[context] If, however, this pure quicksilver floats upward in a pure mineral earth, without any gross alloy, it is hardened into the pure
and white sulphur of Nature by being subjected to a very moderate degree of gentle heat, and at length assumes the specific form of silver. Like all the other metals it may still be developed into gold, if it remain under the influence of its natural heat. But if the same pure, unalloyed quicksilver be subjected to a higher degree of natural heat, it is transmuted into the pure red sulphur of Nature, and becomes gold without first passing through the stage of silver. In this form it remains, because gold is the highest possible stage of metallic development.

Quicksilver is the mother of all metals, on account of its coldness and moistness; and if it be once purified and cleansed of all foreign matter it cannot be mixed any more with grossness of any kind, neither can it be changed back into an imperfect metal. For Nature does not undo her work, and that which has once become perfectly pure can never become impure again. Sulphur, on the other hand, is the father of all metals, on account of its heat and dryness. In the following chapter we shall refer to this difference, and speak more in detail about quicksilver.

[margin] CHAPTER II.

There is, then, in all metals true mercury, and good sulphur, in the imperfect as well as in the perfect metals. But in the imperfect metals it is defiled with impure matter, and stands in need of maturing. Hence you see that all metals may be changed into gold and silver, if the golden and silver properties that are in them be freed from all alloy, and reduced by gentle heat to the form of silver or gold. Those metals, indeed, which have been torn up by the roots, that is to say, that have been dug up from their own proper soil in the veins of the earth, can no longer proceed in that course of development which they pursued in their native abode; yet, as much as in them lies, they strive to be perfected.

[context] Hence it comes that, instead of the waters of the Sages,
these inexperienced persons take pyrites, salts, metals, and divers other substances which, though very expensive, are of no use whatever for our purpose. For no one would dream of buying the true Matter at the apothecary's; ay, that tradesman daily casts it into the street as worthless refuse. Yet the matter of our Stone is found in all those things which are used by ignorant charlatans: for it is our Stone, our Salt, our Mercury, our verdigris, halonitre, salmiac, Mars, sulphur, &c. It is not dug out with pick-axes from ordinary mountains, seeing that our Stone is found in our mountains and springs; our Salt is found in our salt-spring, our metal in our earth, and from the same place we dig up our mercury and sulphur. But what we mean by our mines and springs these charlatans cannot understand. For God has blinded their minds and made gross their senses, and left them to carry on their experiments with all manner of false substances. Nor do they seem able to perceive their error, or to be roused from their idle imaginations by persistent failure. Where they should have distilled with gentle heat they sublime over a fierce fire, and reduce their substance to ashes, instead of developing its inherent principles by vitalizing warmth. Again, when they should have dissolved, they coagulated instead, and so on. By these false methods they could, of course, obtain no good result; but instead of blaming their own ignorance they lay the fault on their teacher, and even deny the genuineness of our Art. As a matter of fact, all their mistakes arise from their misinterpreting the meaning of words which should have put them on the right scent. For instance, when the Sages speak of calcining, these persons understand that word to mean "burning," and consequently render their substance useless by burning it to ashes. When the Sages "dissolve," or transmute into "water," these shallow persons corrode with aqua fortis.
[context] They do not understand that the dissolution must be effected with something that is contained within our substance, and not by means of any foreign appliance.

But our material is not bought from any workshop, yet it is found in it daily, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is enough therefore that it be found by grace: But the material of our stone is compared to all those things with which artisans labor: For our stone is our salt, our Mercury, verdigris, halonitrum, sal ammoniac, Mars (iron), sulfur, and countless other things of that kind, not however dug out from wooded and open mountains with hammers and other instruments: But our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs: in our Salt-spring our Salt is found: from our earth our metal, Mercury, and sulfur are produced, and not from wooded, foreign, and open mountains; all of which artisans do not understand, nor can they believe, nor comprehend; for the Lord has obscured and stopped up their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to be done, and aimed least at the goal, nevertheless they persisted in that contrary sense, and obeyed their stubborn heads; as for instance, when they ought to distill gently, there they sublimated with a strong fire, they burned strong waters, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, and reduced them to nothing. But I wonder still more that there are to be found some men, who not only study this Art, but even try to practice it, and yet do not quite know whether it proceeds by natural and legitimate magic, or whether it is not after all a necromantic, or black art, which is exercised by the illegitimate aid of the powers of hell. No, my good friend. The Devil, wicked angels, and wicked men, have no power but that which God suffers them to possess—and with our present glorious Art they positively have nothing whatever to do. It is entirely in the hand of God, who imparts it to whom He will, and takes it away from whom He will; and He does not suffer any votaries of pleasure, or evil Spirits, to partake of it. He gives it only to the pure, true, and humble of heart. This excellence is neither known, nor understood, by the majority of the present generation; and when the sound of it strikes upon their ears, and they do not comprehend it, they straightway call it foolishness. On account of this their blindness, that spirit will always be hidden from their minds, and will at length be entirely taken away from them.

Let me, however, be permitted to impress one thing on the minds of my pious and devout readers. In so far as a man orders his life, soul, heart, and actions aright in the sight of God, in so far will he perceive that he is making good progress in the discovery, preparation, and use of the Stone. This assertion is the result of my own personal experience during many years, and it embodies my deliberate conviction. Therefore, the best preparation for this study is, in my judgment, a diligent amendment of heart and life.

I am aware that I here lay myself open to the objection that
[context] it is possible to enumerate several men who actually possessed this Stone, or Tincture, and with it transmuted base metals into gold and silver;

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that alchemy is a divine gift rather than a demonic art. It emphasizes that only those with a "simple and upright spirit" can succeed, while the "impious" world remains blind to the art's true nature.</meta>

# The Water-Stone of the Wise

But truly, it is even more to be wondered at that some people are found who not only seek this highest art (*Ecclesiastes 7* <note>original: *Eccles. 7*. The author references the scriptural search for wisdom.</note>) but also attempt to handle and practice it, and yet nevertheless doubt whether it be a natural and truly magical art, or indeed a preternatural and necromantic <term>necromantica</term> <note>Necromancy here refers to the forbidden practice of communicating with the dead or using demonic spirits, which the author distinguishes sharply from "natural magic" or alchemy.</note> art which is acquired only through spirits and illegitimate, prohibited means. Not in the least, my good man; the Devil and all the impious do not have that power without divine permission, such that they might touch even the smallest part of this art, much less make it their own or exercise it at their pleasure. Not at all, I say; it consists in the hand and power of God alone, who bestows it upon whom He wills and at the same time takes it away again. For into this art, which takes its origin from and out of God, no pleasure-seekers at all—much less dire and infernal spirits—are admitted; but instead, such a spirit as shall be simple, upright, true, constant, and of a pure and pious essence. Yet the modern world, secure and impious, does not recognize this spirit, and therefore is ignorant of its essence and its supreme mystery in many things. For as soon as it perceives anything about it with its ears, yet cannot quickly comprehend it, then these worldly companions (*Wisdom 1*) call it foolishness: therefore also, because of their blindness, that spirit shall be perpetually hidden from them and at length entirely taken away from them.

<margin><note>A small ink flourish or doodle consisting of several wavy vertical and horizontal strokes appears in the right margin, likely a decorative element added by a reader or the printer.</note></margin>

But lest I perhaps proceed further than is just from my purpose with this remembrance, let me touch upon it again and finally bring it to a conclusion: for that reason, I want this to be properly impressed upon pious craftsmen <term>artificibus</term> in place of a friendly exhortation: namely, that to the extent that one directs their heart, soul, indeed their life and actions toward God (*Ecclesiasticus 18 & 29*), to that extent will they perceive a remarkable benefit in the progress of the stone and their labor, every day and even every hour: which I myself have observed with the greatest diligence and great devotion every day, and thus have experienced by the deed itself. Wherefore everyone, right from the beginning, ought to direct their actions to this end and prepare themselves so that they may afterwards be able to attain a more successful end in both works <note>original: *in utroque opere*. In alchemical literature, the "two works" often refer to the "Greater Work" (the creation of the Philosopher's Stone for gold) and the "Lesser Work" (the spiritual transformation of the soul), or alternatively, the internal and external processes.</note>.

[context] Truly, indeed, they are, in order that such errors may be avoided, and patients may advance to those sure arcana which God has designed for their use and requirement.
You will gather from hence how necessary it is to act on my prescription rather than on yours. In this respect you have to follow me, not I to follow you. Though you fulminate ever so much against me, nevertheless, my monarchy shall stand, while yours goes to destruction. It is not in vain that I write at such length concerning Alchemy, but I do it with this purpose and for this end, that you may well and surely know what is latent therein, and how it should be understood. Nor should you be offended hereby because you get no gold or silver by it. Rather its result should be that by means thereof arcana shall be unveiled, and the seductions of the ointment-sellers shall be brought to light, since by these the ignorant folk are deceived, while they sell them for a florin what they would not buy back for a penny. So precious, in this sense, are their secrets!

Who will deny that even in the very best things a poison may lie hid? All must acknowledge this. And if this be true, I would now ask you whether it is not right that the poison should be separated from what is good and useful, that the good should be taken and the evil left. Such should certainly be the case. If so, tell me how it is separated in your surgeries. With you all these elements remain mixed. See your own simplicity, then, if you are forced to confess that a poison lies hid, and are asked how it is to be got rid of. Then you bring forward I know not what correctives, which shall drive out and take away the poison. Comfrey, for example, they use to correct scammony, which is then called diagridium. But what kind of a corrective is this? Does not the poison remain afterwards as before? And yet you boast that you have so corrected it that the poison no longer harms. Whither has it gone? It remains in the diagridium. Try it, if you are wise. Exceed the proper dose, and you will soon see where the poison is. You will not be long in finding out. So you correct turbith also, and then call it diaturbith. These are your methods of correction, fit only for clowns, and useful to drench horses with! Risk an excessive dose; you will see whether you do not feel the poison. To correct is to take that which has been corrected. A criminal who has broken the law is punished; but his correction is not extended farther than the free will of the culprit lasts. Such are your corrections. The power is in them, not in you. In such a case, all the physician thinks of is how to eliminate the poison. This must be done by separation. For example, a serpent is venomous, and yet it is used for food. If you take away the poison you can eat the flesh without injury. And so it is with all other substances; only a similar separation is absolutely necessary. If this is not brought about, you cannot be sure of your work, unless, indeed, it come to pass that Nature supplies your place, or some special interposition of providence favours you. You have no protection in your art. If a sure foundation be necessary for the extraction of the poison, that is afforded by Alchemy. It must be so arranged that if there be Mars in Sol, Mars must be taken away; or Saturn in Venus, the Saturn must be separated from the Venus. As many ascendants and impressions as there are in natural substances, so many bodies are there in them. But when the bodies are contrary, it is absolutely necessary that one of them should be taken away and removed, so that in this way all contrariety should be eliminated, and so the evil which you are searching for should be separated from the good. As gold is useless except it shall first have passed through the fire, so medicine is much less useful unless it, too, shall have passed through the fire. It is necessary that everything which is to benefit man shall have passed by fire to a second birth. Should not this, then, be deemed the right fundamental principle of every physician? A physician should exhibit not poisons, but arcana. But all the preparations of your surgeries, how many soever they be, do not contribute the smallest tittle of learning. They are employed simply in correcting, which is just as if a dog should break wind in a room and you should kill the stink with fumigations and juniper wood; but does not the smell remain in the room as much after as before that process? Although the smell is not perceptible by the olfactory organs, could anybody say that the stink was separated and no longer remained? It is there, though corrected by the fumigation. The stink and the fumigation enter the nose together. Of such a sort also are the corrections of the drug-vendors who disguise aloepaticum with sugar, that it may not offend the palate. The sugar and the honey form a magistery in this case. So, too, they correct theriacum with gentian. Are not all these operations instances of asinine ignorance? And yet these people boast themselves the physicians of princes, and sell their skill for money! Yet who is so dense as not to scent the fact forthwith that all this is worthless? What else can they trumpet forth about their remedies beyond saying "This electuary is sweet, being compounded of spices, sugar, honey,
[context] and other condiments, and is held in very great esteem?"

<meta>This page transitions from Paracelsus’s critique of the medical establishment to his specific defense of alchemy as the foundation of medicine. He moves from broad accusations of ignorance to explaining how the alchemical process of separation is the only way to make medicine safe and effective.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>ON ALCHEMY.</header>

### ON ALCHEMY.

<margin>The goal of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but mysteries.</margin>
...destined, let them penetrate. From these things conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my instructions, and by no means according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still hurl more thunderbolts against me, my <term>Monarchy</term> <note>Paracelsus often used "Monarchy" to describe his supreme system of medical and natural philosophy.</note> shall nonetheless stand, while all of yours goes to ruin. I do not write so extensively about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and goal: that from these things you might nearly and solidly recognize what lies hidden within it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by this: that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it. Rather, this is what must be carefully seen to: that through alchemy the <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcana"; the hidden, inner virtues or "secrets" of a substance that provide its healing power.</note> may be uncovered, and the deceptions of the <term>druggists</term> <note>original: "seplasiariorum"; these were sellers of perfumes and ointments, whom Paracelsus often accused of being fraudulent medicine-sellers.</note> may be exposed, by which the unrefined common folk are deceived, while these men serve them for one florin what they would not redeem for a single penny. So "precious" are their secrets.

<margin>Poison is even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that even in the best things poison lies hidden and dwells within? Everyone is forced to admit it. If this is true, I now ask of you: must the poison not be separated from what is good and useful? Should the good be accepted and the bad left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If it must be so, I pray you, tell me: how is that separation performed in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed together. To be sure, in order to protect your simplicity—if you have been convicted into admitting that poison lies there—and you are asked where it eventually goes, then you bring forth I-know-not-what regarding "corrections," which are supposed to drive out and take away the poison;
<margin>The "correction" of the Physicians is examined.</margin>
just as they say <term>Quinces</term> <note>original: "Cotonea"</note> correct <term>Scammony</term> <note>original: "Scammoneam"; a harsh plant-based purgative.</note>, or as they say of <term>Diagridium</term> <note>A preparation made from the juice of scammony, often baked in a quince to "mellow" it.</note>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you, meanwhile, boast that you have "corrected" it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it vanish to? 
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test it, if you are wise: exceed the proper measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will find that out soon enough! You "correct" <term>Turpeth</term> <note>original: "Turbith"; another potent purgative root.</note> in the same way, and you call it "Diaturbith." Those are your kinds of corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be fed to pack-horses. Try the experiment by exceeding the measure and increasing the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. 
<margin>What "I correct the physician" means.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected thing.* <note>The Latin "Corrigere est correctum sumere" implies that true correction means only using the refined substance after the bad part is gone.</note> He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction extends no further than the will of the one who was punished lasts. These "corrections" of yours are of such a kind; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now indeed, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. For example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted as food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same is to be understood equally for all other things: that there is a need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation—unless by chance it happens that nature makes up for your failings, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection remains.

Now, therefore, let us finally look at that true foundation, if it is required, which removes poison, and how Alchemy provides it. For it must be done in such a way that if <term>Mars</term> is in the <term>Sun</term>, Mars is removed; and if <term>Saturn</term> is dwelling in <term>Venus</term>, it is separated from her. <note>Paracelsus uses the names of planets to refer to metals or qualities: Mars (Iron/Choler), Sun (Gold/Vitality), Saturn (Lead/Melancholy), Venus (Copper/Flux). He is describing the chemical purification of mixed elements.</note> For as many "ascendants" and "impressions" as there are in the things of nature, just as many bodies exist within them. Truly, when bodies are contrary to one another, it is absolutely necessary for one of them to be taken away and removed, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is taken away from the good which you seek.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so much less useful is a Medicine which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into a second generation, through which it ought to benefit and help mankind. And should this not be rightly judged the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to employ poisons, but rather arcana. 
<margin>The Pharmacies are rebuked.</margin>
However, all those preparations of the workshops—as many as there are—do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are occupied simply with "correcting"; as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were put to sleep either by <term>troches</term> <note>medicinal lozenges</note> and incense, or by juniper wood. I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room just as much afterward as before? And although it might not be perceived by the sense of smell, is anyone permitted to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? No, it is there, but "corrected" by the fumigation. Thus, the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who dull the <term>Aloe-mixture</term> <note>original: "Aleopaticum"</note> with sugar, so that it inflicts no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their "mastery." In this way, they also "correct" <term>Gentian</term> and <term>Theriac</term> <note>An ancient, complex herbal "cure-all" that Paracelsus often mocked for being a messy soup of ingredients.</note>. Are these not the works of donkey-like ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of Princes. Who is so stupid as not to smell immediately that these things are worthless? Regarding their remedies, what else can they boast, I pray, except to say, *“This Electuary is sweet, made of spices, sugar, and honey”*?

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the true purpose of alchemy in medicine is the chemical separation of poisons from healing virtues, rather than the pursuit of gold. He mocks traditional pharmacists for merely masking the bad taste or harsh effects of drugs with sugar or quinces, comparing it to using incense to hide a foul odor without removing the source.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, separation, poison, arcana, pharmacy critique, fire, Mars, Saturn, Diagridium, Scammony, medicinal preparation</keywords>

<summary>Paracelsus critiques contemporary medical and pharmaceutical practices, arguing that their methods of "correcting" toxic substances are mere deceptions that mask poison rather than separating it through alchemical fire.</summary>

<header>DE ALCHIMIA.</header>

### DE ALCHIMIA.

<margin>Alchimię finis non aurum & argentũ. sed arcana.</margin>
destinauit, penetrent. Ex his colligite, necesse esse, vt ad præscriptum meum procedatur, & minimè ad vestrum. Hic opus est, vt me sectemini, non ego vos. Et licet quidem aduersus me adhuc plura defulminetis: mea tamen nihilominus Monarchia stabit, vestrā cuncte pessum. Frustra de Alchimia tam prolixè non scribo, sed id hoc animo & fine facio, vt ex his propè & solidè cognoscatis, quid in ipsā lateat, & quî intelligi debeat. Nec ex hoc offendi debes, quod ex eā nec aurum, nec argentum prodit: Sed hoc potius accurandum est, vt per eam arcana detegantur, & seductiones seplāsiariorum prodantur, quibus rude vulgus decipitur, dum his pro floreno vno ministrant, quod nummo vno non redimerent. Tam pretiosa eorum arcana sunt.

<margin>Venenū etiam in reb. optimis.</margin>
Quis est, qui inficiari ausit, etiam in rebus optimis venenum latere & inesistere? Fateri id omnes coguntur. Hoc ergò si verum est, ex vobis iam quæro an non à bono & vtili venenum separandum sit? & bonum accipiendum, malum relinquendum? Imò verò, ita oportet. Si itaq; oportet: quæso enarrate mihi, qui id in vestris officinis separetur? Apud vos enim omnia permixta manent. Vt verò simplicitatem vestram tueamini, si conuicti estis ad fatendum, ibi venęnum latere & quò tandem illud abeat, rogamini: tunc nescio quid de correctionibus profertis, quæ venenum exigant & auferant,
<margin>Correctio Medicorum ventilatur.</margin>
veluti Cotonea Scammoneam, post Diagridium, dictum corrigūt. Quid id verò correctionis est? An non manet venenum postea ceu primò? Et tu tamē interim gloriaris, quod correxeris, adeò vt venenum ampliùs non noceat. Id verò quò euasit? 
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
In Diagridio manet. Id tenta, si sapis: modum excede, & videbis, vbi venenum sit. Nam id haud segniter scies Sic corrigis etiam Turbith, & vocas ipsum Diaturbith. Istiusmodi correctiones vestrę sunt, quæ rusticos decerent, & caballis propinandæ essent. Excedēndo modum periculum fac, & dosin auge: videris an venenum non sensurus sis. 
<margin>Corrigo Medicu quid</margin>
*Corrigere est correctum sumere.* Qui malitiosus est, & peccauit: is si plectitur, correctio non extēditur longius, quàm voluntas durat eius, qui plexus est. Tales hæ quoque correctiones sunt, penes ipsas fitum est, non penes te. Iam verò hoc casu nihil considerandum Medico est ampliùs, quàm vt venenum dematur. Id per separationem fieri oportet: Vt, exempli gratia: serpens venenosus est: & tamen in cibum adoptatur. Si ipsi venenu demis, comedas nullā noxā. Idem de rebus cæteris vniuersis æquè intelligendum est, nimirùm simili separatione opus esse. Eā nondum factā, operationis tuæ securus esse non possis: nisi forte fiat, vt vices tuas natura suppleat, aut cœli maior benignitas faueat. In arte etenim tuā præsidij nihil superfuerit.

Iam ergò tandem verum illud fundamentum si oportet, quod venenum aufert, qualiter id Alchimia præstat. Hoc enim ita fieri necesse est, vt, si Mars in Sole sit, Mars dematur, & si Saturnus in Venere versetur, is ab eā separetur. Quot enim ascendentes & impressiones in rebus naturæ sunt, tot etiam corpora in illis existunt. Quæ verò corpora contraria sunt, eorum omninò aliquod demi & auferri opus est, vt hoc pacto omnis contrarietas tollatur, & à bono malum, quod quæris, adimatur.
<margin>Ignis omnia perficit.</margin>
Ut aurum ad nihil vtile est, nisi priùs in ignem coniiciatur: sic multò minùs vtilis Medicina est, quæ per ignem non transit. Per ignem enim necesse est omnia transire in generationem alteram, quā homini conducere & opitulari debet. Et hoc non meritò probum fundamentum cuiuslibet Medici censeri debeat? Nec enim Medicus venena, verū arcana adhibere debet. 
<margin>Officinę reprehend.</margin>
Omnes autem illæ officinales præparationes, quotquot earum sunt, isti doctrinæ ne quidem literulam conferunt: sed in corrigendo simpliciter occupantur, velut; si canis in conclaui pepedit, & fœtor ille aut trochiscis & thymiamate, aut ligno iuniperino sopiatur: an non quęso fœtor tam postea, quàm antea in cōclaui remanet? Et licet quidem olfactu non percipiatur: an ideò cuipiam dicere liceat, fœtor separatus est, nec restat ampliùs? Imò adest, sed correctus suffitu. Sic ergò suffitus & pedor nares vnà ingrediuntur. Huiusmodiquoque sunt correctiones Pharmacopœorum, qui saccharo obtundunt Aleopaticum, vt sic nullam noxam infligat. Ita saccharū & mel ipsorum magisteriū est. Sic gentianā etiā corrigūt theriacam. An verò hæc non asininæ inscitiæ opera sint? Ipsi tamen se principum Medicos iactant & venditant. Quis verò ita stupidus est, vt hæc nihili esse, non illicò olfaciat? De remediis suis quid quæso iactare possunt aliud, quàm vt dicant, *Hoc Electuarium suaue est, ex aromatis, saccharo, melléque*

[context] Those things are called growing in this place which fall and grow again, as herbs, leaves, and the like. For extracting the quintessences of these, several methods also have been found out by the addition of other things.
But they should be extracted without the admixture of anything, so that they may retain their taste, colour, and odour; and that these properties may be increased in them, not diminished. Thus, if the quintessence be extracted from musk, amber, and civet, their body afterwards stinks, so that they are no longer of any account in taste, in odour, or in nature. So of other things in this class it must be understood, so far as relates to the extraction of their quintessences. But we do not discuss musk, amber, and civet in this chapter, because we write specially of them elsewhere, and at present we are only treating of growing things, as the lily, spike, leaves; for the extraction of the quintessence from which the following is the process.

Take growing things, bruised as completely as possible. Put them in some fitting vessel, and set this in a venter equinus for four weeks. Afterwards distil them by means of a bath; again let them be placed in horse-dung for eight days, and once more distilled by the bath of Mary.

Thus the quintessence will ascend by the alembic, but the body will remain at the bottom. If any of the quintessence shall have remained at the bottom, putrefy it still further, and proceed as before. Then take at length this distilled water, add it again to this growing thing, and so, by means of a pelican, let them be digested together six days. Thereupon the colour will be dense. Abstract this by means of the balneum maris, when the body will disappear, the quintessence remaining at the bottom. Separate this by a retortive process, that is, by pressure, from the dregs, and let this quintessence digest for four days.
[context] In this way you will have it perfect in odour, in juiciness, in taste, and in virtue, as well as consisting of a thick substance.

Ours is the 1569 Latin Archidoxae (Rupertus Finck dedication), where the same chapter is Lib. III, Cap. VI 'De extractione Quintae Essentiae ex Crescentibus'.
reference_meta.coverage_note: ~95%. The page opens mid-clause ('[cum oporteat absque omni infectione aliarum] additionum eas fieri'). The first English sentence 'But they should be extracted without the admixture of anything' straddles the page break: its main verb ('eas fieri') is on this page, but 'without the admixture' renders the end of the previous page. The page ends mid-word at 'quatu-[or dies]', so the English cut ends at 'digest for four days'. Small differences: 'lilies, spike, leaf (Lilijs, Spica, Folio)' becomes 'the lily, spike, leaves'; 'quas impositas ollae' becomes 'Put them in some fitting vessel'; 'quem cola, colatum distilla per balneum, et exibit corpus' is condensed to 'Abstract this by means of the balneum maris, when the body will disappear'. Sentences otherwise correspond one to one.

alignment_note: Printed p. 66 of the 1569 Archidoxae, book III ('De Quinta Essentia' running head), cap. VI. Found via 'musk, amber, and civet' in Waite. The book numbering differs from Waite's: his Book IV is our Lib. III. The text itself matches sentence for sentence.

reference_text:
[context] But if the circle be composed of some envenomed substance,
the spider will have no difficulty in crossing the line, which is homogenous to its own nature.

Any similar experiment would yield the same result. Hollow out a silver coin, and let it float on the water like a boat. Then hold close to it, yet without making actual contact, a particle of a true unicorn. The coin will be as surely repelled and moved backward as the duck which sees the sportsman taking aim at it with his gun.

That homogeneous substances always attract each other you may learn from the fact, that if you place a piece of pure, unadulterated bread in a bowl of water, so that it floats on the surface, and hold, not very far from it, a piece of true unicorn,
[context] the bread will float in any direction in which the piece of unicorn is moved.

then there will be seen, about the thirtieth day of this Reign, an orange colour, which, within two weeks from its first appearance, will tinge the whole substance with its own hue.

[margin] CHAPTER XXX. Of the Regimen of the Sun.

As you are now approaching the end of the work, the substance receives a golden tinge, and the Virgin's Milk which you give your substance to drink has assumed a deep orange colour. Pray to God to keep you from haste and impatience at this stage of the work; consider that you have now waited for seven months, and that it would be foolish to let one hour rob you of the fruits of all your labour. Therefore be more and more careful the nearer you approach perfection. Then you will first observe an orange-coloured sweat breaking out on the body; next there will be vapour of an orange hue. Soon the body below becomes tinged with violet and a darkish purple. At the end of fourteen or fifteen days, the substance will be, for the most part, humid and ponderous, and yet
[context] the wind still bears it in its womb.

The meadows were studded with a large variety of beautiful and fragrant flowers. The slopes of the hills were clad with vines, olives, and cedars. The roads were overhung by the intertwining branches of laurels and pomegranate trees, which afforded grateful shade to the wayfarer. The plains were covered with groves of orange and lemon trees. In short, the island was an epitome of earthly beauty. Concealed under a rock, Neptune shewed me two minerals of that island, gold and chalybs (steel). Then I was conducted to an orchard in the middle of a meadow, which was at no great distance, the same being planted with a great variety of beautiful trees. Among these he shewed me seven enriched by particular names; and two of them towered above the rest. One bore fruit which shone like the sun, and its leaves resembled gold; the fruit of the other was whiter than lilies, and its leaves were like fine silver. Neptune called the first the Solar, and the second the Lunar tree. The only thing which it was difficult to obtain in the island, was water. The inhabitants had tried to get it from a spring by means of a conduit, and to elicit it from many things. But the result was a poisonous water, and the only water that could be drunk was that condensed out of the rays of the sun and moon. The worst of it was, that no one could attract more than ten parts of this water. It was wonderful water, I can tell you; for I saw with my eyes, and touched with my hands its dazzling whiteness, which surpassed all the splendour of the snow. While I stood wrapt in admiration, Neptune vanished from my sight, and there stood before me a tall man, on whose forehead the name of Saturn was inscribed. He took a vessel, and scooped up ten parts of the water,

[context] This they have pretended to fix, and by it to turn copper into silver. This, however, is merely a sophistical whitening,
for arsenic cannot be fixed unless the operator be an Artist, and knows well its tingeing spirit. Truly in this respect all the philosophers have slept, vainly attempting to accomplish anything thereby. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant as to this spirit, cannot have any hopes of fixing it, or of giving it that power which would make it capable of the virtue of transmutation. So, then, I give notice to all that the whitening of which I have just now spoken is grounded on a false basis, and that by it the copper is deceitfully whitened, but not changed.

Now the sophists have mixed this counterfeit Venus with twice its weight of Luna, and sold it to the goldsmiths and mint-masters, until at last they have transmuted themselves into false coiners — not only those who sold, but those who bought it. Some sophists instead of white arsenic take red, and this has turned out false art; because, however it is prepared, it proves to be nothing but whiteness.

Some, again, have gone further and dealt with common sulphur, which, being so yellow, they have boiled in vinegar, lixivium, or sharpest wines, for a day and a night, until it became white. Then afterwards they sublimated it from common salt and the calx of eggs, repeating the process several times; yet, still, though white, it has been always combustible. Nevertheless, with this they have endeavoured to fix Mercury
[context] and to turn it into gold; but in vain.

for Truth is accompanied with the Good, together also with Life and Light. 44. And there came no more any torment of Darknesse, but being overcome, they all fled away suddenly, & tumultuarily. 45. Thou hast understood, O Son, the manner of Regeneration; for upon the coming of these Ten, the Intellectuall Generation is perfected, and then it driveth away the Twelve; and we have seen it in the Generation it self. 46. Whosoever therefore hath of Mercy obtained this Generation, which is according to God, he leaving all bodily sense, knoweth himself to consist of divine things, and rejoyceth, being made by God stable and immutable. 47. Tat. O Father, I conceive and understand, not by the sight of mine eyes, but by the Intellectuall Operation, which is by the Powers. I am in Heaven, in the Earth, in the Water, in the Air; I am in living Creatures, in Plants, in the Womb, every where. 48. Yet tell me further, this one thing, How are the torments of Darknesse, being in number Twelve, driven away and expelled by the Ten powers? What is the manner of it, Trismegistus? 49. Herm. reference_text:
[context] 15. But the Workman, Mind,
together with the Word, containing the Circles and Whirling them about, turned round as a Wheel his own Workmanships; and suffered them to be turned from an indefinite Beginning, to an undeterminable End; for they alwayes begin where they end. 16. And the Circulation, or running round of these, as the Minde willeth, out of the lower, or downward-born Elements brought forth unreasonable or bruitish Creatures, for they had no reason, the Air flying things, and the Water such as swim. 17. And the Earth and the Water were separated, either from other, as the Mind would; and the Earth brought forth from her self, such Living Creatures as she had, four-footed and creeping Beasts, wild and tame. 18. But the Father of all things, the Minde being Life and Light, brought forth Man, like unto himself, whom he loved as his proper Birth; for he was all beauteous, having the Image of his Father. 19. For indeed God was exceedingly enamoured of his own Form or Shape, and delivered unto it all his own Workmanships: But he seeing and understanding the Creation of the Workman in the whole; would needs also himself fall to work, and so was separated from the Father, being in the sphere of Generation or Operation. 20. Having all Power, he considered the Operations or Workmanships of the Seven; but they loved him, and every one made him partaker of his own Order.

candidates.text: ...the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift rapacity, bent its own machinery to itself, and commanded it to revolve from a beginning without a beginning to an end without an end. For it always begins from there, where it ends. Truly, the circuit of all these things, just as the Mind itself willed, fashioned animals lacking reason from the inferior elements; for it did not provide reason. The air produced winged creatures, and the water produced swimming ones. The water and the earth were also distinguished from one another in the manner which had pleased the Mind. Afterward, the earth brought forth the living creatures it had held within: namely, quadrupeds, creeping things, wild beasts alike, and domesticated ones. But the Father of all, the Intellect, being life and brightness, procreated man like unto himself, and congratulated him as his own son. For he was beautiful, and bore the image of his Father. For God, having delighted in his own true form, granted all his works to human use. But man <margin>note the sin of the philosophers <unclear>what it is</unclear></margin> when he had considered the procreation of all things in his Father, he also wished to fashion things. Whence he fell down from the contemplation of the Father to the sphere of generation. And when he possessed power over all things, he took note of the creations of the seven governors. These, however, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each bestowed a part of their own order...

[context] For that a lofty reasoning, and much more one that is too godlike for the mental grasp of [average] men, if that the speaker's words are not received with more attentive service of the ears, — will fly and flow beyond them; or rather will flow back [again],
and mingle with the streams of its own source. 2. There are, then, [certain] Gods who are the principals of all the species. Next there come those whose essence is their principal. These are the Sensible, each similar to its own dual source, who by their sensibility affect all things, — the one part through the other part [in each] making to shine the proper work of every single one. Of Heaven, — or of whatsoe'er it be that is embraced within the term, — the essence-chief is Zeus; for 'tis through Heaven that Zeus gives life to all. Sun's essence-chief is light; for the good gift of light is poured on us through the Sun's disk. 3. The "Thirty-six," who have the name of Horoscopes, are in the [self] same space as the Fixed Stars; of these the essence-chief, or prince, is he whom they call Pantomorph, or Omniform, who fashioneth the various forms for various species. The "Seven" who are called spheres, have essence-chiefs, that is, [have each] their proper rulers, whom they call [all together] Fortune and Heimarmene, whereby all things are changed by nature's law; perpetual stability being varied with incessant motion. The Air, moreover, is the engine, or machine, through which all things are made — (there is, however, an essence-chief of this, a second [Air]) — mortal from mortal things and things like these. 4. These hierarchies of Gods, then, being thus and [in this way] related, from bottom unto top, are [also] thus connected with each other, and tend towards themselves; so mortal things are bound to mortal, things sensible to sensible. The whole of [this grand scale of] Rulership, however, seems to Him [who is] the Highest Lord, either to be not many things, or rather [to be] one. For that from One all things depending, and flowing down from it, — when they are seen as separate, they're thought to be as many as they possibly can be; but in their union it is one [thing], or rather two, from which all things are made; — that is, from Matter, by means of which the other things are made, and by the Will of Him, by nod of whom they're brought to pass. XX. 1. Asc. Is this again the reason, O Thrice-greatest one? Tris. It is, Asclepius. For God's the Father or the Lord

Having established that the world exists within God and is animated by a divine spirit, Hermes now describes the specific "Rulers of Essence" who govern different realms of the universe, from the highest heavens to the stars and the planetary spheres.</meta>

...and it shall mix itself with the liquids of the fountain. There are, therefore, gods who are the heads of all species. These are followed by the gods whose prince is **Essence** <note>original: "ουσια" (ousia). In this context, it refers to the fundamental substance or "being" of a thing.</note>. These are perceptible to the senses and resemble both origins; they complete all things through their sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work through the other.

Of heaven—or whatever is contained by that name—the **Ruler of Essence** <term>ousiarches: a Greek term meaning "ruler of substance" or "head of being."</term> is Jupiter. For through heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. The Ruler of Essence of the sun is **Light**. For the benefit of light is poured into us through the sun's orb.

Concerning the thirty-six <note>Known as the "Decans" in Egyptian and Hermetic astrology, these are 36 spirits who rule over ten-degree segments of the zodiac.</note> (whose name is "the Horoscopes") among the stars that are always fixed in the same place: their Ruler of Essence or prince is the one they call **Pantomorphos** <note>original: "Pantomorphon", meaning "the All-Formed One."</note>, or the "One of All Forms." It is he who creates different forms for different species.

The seven spheres which are called "erratic" <note>The "erratic" stars are the planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, plus the Sun and Moon), so-called because they appear to move against the background of the "fixed" stars.</note> have their own Rulers of Essence—that is, their own princes—whom they call **Fortune** or **Fate** <note>original: "ειμαρμενηρ" (heimarmene). This represents the rigid, cosmic law of cause and effect.</note>, by whom all things are changed by the law of nature with the firmest stability, varied by eternal motion.

**Air**, indeed, is the instrument or the engine of all, through which all things are done. However, the Ruler of Essence of this air is the "second" one. It provides mortal things to mortals and things similar to them.

Because these things are so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things are naturally connected to one another: so that mortal things are linked to mortals, and things perceived by the senses are linked to the sensible. But the peak of governance obeys that supreme Lord, so that they are not many, but rather **One**. For all things hang from the One, or rather flow from Him; when they are seen from a distance, they are believed to be many separate things. But joined together, they are one, or rather two: the source from which all things are made, and the one by whom they are made. That is, they consist of the **matter** out of which they are made, and the **will** of Him by whose command all other things are brought about.

**ASCLEPIUS:** What then is this reasoning, O Trismegistus?

**TRISMEGISTUS:** It is this, O Asclepius. For God—either the Father, or the Lord...

[context] 3. This, then, is how the good will differ from the bad.
Each several one will shine in piety, in sanctity, in prudence, in worship, and in service of [our] God, and see True Reason, as though [he looked at it] with [corporal] eyes; and each will by the confidence of his belief excel all other men, as by its light the Sun the other stars. For that it is not so much by the greatness of his light as by his holiness and his divinity, the Sun himself lights up the other stars. Yea, [my] Asclepius, thou should'st regard him as the second God, ruling all things, and giving light to all things living in the Cosmos, whether ensouled or unensouled. For if the Cosmos is a living thing, and if it has been, and it is, and will be ever-living, — naught in the Cosmos is subject to death. For of an ever-living thing, it is [the same] of every part which is; [that is,] that 'tis [as ever-living] as it is [itself]; and in the World itself [which is] for everyone, and at the self-same time an ever-living thing of life, — in it there is no place for death. 5. And so he should be the full store of life and deathlessness; if that it needs must be that he should live for ever. And so the Sun, just as the Cosmos, lasts for aye. So is he, too, for ever ruler of [all] vital powers, or of [our] whole vitality; he is their ruler, or the one who gives them out. God, then, is the eternal ruler of all living things, or vital functions, that are in the World. He is the everlasting giver-forth of Life itself. Once for all [time] He hath bestowed Life on all vital powers; He further doth preserve them by a law that lasts for evermore, as I will [now] explain.

Mead's bracketed insertions kept; footnotes omitted.

CHAP. XLV. Of the Images of the head and Tayle of the Dragon of the Moon.
They made also the Image of the head and taile of the Dragon of the Moon, namely betwixt an Aeriall and fiery circle, the likeness of a Serpent, with the head of an Hawke tyed about them, after the manner of the great letter Theta, & they made it when Jupiter with the head obtain'd the midst of Heaven: which Image they affirm to availe much for the success of Petitions, and would signifie by this Image a good and fortunate Genius, which they would represent by this Image of the Serpent; for the Egyptians and Phenitians do extoll this creature above all others, and say it is a divine creature and hath a divine nature; for in this is a more acute spirit, and a greater fire then in any other, which thing is manifested both by his swift motion without feet, hands or any other instruments and also that it often reneweth his age with his skin, and becometh young again: but they made the Image of the taile like as when the Moon was Ecclipsed, in the Taile, or ill affected by Saturn or Mars, and they made it to introduce, anguish, infirmity and misfortune; and they called it the evill Genius; such an Image a certain Hebrew had included in a golden Belt full of Jewels, which Blanch the daughter of the Duke of Borbon (either willingly or ignorantly) bestowed on her husband Peter King of Spain, the first of that name, with which when he was girt, he seemed to himself to be compassed about with a Serpent; and afterwards finding the Magicall virtue fixed in the girdle, for this cause he forsook his wife.
CHAP. XLVI. Of the Images of the Mansions of the Moon.
They made also Images for every Mansion of the Moon; in the first for the destruction of some one, they made in an Iron ring the Image of a black man in a garment made of haire, and girdled round, casting a small lance with his right hand; they sealed this in black wax, and perfumed it with liquid Storax, and wished some evil to come. In the second, against the wrath of the Prince, and for reconcilation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastick, the Image of a king crowned, and perfumed it with Lignum Aloes; In the third, they made an Image in a silver ring, whose table was square, the figure of which was a woman well clothed, sitting in a chair, her right hand being lifted up on her head; they sealed it and perfumed it with muske, Camphire and Calamus Aromaticus. They affirmed that this giveth happy fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for revenge, separation, enmity and ill will, they sealed in red wax the Image of a souldier sitting on an horse, holding a Serpent in his right hand; they perfumed it with red myrrhe, and Storax; in the fifth, for the favor of Kings and officers, and good entertainment, they sealed in Silver the head of a man, and perfumed it with Sanders; in the sixth, for to procure love betwixt two, they sealed in white wax two Images imbracing one another, and perfumed them with Lignum Aloes and Amber; in the seventh, for to obtain every good thing, they sealed in Silver the Image of a man well clothed, holding up his hands to heaven

It transitions from the seven classical planets to the lunar nodes (the Dragon’s Head and Tail) and begins the sequence of the twenty-eight Mansions of the Moon, detailing the specific images, materials, and rituals used to harness their influences.</meta>

### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon’s dragon. Chapter 45.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</image-desc>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon <note>original: "capitis & caudæ draconis Lunæ"—referring to the North and South Nodes of the Moon, where its orbit intersects the ecliptic</note>; specifically, the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter theta <note>original: "thita" (Θ). The serpent biting its tail is a common symbol for the Nodes in Renaissance magic.</note>. They made this when Jupiter, along with the Head <note>The North Node, or "Caput Draconis"</note>, held the <term>midheaven: the highest point of the zodiac at the time of the calculation</term>. They affirm that this image contributes greatly to the success of petitions. They intended to represent a good and happy <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or celestial entity, not necessarily an evil "demon"</term> through this image, and they chose to figure it as a serpent. Indeed, the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this animal as divine above all others, noting its divine nature because there exists within it a sharper spirit and a more abundant fire than in other animals. This is shown by its swift movement without any feet or hands or other limbs, and because it periodically renews its age and grows young again by shedding its skin.

However, they made the image of the Tail <note>The South Node, or "Cauda Draconis"</note> in a similar fashion when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was poorly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made this to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an "evil genius" <note>original: "malum genium"—a malevolent spirit or influence</note>. A certain Hebrew man had enclosed such an image in a golden double-belt which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first King of Spain of that name <note>Peter of Castile, known as "the Cruel" (1334–1369). Historical legend suggests he abandoned his wife Blanche almost immediately, with some accounts blaming a cursed belt.</note> (whether she was aware of it or was ignorant). When he was girded with it, it seemed to him that he was cinched by a serpent. Once the magic power inserted into the belt was discovered, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter 46.

They also made images in the individual <term>mansions of the moon: 28 divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon travels daily</term>. 

In the **first** mansion, for the destruction of someone, they made on an iron ring the image of a black man clothed and girded in hair-cloth <note>original: "cilicio"—a coarse garment made of goat's hair, worn for penance</note>, throwing a small spear with his right hand. They sealed this in black wax, smoked it with liquid storax <note>a fragrant resin</note>, and made imprecations. 

In the **second**, against the wrath of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and smoked it with aloeswood. 

In the **third**, they made an image on a silver ring of square measure, the figure of which was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised over her head. They sealed it and smoked it with musk, camphor, and "aromatic claw" <note>original: "ungula aromatica"—likely the operculum of certain sea snails, used in incense</note>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. 

In the **fourth**, for revenge, separation, enmity, and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and smoked it with red myrrh and storax. 

In the **fifth**, for the favor of kings and officials and for a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and smoked it with sandalwood. 

In the **sixth**, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and smoked them with aloeswood and amber. 

In the **seventh**, to acquire every good thing, they sealed in silver the image of a well-dressed man, with hands stretched toward heaven for...

### De imaginibus capitis & caudæ draconis Lunæ. Cap. XLV.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</image-desc>

Faciebant etiam imaginem capitis & caudæ draconis Lunæ, scilicet inter circulum aëreum & igneum serpentis effigiem, cum capite accipitris illos circundantem, ad instar Græce literæ thita, faciebātq́; quando Iupiter eum capite medium cœlum obtinebat, quam quidē imaginem ad successus petitionum multum conferre affirmant, uolebantq́; per eam imaginē bonum ac felicem dęmonem notare: uolebantq́; eum per serpentis imaginem figurare: hūc enim Aegyptii atq; Phœnices super omnia animalia esse diuinum animal, atq; eius diuinam naturam celebrāt: quia in eo super cętera animalia spiritus acrior atq; amplior ignis existat: quę res cū ex illo celeri gressu ostenditur, sine ullis pedibus manibusq́; uel aliis instrumentis, tum quod ætatem subinde cum eximiis renouat ac iuuenescit. Caudæ uero imaginem faciebant consimilem, quando luna in cauda erat eclipsata, aut à Saturno uel Marte male affecta: faciebantq́; illam ad anxietatē & infirmitatem inducenda: & uocabant illā malum genium. Talem imaginē Hebręus quidā incluserat aureo geminatoq́; baltheo quem Blancha ducis Borbonii filia marito suo Petro Hispaniarum regi eius nominis primo (siue conscia siue ignorās) dono dedit: quo cū ille cingeretur, serpente succinetus sibi uidebatur: cōpertoq́; deinde uim magicam cingulo insertam, eam ob causam uxorem repudiauit.

### De imaginibus Mansionum lunæ. Cap. XLVI.

Faciebant etiam imagines in singulis māsionibus Lunæ. [context] Now, as concerning the reason of Seeing, there are sundry and different Opinions.
Plato thinks that the sight proceeds from an equal clearness in the Eye, and the Object; the clearness from the Eye, being caus'd by the flowing of the Light to one extrinsick Air; that which proceeds from the Body, being caus'd by a reverberation of the Sight to the Eye; the middle clearness about the Air, being easily fluid, and apt to receive shape, according to the force of the Sight that always extends it self in a firy Form. Galen agrees with Plato. But Hipparchus saith that the Beams extended from the Eyes to the Bodies themselves, touching them as it were with a certain Palpitation, returns back the apprehension thereof to the Sight. Aristotle is of Opinion, that the Images of things pass from the Object to the Sight according to their quality, through the alteration of the middle Air. Porphyrius believes, neither Beams nor Images, nor any thing else to be the Cause of Sight, but that the Soul knowing her self, apprehends and sees her own self in all visible beings. But the Geometricians and Opticks coming near to Hipparchus, have invented certain Cones made by the co-incidence or falling together of the Beams, which are emitted through the Eyes, so that the Eye apprehends many visibles at one time; but those most certainly, where the Beams meet together. But Alchindus teaches another thing, which St. Austin thinks to be most true, That the Power of the Soul doth act something in the Eye, which is above humane Wisdome to find out. This Art therefore much conduces to the understanding the variety of Coelestial Bodies, their Distance, Magnitude, Motions, and Reflections; and is also a great help to Architecture, in the measuring, adorning, and perfecting great Buildings. But in the Art of Painting and making of Landskips, is of so great use, that neither can be done without it. For it shews us how to make Figures seem undeformed, and in Symmetry, at whatsoever height or distance they are to be seen.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of vision and the science of optics, transitioning from general definitions to specific philosophical schools of thought.</meta>

# ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE

<page-num>56</page-num>

->ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE<-

For Plato believes that sight occurs through a "co-brilliance," <note>original: "conclaritatem"; a term referring to the merging of internal and external light</note> namely, that the light flowing out from the eyes meets the light reflected from bodies in the external air. This occurs because the air in between is easily diffused and transformed, extending along with the fire-like power of sight. Galen feels in harmony with Plato. However, Hipparchus says that rays extended from the eyes reach out to those bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and return the perception of them to the sight. The Epicureans, on the other hand, assert that "images" <note>original: "simulacra"; the Epicurean theory of thin films or atoms shedding off objects</note> of things that appear cast themselves into the eyes. Aristotle, however, judges that these images are not bodies themselves, but reach the sight from visible things through a quality—an alteration of the surrounding air. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> truly believes that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing; rather, it is the soul itself, recognizing itself as visible—and since the soul is one in all things, it recognizes itself in everything that exists.

But the Geometricians and experts in optics, agreeing in a certain way with Hipparchus, describe certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays which are emitted through the eyes. From this, the sight comprehends many visible things at once, but those are seen most certainly wherever the rays coincide. Yet Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; a 9th-century Islamic philosopher and pioneer of optics</note> teaches something else entirely regarding aspects, while it seems to Augustine that the power of the soul effects something in the eye which has not yet been fully investigated by students of wisdom.

Therefore, this science contributes greatly to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves architecture in the measuring of buildings. Most closely, however, it brings the greatest ornament to the art of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, so that without it, these arts cannot be perfected. For it demonstrates by what reasoning we may avoid creating images that are either out of proportion or deformed when they are perceived due to distances and heights.

<summary>This page surveys historical theories of vision, ranging from Plato's "co-brilliance" and the Epicurean "images" to the geometric ray theories used by Al-Kindi and architects. It emphasizes optics as a foundational science for astronomy, architecture, and the visual arts.</summary>

<keywords>optics, theory of vision, Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, Al-Kindi, perspective, geometry, painting, reflection, refraction</keywords>

## ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE.

For Plato believes that vision is formed according to clarity, namely that which flows from the eyes to the external air as one, and that which is brought back from light originating from bodies to meet it. Furthermore, he posits that the vision which exists in the intermediate air is easily diffused and turns, being coextensive with the fire-like faculty of sight. Galen agrees with Plato, but Hipparchus says that rays are extended from the eyes to the bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and that this renders them perceptible to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that the images of things that appear insert themselves into the eyes. Aristotle believes that the images are not themselves bodies, but that they arrive from visible objects to the sight through an alteration of the air which surrounds them. Porphyry, however, considers neither rays nor images, nor anything else, to be the cause of seeing; rather, it is the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible, and being one for all, knowing itself in all things that exist. But the geometers and opticians, leaning somewhat toward Hipparchus, subscribe to certain cones formed from the coincidence of rays, which are emitted through the eyes. From this, they believe that sight comprehends many visible things at once, but those things most accurately where the rays coincide. But indeed, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; the Latinized name of the 9th-century philosopher Al-Kindi</note> teaches something else entirely regarding aspects. To Augustine, it seems that the power of the soul in the eye effects something which has not yet been investigated by scholars of wisdom. Therefore, this science contributes much to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves architecture in measuring buildings. It is closest, however, to the art of painting, and confers great ornament upon the construction of mirrors, such that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it shows by what reasoning we may neither miscount nor shape things in a deformed manner within the images that are perceived on account of intervals and altitudes.

But Porphyry claims that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing: rather, he believes it is the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible—and being the one soul of all things—that recognizes itself in everything that exists.

Yet the Geometricians and the practitioners of optics, following Hipparchus in a certain way, describe certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays which are emitted through the eyes: from which they say the sight grasps many visible things at once, but those most clearly where the rays have coincided. However, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; a 9th-century Arab philosopher and scientist known for his work on optics</note> teaches something entirely different regarding appearances, while to Augustine it seems that the power of the soul performs something in the eye that has not yet been fully investigated by the students of wisdom. 

Therefore, this science contributes greatly to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of the celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves Architecture in the measurement of buildings. Furthermore, it brings a great deal of ornament to the craft of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, such that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it demonstrates the method by which we avoid creating disproportionate or deformed things in images that are seen, due to the effects of distance and height.

<summary>Agrippa surveys classical and medieval theories of vision—from Plato and Aristotle to Al-Kindi and Porphyry—and outlines the practical applications of Optics in astronomy, architecture, and art.</summary>

...among the ancients. For Plato thinks that vision occurs through a shared brilliance, namely the light flowing out from the eyes to the surrounding air, meeting the light reflected back from bodies. He suggests that the light in the middle air easily flows into and joins with the fire-like power of sight, which is capable of expansion and transformation. Galen <note>An influential Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> agrees with Plato on this point. However, Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note> says that rays extended from the eyes as far as those bodies, touching them as if with a kind of palpitation, return the perception of them to the sight. 

The Epicureans <note>Followers of the philosophy of Epicurus</note>, on the other hand, affirm that <term>simulacra</term> <gloss>images or likenesses</gloss> of things that appear actually force themselves into the eyes. Aristotle, however, believes that these images are not physical bodies, but that they reach the sight from visible things through a change in the quality of the surrounding air. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher</note> maintains that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing; instead, he believes the soul itself, recognizing itself as visible—and being the one soul shared by all things—recognizes itself in everything that exists. 

Furthermore, Geometers and experts in optics, following Hipparchus in a certain way, describe certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays which are emitted through the eyes. From this, they believe the sight grasps many visible things at once, but those things are seen most clearly wherever the rays coincide. But indeed, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; a prominent Arab philosopher and scientist known for his work on optics</note> teaches something entirely different regarding aspects. Truly, it seems to Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, the influential Christian theologian</note> that the power of the soul effects something in the eye that has not yet been fully investigated by those devoted to wisdom. 

Therefore, this science contributes greatly to detecting the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of the celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions. It also serves architecture in the measurement of buildings. Most closely, however, it provides a great deal of ornament to the art of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, such that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it demonstrates by what method we may avoid creating disproportionate or deformed figures in images that are viewed, accounting for distances and heights.

<summary>Agrippa catalogues various classical and medieval theories on the mechanism of sight before discussing the practical applications of optics in astronomy, architecture, and painting.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Galen, Hipparchus, Epicureans, Aristotle, Porphyry, Al-Kindi, Augustine, optics, vision, light rays, perspective, art theory</keywords>

# ON OPTICS OR PERSPECTIVE

For Plato believes that vision is formed according to clarity, specifically through light flowing out from the eyes toward an external air, and light from bodies being carried to meet it. This light, which exists in the intervening air, is easily extended alongside the fire-like faculty of sight, which is capable of being poured forth and turned. Galen agrees with Plato, but Hipparchus claims that rays extended from the eyes reach out to bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and thus render their perception to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that images of what appears force themselves upon the eyes. Aristotle, on the other hand, believes that images are not bodies themselves, but that the quality comes from visible objects to the sight through an alteration of the air that surrounds us. Porphyry argues that neither rays, nor images, nor anything else is the cause of seeing; rather, the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible and one with all things, recognizes itself in all that exists. Yet geometers and opticians, leaning somewhat toward Hipparchus, propose certain cones formed by the coincidence of rays emitted through the eyes. From this, they conclude that the sight comprehends many visible things at once, but perceives those most clearly where the rays coincide. But Al-Kindi <note>original: Alchindus</note> teaches something entirely different regarding aspects, and indeed it seems to Augustine that the power of the soul effects something in the eye which has not yet been investigated by those studious of wisdom. Therefore, this science contributes much to understanding the variety, distance, magnitude, and motion of celestial bodies, as well as their reflections and refractions; it also serves architecture in measuring buildings. It contributes most, however, to the art of painting and the manufacture of mirrors, to the extent that these arts cannot be perfected without it. For it shows by what reasoning we should not create incorrect or deformed images when accounting for distances and heights.

<summary>This passage outlines various classical and medieval philosophical theories regarding the nature of vision, including the ideas of Plato, Aristotle, and Al-Kindi, before noting the practical applications of optics in architecture and art.</summary>

Aristoteles autem simulacra non quidem corpora, sed secundum qualitatem per alterationem aëris, quæ in circuitu est, à visibilibus usque ad visum devenire censet. Porphyrius vero neque radios, neque simulacra, neque aliud quicquam videndi causam: sed animam ipsam seipsam cognoscentem visibilem, & quæ una est omnium, seipsam in omnium, seipsam in omnibus quæ sunt, cognoscere. Hæc itaque scientia ad deprehendendum cœlestium corporum varietatem, distantiam, magnitudinem, motum, eorumque reflexiones & refractiones permultum conducit, architecturæ etiam in metiendis ædificiis inservit. Proxime tamen pingendi artificio, atque speculorum fabricæ plurimum confert ornamenti, ut sine ipsa hæ artes perfici non possint. # ON MORAL PHILOSOPHY

Christ teaches that one must do good to all, that even enemies must be loved, that one must give freely without expecting a return, that vengeance should not be taken against anyone, and that one should give to every requester. On the contrary, the philosophers say one should only give to those who compensate a benefit with a benefit; otherwise, it is permissible to be angry, to hate, to contend, to wage war, and to charge interest. Furthermore, they have given us, with their free will and the dictates of right reason and the light of nature, the Pelagian heretics. Moreover, all of moral philosophy (as Lactantius witnesses) is false and empty, neither instructing in the duties of justice nor confirming the office of man and his reasons. Finally, it is entirely repugnant to divine law and to Christ himself, so that its glory is owed to no one other than Satan.

# ON POLITICS
### Chapter LV

<column-break/>
rich men, or wise men; and Democracy, which is the rule of the people. And related to all these are tyrannies, oligarchies, and anarchies. But all these things must be referred to that which comes to each person. For although the philosophers wish to define which is best, they follow diverse opinions. Some admit that Monarchy is the truer form of good government, just as there is one God in heaven, one head in the members, and one leader among the bees. Likewise, others contend that Aristocracy or Democracy is the form of government that is equal and by which liberty is preserved. Above others, however, are Plato, Aristotle, Apuleius, and others, who are not only from our own traditions but also from the barbarians. [context] So the litle fish Echeneis stops the ships, and the Basilisk, and Catablepa kill with their sight, when they are alive; but when they are dead
do no such thing. So they say that in the Colick, if a live Duck be applyed to the belly, it takes away the pain, and her self dies: like to this is that which Archytas sayes. If you take a heart newly taken out of an Animall, and whilest it is yet warm, and hang it upon one that hath a quartane feavor, it drives it away. So if any one swallow the heart of a Lapwing, or a Swallow, or a Weesel, or a Mole whilest it is yet warm with naturall heat, it shall be helpfull to him for remembring, understanding, and foretelling: Hence is this generall rule, viz. That whatsoever things are taken out of Animals, whether they be Stones, any Member, Excrements, as Haire, Dung, Nailes, they must be taken from those Animals, whilest they be yet living; and if it be possible, that so they may be alive afterwards. Whence they say, when you take the tongue of a Frog, you must put the Frog into the water again, and if you take the tooth of a Wolf, you must not kill the Wolf; and so of the rest. So writes Democritus, if any one take out the tongue of a water-Frog, yet living, no other part of the body sticking to it, and she be let go into the Water again, & lay it upon the place where the heart beats, of a woman, she shall answer truly whatsoever you ask her. Also they say, that if the eyes of a Frog be before Sun rising bound to the sick party, and the Frog be let go again blind into the Water, they will drive away a tertian ague; as also that they will, being bound with the flesh of a Nightingale in the skin of a Hart, keep one alwaies watchfull without sleep. Archytas <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician of the 4th century BCE</note> says something similar: if a heart recently extracted from an animal, still warm and living, is hung over a patient suffering from a quartan fever <note>A fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>, it removes it. Likewise, if anyone swallows the heart of a Hoopoe, or a Swallow, or a Weasel, or a Mole, while it is still living and pulsating, it grants him memory, recollection, understanding, and divination.

From this arose a general precept, namely that whatever things are to be collected from animals, whether stones, members, or excrements such as hair, dung, or hooves, these must be taken from those animals while they are still living, and even, if possible, while they remain alive afterward. Hence they instruct that when you collect the tongue of a Frog, you should return it alive into the water; if you collect a tooth or an eye from a Wolf, do not kill the Wolf; and so on with similar cases. 

Thus Democritus <note>The Greek "laughing philosopher" to whom many magical and medical works were apocryphally attributed</note> reports that if one extracts the tongue from a living sea-frog <note>original: "Ranæ marinæ"; likely referring to the Anglerfish or Monkfish</note>, with no other part of the body adhering to it, and after releasing it back into the sea, places the tongue over the heart-palpitation of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever questions are asked of her. In a similar way, they promise that the eyes of frogs, tied to a sick person before sunrise in such a way that the frogs are released blind into the water, drive away tertian fevers <note>A fever recurring every third day</note>. They also report that these same eyes, tied on in deerskin with the flesh of a Nightingale, maintain wakefulness and put sleep to flight. Similarly, the spine of a stingray <note>original: "Pastinacæ radius"; the venomous tail-spine of the common stingray</note> tied to the navel is said to make births easy.
