<meta>This page continues a medieval lapidary—a treatise on the magical and medicinal properties of gemstones. The text follows a formulaic "If you wish [X], take [Stone Y]" structure common in Albertus Magnus's "Book of Secrets" or similar pseudo-Aristotelian works.</meta>

<sig>C 2</sig>

...ries: and he grants the power of prophesying: and the interpretation of all dreams: and he makes one able to understand riddles. <note>The beginning of this sentence is truncated from the previous page; it likely refers to a specific stone or spirit associated with wisdom.</note>

¶ If you wish to have a good understanding of the senses: and to be unable to become drunk: Take the stone which is called **Amethyst**: and it is of a purple color: and the best kind is produced in India and is powerful against drunkenness. It also bestows a good understanding of scholarly matters. <note>The name Amethyst comes from the Greek 'a-methystos', meaning 'not drunken'.</note>

<margin>+</margin>
¶ If you wish to overcome enemies and escape lawsuits. Take the stone which is called **Beryl**: and it is of a pale color with transparent light like water: Carry it with you and you will win all lawsuits and put enemies to flight: and it shall make an enemy mild. It renders power effective in one's character: just as Aaron says. <note>Refers to the biblical Aaron, often cited in medieval magic as an authority on the virtues of stones in the High Priest's breastplate.</note> It also gives a good understanding of scholarly matters.

¶ If you wish to divine the future. Take the stone which is called **Chelonite**: and it is of a purple and varied color: and it is found <margin>-</margin> in the body of a tortoise. <note>original: "testudinis". Chelonite was a mythical stone believed to be found in the heads of tortoises.</note> If anyone, however, carries this stone under their tongue, they shall divine and predict the future. Nevertheless, it has no power unless the first light <note>The new moon</note> has been kindled: and as the moon grows until it finally wanes. So wills Aaron concerning the virtues of stones and herbs.

<margin>+</margin>
If you wish to pacify tempests and cross over rivers. Take the stone which is called **Coral** and it is red, and another kind is white. And it is proven that it immediately stanches blood and, when carried, drives away foolishness: and provides wisdom: and this has been proven by certain people in our own time: and it is powerful against storms: and the dangers of rivers.

<summary>This page describes the occult virtues of Amethyst, Beryl, Chelonite, and Coral, focusing on their abilities to prevent drunkenness, win legal disputes, predict the future, and ensure safe travel across water.</summary>

Translator compresses the subject 'tenentem / habeant' into 'about you'; Latin 'peristereon herbam' = 'Vervain'; 'Alas si oleo illeveris' (anoint the wings) rendered 'under the shoulders'; the Latin clause 'pro vehementi, ac nimis in pugnam procliui' is paraphrased by 'ready and earnest to fight'. EEBO-TCP A55484 has many gaps on this page, so the archive.org OCR of the 1658 print was used and cleaned (long-s, OCR misreads); the Greek word was garbled by OCR and is restored from the Latin (form uncertain). Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero known for his works on magic and nature</note> says that dogs flee the sight of one who pulls a tick from a pig and carries it for a little while. You shall encourage the bird against the prey, so that it attacks large birds; moisten the bait, which it uses during the hunting time, with wine; or if it is a goshawk <note>original: "astur"</note>, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into a pigeon chick's beak, then make it fly. Thus,

### *You will make partridges more combative,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti ramulos"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; from which, most wittily in Old Comedy <note>Likely referring to the playwright Aristophanes</note>, they are called *garlic-fed* <note>original Greek: ἐσκοροδισμένοι (*eskorodisménoi*)</note>, that is, seasoned with garlic, a term for one who is vehement and too inclined toward battle.

Pluck the tail feathers that direct the course upward; thus it will fly below in a circle. If you wish

### *That a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without further harm <note>original: "sine noxa," implying the bird survives but is grounded</note>; the bird will not fly, and in this manner they do not escape from aviaries.

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; for this reason, in the Old Comedy <note>Ancient Greek theatrical style, notably Aristophanes</note>, they were most wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>original: ἐσκοροδισμένοι</gloss>, that is, "garlic-fed," meaning a person who is violent and too prone to a fight.

### Lest a bird fly too high,

Pluck the tail feathers which direct the flight upward; thus it will fly in circles below. If you wish

hairs, or excrement, or those who carry the herb <term>peristereon</term> <gloss>vervain</gloss>. A black stone similar to a bean is found in the Nile; when it is seen, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog’s tongue placed in your shoe under your big toe, or if you carry a dried dog’s heart with you, according to Sextus. Use hare hair or excrement, according to Pliny. Or, you shall carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give a frog to the dog in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs will flee from the sight of a person all day if he expels a tick from a pig and carries it for a while. Oppian writes:

> If you carry a little piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Immediately the whelps and fierce dogs,
> Struck with bitter terror, will not bark at you
> As you walk past, even if they were barking before.

### That a dog cannot run.

If you smear its wings <note>Note: referring to the dog's legs/feet in the context of animal speed</note> with oil, it will be hindered in running; this is how it will happen.

### That a hawk may be spirited.

You will invigorate a bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food it uses during the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish for it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into the beak of a pigeon chick, then make it fly. Thus,

### You will make partridges more combative,

If you give them branches of maidenhair fern <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. And,

### Roosters become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food shortly before they are to fight, from which the term <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed</gloss> is most wittily derived in ancient comedy, that is, one who is seasoned with garlic as a term for someone who is vehement and overly inclined toward fighting.

### That a bird may not fly high.

Pluck the tail feathers that direct the course upward; thus, it will fly in a circle below. If you wish,

### That a bird may not be able to fly.

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains unharmed; the bird will not fly. In this way, they do not escape from aviaries.

Therefore to have vitiated the entireness, continuation or holding together, and digestion of the parts, next, to have converted the venal Blood into corrupt Snotty matter, is reputed the very same thing in the Schools, as to have gone to prevent Catarrhs or Rheums; or thorow the hole of a Cautery, to have extracted from the Head (from whence they originally fetch all Rheums) an excrementous humor, which otherwise had threatned to fall down on a noble part; whether in the mean time, there be an agreement between the Head, and the Wounded part or not; for it is all one, so the Skin be deteined Wounded, whether that excrementous humour be Blood, or be made snotty pus, or liquid Sanies, is all one, so by the thred-bare words of Catarrhe, prevention, derivation, revulsion, and an Issue, the world be circumvented. For I behold a small Infant of a Year old, now breeding Teeth, and to suffer a Fever, froath of the Mouth, and Spittle, without ceasing; And at length that there are wringings of the Bowels, and Stools of Yellow-Green-coloured excrements: At least that Tooth is a part of the Head, wherefore the Flux shall be a Rheum of the Head: But what consent is there of a Tooth about to break forth, or a swollen Gum with a Bowel? Or what power thereof is there of begetting or sending away that Catarrhe out of the Stomack of a little Infant, unto his Head? And from thence into the Ileos? By what right shall a vapour dropped or stilled out of the Stomack, be made Cankered Choler in the Head? Hath perhaps the shop of Choler now wandred from the beginning of Life unto the Head? Could a Cautery (if an Infant were for undergoing it) suck unto it a leeky Flux into it self? And by a few small drops of corrupt matter, recompence or Ballance the leeky Choler of some pounds? Why doth the Stomack of a small Infant frame a Catarrhe by reason of the pain of his Tooth? Why is it sent into a Bowell, and not unto the paining Tooth? Doth not the reader yet see, that a Flux is not a Rheum? But that the Archeus (wheresoever yee will have it) being enraged, is ready in the Bowels, to transchange the nourishable juyce into excrements, which by the Schools are reckoned Choler, Phlegme, &c. If therefore the Flux be not a Rheume, and the Archeus being wroth, can transchange any thing into a troublesom Liquor, if the Gum be but afflicted; shall not he be able, on every side to unload himself by the appointed emunctories? And not to wait for the Skin to be opened by a Caustick? Alass, hath cruel dullness caused the Schools to be cruel towards their mortal kinsfolks?

<meta>This page continues Van Helmont’s physiological critique of the "Schools" of medicine. He argues that the fluids discharged from an artificial wound (cautery) are not "catarrhs" or waste products drawn from the brain, but are simply local blood being corrupted at the site of the injury by the body's internal director, the Archeus.</meta>

# THE CAUTERY #

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is simply blood that has been spoiled in the area where the wound is located; it is the result of a corrupted digestion in that specific place. To have damaged the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the body's parts, and finally to have converted the blood into pus—this is exactly what is regarded in the **Schools** <note>original: "Scholis"; the academic medical establishment of the time</note> as having countered **Catarrhs** <note>original: "Catarrhis"; from the Greek "to flow down," a medical theory that many illnesses were caused by mucus flowing from the brain to other organs</note>. They claim they have extracted an excrement-like humor through the opening of the cautery—humor which was otherwise threatening to settle in a **noble part** <note>a vital organ like the heart or liver</note>—either from the head (where they believe all catarrhs originally seek their source) or elsewhere. They maintain this whether or not there is a "consensus" <note>a sympathetic connection</note> between the head and the wounded part; it is all the same to them, provided the wounded skin is kept open. Whether that excrement-like humor is blood, or becomes pus, or is **sanies** <note>a thin, foul-smelling discharge</note>, it is all the same, so long as the world is deceived by the well-worn vocabulary of Catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and the **fontanelle** <note>original: "fontanellæ"; an "issue" or artificial wound kept open to drain fluids</note>. 

For I observe a year-old infant, currently teething, suffering from fever, foaming at the mouth, and constant saliva. And finally, there are griping pains and stools that are greenish-yellow. Surely that tooth is a part of the head; therefore, the diarrhea must be a "catarrh of the head" <note>Van Helmont is being sarcastic here to show the absurdity of the "Schools" logic</note>. But what is the "consensus" of a tooth about to erupt, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? What power does the tooth have to create and send a catarrh from the infant’s stomach to the head, and from there into the **ileum** <note>original: "Ileon"; the final section of the small intestine</note>? By what law does a vapor distilled from the stomach become "aeruginous" <note>rust-colored or copper-green</note> bile in the head? Has the workshop of the bile perhaps migrated to the head from the very beginning of life? Could a cautery (if an infant could tolerate it) drive away that leek-green diarrhea into itself? Could a few drops of pus compensate for several pounds of leek-green bile? Why does the infant's stomach manufacture a catarrh because of a toothache? Why is it sent to the intestine and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a catarrh? Rather, it is the **Archeus** <note>original: "Archeum"; Van Helmont's term for the internal "master builder" or vital spirit that governs the body’s chemistry</note>, indignant and provoked anywhere in the body, which is ready in the intestine to transform the nutritional "cream" into excrement—which the Schools then think is bile, phlegm, and so on. If, therefore, diarrhea is not a catarrh, and if the indignant **Archeus**—

<column-break/>

—is able to transform anything into a hostile liquid if only the gum is afflicted, can it not then discharge itself in any direction through the established **emunctories** <note>natural disposal organs/routes like sweat or urine</note>? Does it really need to wait for a piece of skin to be opened by a caustic? Ah, what cruel dullness has made the Schools so ferocious against their own fellow mortals?

<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not even consider that in women and the obese, there is a fleshy membrane around the ordinary locations for a cautery—mere **axungia** <note>soft body fat or lard</note> to a thickness of at least two fingers—yet these are the very persons for whom cauteries are more frequently and "profitably" urged. Consequently, the bottom of the fontanelle will barely reach the middle of that fat. 

<margin>17.</margin>
There is, therefore, no path by which the evil, fictional humor of the outlawed **Catarrh** can rush from the brain, or between the skull and the skin, through the middle of that fat. For what, in the end, is that "solitary humor," which, having been outlawed by its own sin from the part that sent it, descends unmixed through the substance of the fat and degenerates into pus? If it is an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why is it not more frequent in younger people and those with "hot" stomachs, rather than in the weak, the old, and the "cold"? In what way does that water, distilled from vapor, take on the form of pus? How will it hurry through the brain, the **meninges** <note>original: "menynges"; the membranes covering the brain</note>, and the skull to find the hole made by the cautery, so that it might flow out and be purged there alone? Why does the vapor not fly out into the air a hundred times over before it reaches the place so conveniently designated for the cautery? How can water rising from the stomach already be blood and the mother of pus? How can blood (which is the material of pus, according to **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Roman physician whose theories Van Helmont is attacking</note>) be the material of "Catarrh"? Why should blood be reduced to the rank of "bad humors" when it is not yet contaminated and is being dispensed by nature to the wounded site? Why, once a wound is made, would nature stop casting down the condemned matter through and into its accustomed places? If the skin is opened at the doctor's whim, will nature suddenly lose its way? Or did it perhaps struggle so much just to find an exit somewhere, and now that the hole is made, will it henceforth become the servant of the one who wounded it? Therefore, these four things are false: namely,

# C A U T E R I U M.

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is blood corrupted in the very part where the wound is, and it is the effect of a digestion that has been corrupted there. At least that tooth is a part of the head: therefore, diarrhea will be a Catarrh of the head. But what is the consensus of an erupting tooth, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what is its power of generating, of sending a Catarrh from the infant’s stomach to the head? And thence into the *Ileon*? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become greenish bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile perhaps migrated to the head since the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were capable of enduring it) drive the porraceous <note>resembling leeks, often referring to a green, bilious discharge</note> diarrhea into itself? And compensate for several pounds of porraceous bile with a few tiny drops of pus? Why does the infant’s stomach manufacture a Catarrh because of a toothache? <column-break/>

transmute whatever he likes into a harmful liquid, provided the gum is afflicted, could he not exonerate himself in every direction through established emunctories <gloss>cleansing or excretory organs</gloss>? And not wait for the skin to be opened by a caustic? Ah, cruel dullness, has it made the *Schools* behave fiercely toward mortals born of the same stock?
<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not consider that, in women and obese people, the fleshy membrane around the ordinary sites of the cautery is mere lard to a thickness of at least two fingers, yet it is to these persons that more frequent and more beneficial cauteries are recommended. Wherefore, the base of the *fontanella* will scarcely be in the middle of the fat. 
<margin>17.</margin>
There is therefore no path by which the evil, fictitious humor—proscribed as a *Catarrh*—may rush from the brain, or from between the cranium and the skin, through the middle of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor, which, having been proscribed by its own fault by the part sending it, descending unmixed through the substance of the fat, degenerates into pus? If it were an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why would it not be more frequent in the young, and those with warm stomachs, than in the weak, the old, and the cold? In what way will this water, distilled from vapor, put on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the meninges, and the cranium to find the opening made by the cautery, so that it may flow out and be purged only by that path? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place designated by the compliant cautery? How will water climbing from the stomach be blood and the matter of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen*) be the matter of *Catarrh*? Why must blood be reduced to the series of bad humors, which, not yet contaminated, is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once a wound is made, will nature cease to disturb the condemned matter through and into its accustomed places? For once the skin is opened at the pleasure of the healer, will it become ignorant of deviations? Or has it perhaps labored only to find an exit somewhere? And having done so, will it henceforth come to the bidding of the one inflicting the wound? Thus these four are false,

<header>C A U T E R I U M.</header>

<margin>15.</margin>
Ergò pus, est cruor vitiatus in illa parte qua vulnus est, effectusque vitiatæ ibidem digestionis. Vitiâsse ergo partium integritatem, continuitatem, atque digestionem, cruorem denique in pus convertisse, idipsum est in *Scholis* reputatum, *Catarrhis* obviam ivisse : sive à capite (undè omnes *Catarrhos* originaliter petunt) humorem excrementosum (qui alioquin ad partem nobilem comminatus erat decumbere) per foramen cauterii extraxisse : sive interim capiti, cum parte vulnerata, sit consensus, vel non: perindè enim est, modo cutis faucia detineatur. Sivè humor ille excrementosus, sit cruor, sivè pus fiat, vel sanies, perindè, modò per trita vocabula Catarrhi, præcautionis, derivationis, revulsionis, & fontanellæ, mundo fit circumventum. Contueor enim hornotinum infantulum, jam dentientem, ac pati febrim, spumam oris, atque indefinentem salivam. Ac tandem adesse tormina, & secessus ex viridi flaventibus. Saltem dens ille est capitis pars: quapropter diarrhœa erit Catarrhus capitis. Ast quis est dentis erupturi, vel tumidæ gingivæ consensus cum intestino? quæve potestas ejus gignendi, immittendi Catarrhi, è stomacho infantuli ad caput? atque indè in *Ileon*? quo jure stillatus è stomacho vapor, fiet æruginosa bilis in capite? fortè nè ab vitæ initio jam biles officina migravit ad caput? An cauterium posset (si infans esset tolerando) diarrhœam porraceam in se affugere? paucisque puris guttulis compensare aliquot librarum bilem porraceam? Cur fabricat Infantuli stomachus Catarrhum, propter dentis dolorem? Cur mittitur in Intestino, & non ad dentem dolentem? An nondum cernit lector, diarrhœam non esse Catarrhum? Sed indignatum *Archeum* ubilibet, in Intestino promtum esse, ad transmutandum alimentarium cremorem in excrementa, quæ à *Scholis* putantur bilis, pituita, &c. Si itaque diarrhœa non fit Catarrhus, possitque *Archeus* indigna-

<column-break/>

tus transmutare quilibet in infestum liquorem, si modo gingiva affligatur; An non poterit quaqua versus se exonerare per statuta emunctoria? nec præstolari apertam pellem caustico? Ah crudelis hebetudo, ferocire *Scholas* fecit in mortales sibi agnatos?
<margin>16.</margin>
Neque enim considerant, quod in mulieribus, & obesis, carnosa membrana sit circa ordinaria loca cauterii, mera axungia ad duorum saltem digitorum spissitudinem, quibus tamen personis frequentiora, magisque proficua, persuadentur cauteria. Quare etiam vix in medietate axungiæ fundus fontanellæ erit: 
<margin>17.</margin>
Non est ergò via, qua è cerebro, vel inter cranium, & cutim, ruat malus, *Catarrhi* proscriptus humor fictitius, per medium adipis. Sed quis demum humor ille solitarius, suo qui peccato à parte mittente proscriptus, per axungiæ substantiam, impermistus descendens, in pus degenerat? Si sit exhalatio vaporum è stomacho, cur non erit frequentior junioribus, & calidis stomachis, quam debilibus, senibus & frigidis? Quo pacto aqua ista, è vapore stillatitia, formam puris induet? Quomodo per cerebrum, menynges, & cranium, festinabit invenire factum foramen à cauterio, ut isthac tantum defluat, & purgetur? Cur centies non prius in auras vapor evolat, antequam ad locum cauterio lubenti designatum pertingat? Quomodo aqua scandens à stomacho, jam erit cruor, & puris mater? Quomodo cruor (materia puris, juxta *Galenum*) erit *Catarrhi* materia? Quare cruor redigendus in seriem malorum humorum, qui nondum contaminatus, à natura dispensatur ad locum vulneratum? Quare, facto vulnere, cessabit natura damnatam materiam, per & in loca sibi consueta, deturbare? An enim aperta, ad medentis lubitum, cute, fiet deviarum nescia? An forte laboravit tantum, ut exitum alicubi reperiret? eoque jam facto, deinceps in obsequium vulnerantis veniet? Itaque falsa sunt hæc quatuor nempè,

[context] For as diseases arising from depraved meat and drink, from Animals, Vegetables, and fruites of the Earth; with Arcanums of Herbs and Roots are healed; so if from Mettals and Minerals, with their Arcanums also, in such Arcanums of Vegetables are refused. In the same manner
plainly, the greatest part of diseases, coming from Celestial Influence, and from the Astral Impression of the greater and lesser Worlds firmament, admit not of cure with promiscuous Remedies, as by Arcanums of Herbs, Minerals, and Metalls, but by Astronomick Influence, the cure is instituted with such things only as have an Analogy to the greater and lesser World, in which is the true Magnetick force of the Firmament, and a Celestial Impression of resisting diseases, caused by the Firmament of the greater and lesser World, as is apparent in Arsemart, the greater Comphry, Dragonwort, and the greater Wallwort. If supernaturally, the disease or dolour take its beginning from Inchantment or by Magical Impression of Ascendants, the endeavouring the Cure by the three former ways is fruitless and unprofitable; but according to Paracelsus, process must be made Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil by the same means it was inferr'd must again be expell'd. In the aforesaid Simples there is an Influential Attractive, and all according to Divine Ordination, Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically cure; because in them is Medicine, and in Man the Magnet.
For as the Sun and Stars have power of attracting humidity from Inferiours, so Man (by the Magnetick attractive virtue placed in him, attracts Spirit instead of Nutriment, as a Loadstone draws Iron) and Inferiors have the same power of attracting from Superiors, as we see in time of the Pest; and these
[margin] ... Astral, Venenate, and Spiritual, the fift is such as are inflicted as a Scourge.
[margin] These Astral and Firmamental Infections are known by the ingenious Physician, and Firmamentally cured, for Art hath obtained a Medicine which impowers the Phy[s]itian ... to know and expell Firmamental diseases.
[margin] The Magnet of Man is Magical Cure, in which is a Celestial Impression after Contact of the Herb, the Herb until it be putrefied, attracts Medicine into the Ulcer, and so cures it.

[context] and moreover in this Hydropick Specifick, he joyns it with the Extract of black Hellebore and Colequintida,
that their virtues may be rendred more strong in expelling, and also the doses of precipitate Mercury, for their more commodious exhibiting he appoints to be made up in Pills. Therefore this precipitate Mercury, is by him highly praised and commended, and not without cause, for it powerfully helps in this case. Of like virtue is Mercurius vitae, or Flowers of Butter of Antimony, of which above, if from four granes to twelve thereof, be exhibited for three days together in extract of Hellebore and Colequintida; they happily expell the resolved Salt. But afterward Sweats and Urine must be provoked, with a decoction of Sarsaparilla, Lignum Sanctum, or root of Colts-foot, adding always a little Spirit of Tartar, or other Diaphoreticks and Diureticks, of which above; but especially adding Arcanum of Wormwood, or Carduus Benedictus. But this is to be noted, that the exhibiting of Mercurius vitae three days together, in those of ripe age, is often wont to cause the falling down of the Fundament, which is afterward rarely, or at most very difficultly cured. Yet it is needful in cure of the Dropsie, that such Purgations be adhibited in the beginning, but afterward Diureticks and Hydroticks must succeed. For otherwise, viz. ὕστερον πρότερον, this will happen, the Whey, or Watery humidity will all be devolved to the Reins Urinal Passages, from whence afterward, by reason of aggravation, very often most pertinacious Symptomes are wont to arise. Moreover in preparation of the Extract of Root of black Hellebore, it will be more safe instead of Spirit of Wine, to take Wine it self, with which the Root must only be gently Boiled without noise, and this done with fresh Wine, so long as until all the Essencified force be Extracted from the Root, afterward by evaporating or distilling reduce the Extract to the thickness of Honey. For Spirit of Wine, by reason of its attraction, which it rather acts upon the Sulphur, then the
[context] Mercurial liquor, in which the purging virtue consists, is less profitable, therefore Wine is better.

[context] “But
to return to their manner of living in society: the oldest man of every family, as has been already said, is its governor; wives serve their husbands, and children their parents, and always the younger serves the elder. Every city is divided into four equal parts, and in the middle of each there is a market-place. What is brought thither, and manufactured by the several families, is carried from thence to houses appointed for that purpose, in which all things of a sort are laid by themselves; and thither every father goes, and takes whatsoever he or his family stand in need of, without either paying for it or leaving anything in exchange. There is no reason for giving a denial to any person, since there is such plenty of everything among them; and there is no danger of a man’s asking for more than he needs; they have no inducements to do this, since they are sure they shall always be supplied:

# VTOPIAE THOMAE MORI

to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and happy. Fabricius, a man of upright and lofty spirit, certainly understood this himself when he replied that he would rather rule over the rich than be rich himself. And indeed, for one man to flow in pleasure and delicacies while others are groaning and lamenting on all sides, this is not being a king, but a jailer. Finally, just as he is a most unskilled physician who knows not how to cure a disease except by causing another, so he who does not know how to correct the lives of citizens except by taking away the comforts of life should admit that he does not know how to rule free men. Rather, he should change his own laziness or pride; for it is generally through these faults that the people either despise him or hate him. He should live harmlessly from his own means, adjust his expenses to his revenues, curb crimes, and prevent them through the proper upbringing of his people rather than allowing them to grow, only to punish them later. He should not rashly revoke laws that have fallen into disuse, especially those that have been long abandoned and never missed. Nor should he ever take anything in the name of a crime that a judge would not allow a private citizen to take, as if it were unjust and crafty. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarenses, who themselves are not far from Utopia, whose King, on the very first day he enters upon his rule, is bound by a solemn oath, after great sacrifices have been offered, never to have more than a thousand pounds of gold, or its equivalent in silver, in his treasury. They say this law was instituted by a certain excellent King, who cared more for the advantage of the country than for riches

OF THOMAS MORE'S UTOPIA

it is for the dignity of a ruler to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and fortunate. Indeed, Fabricius, a man of an upright and lofty spirit, surely understood this when he replied that he would rather rule over rich men than be rich himself. And in truth, for one person to wallow in pleasure and luxury while others everywhere are groaning and lamenting is to be the jailer, not the ruler, of a kingdom. Finally, just as a most unskilled physician is one who knows not how to cure one disease except by another, so he who does not know how to reform the life of his citizens except by taking away the comforts of life should admit that he does not know how to rule over free men. Rather, let him cast off his own sloth or arrogance; for it is usually through these vices that the people either despise him or hold him in hatred. Let him live innocently upon his own resources, let him adapt his expenses to his revenues, let him curb wrongdoing, and by the right training of his people, let him prevent evils from growing rather than allow them to increase only to punish them later. [context] Whereas if another do but slip a word, and one more quick-sighted than the rest discover it by accident, O Hercules! what uproars, what bickerings, what taunts, what invectives!
If I lye, let me have the ill will of all the Grammarians. I knew in my time one of many Arts, a Grecian, a Latinist, a Mathematician, a Philosopher, a Physitian, a Man master of 'em all, and sixty years of age, who, laying by all the rest, perplext and tormented himself for above twenty years in the study of Grammar; fully reckoning himself a Prince if he might but live so long till he could certainly determine how the Eight parts of Speech were to be distinguisht, which none of the Greeks or Latines had yet fully clear'd: as if it were a matter to be decided by the Sword, if a man made an Adverb of a Conjunction. [context] And whosoever will strive with thee in the law, and take from thee thy coat, yield up to him also thy cloak or mantle.
And whosoever shall compel thee to go with him one mile, go with him two more other. Love your enemies, and do good to them which hate you, and pray for them which persecute you and pick matters against you, that ye may be the sons of your father which is in heaven, which maketh the sun to rise upon good and evil, and sendeth rain upon just and unjust. Thou answerest, he spake not this to me, he spake it to his apostles, he spake it to perfect persons. Heardest thou not how he said that ye may be the sons of your father? if thou care not to be the son of God, that law pertaineth not to thee. Nevertheless he is not good verily which would not be perfect. Hark also another thing: if thou desire no reward, the commandment belongeth not to thee: for it followeth. If ye love them which love you, what reward shall ye have? as who should say, none: for verily, to do these things (that is to say, to love them that loveth thee) is not virtue: but not to do it, is an evil thing: there is debt of neither side where is just recompense made of both sides. Hear Paul, both a great wise man and cunning and an interpreter also of Christ's law. Bless (saith he) them that persecute you, bless them, and curse them in no wise, rendering to no man evil for evil, if it may be as much as in you is, having rest and peace with all men, not defending yourself, my best beloved brethren, but give place and withstand ye not wrath: for it is written, Vengeance shall be reserved to me and I will requite them saith our Lord. But if thine enemy shall be hungry, give to him meat: if he be athirst, give to him drink: for if thou do this, thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, that is to say, thou shalt make him to love fervently. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil in goodness. What shall then follow, sayest thou, if I shall with my softness nourish up the knappyshnes or malice and froward audacity of another man, and in suffering an old injury provoke a new? If thou can without thine own evil either avoid or put by evil, no man forbiddeth thee to do it: but if not, look thou say not, it is better to do than to suffer. Amend thine enemy if thou can, either lading him with benefits, or overcoming him with meekness: if that help not, it is better that the one perish than both: it is better that thou wax rich with the lucre and advantage of patience than that while either to other rendereth evil both be made evil. Let this therefore be a decree among Christian men, to compare with all men in love, in meekness, and in benefits, or doing good: but in striving, hate or backbiting, in rebukes and injury, to give place ever to them that be of lowest degree, and that with good will. But he is unworthy to whom a good turn should be done, or an evil forgiven, yet is it meet for thee to do it, and Christ is worthy for whose sake it is done. I will neither (say they) hurt any man, neither suffer myself to be hurt: yet when thou art hurt, see thou forgive the trespass with all thy heart, providing always that nothing be which any man should remit or forgive unto thee.

[context] Ca. Why in such Haste? Stay a little; pray stay. I'll put on my better Looks, and we'll be merry together.
Eu. What Sort of Cattle have we got here?
Ca. 'Tis the Patriarch of the College: Don't go away, they have had their Dose of Fuddle: Stay but a little While, and as soon as he is gone, we will discourse as we use to do.
Eu. Well, I'll be so good natur'd as to hearken to you, though you would not to me. Now we are alone, you must tell me the whole Story, I would fain have it from your Mouth.
Ca. Now I have found by Experience, of all my Friends, which I took to be very wise Men too, that no Body gave more wise and grave Advice than you, that are the youngest of 'em all.
Eu. Tell me, how did you get your Parents Consent at last?
Ca. First, by the restless Sollicitations of the Monks and Nuns, and then by my own Importunities and Tears, my Mother was at length brought over; but my Father stood out stiffly still: But at last being ply'd by several Engines, he was prevail'd upon to yield; but yet, rather like one that was forced, than that consented. The Matter was concluded in their Cups, and they preach'd Damnation to him, if he refus'd to let Christ have his Spouse.
Eu. O the Villany of Fools! But what then?
Ca. I was kept close at Home for three Days; but in the mean Time there were always with me some Women of the College that they call Convertites, mightily encouraging me to persist in my holy Resolution, and watching me narrowly, lest any of my Friends or Kindred should come at me, and make me alter my Mind. In the mean While, my Habit was making ready, and the Provision for the Feast.
Eu. How did you find yourself? Did not your Mind misgive you yet?
Ca. No, not at all; and yet I was so horridly frighted, that I had rather die ten Times over, than suffer the same again.
Eu. What was that, pray?
Ca. It is not to be uttered.
Eu. Come, tell me freely, you know I'm your Friend.
Ca. Will you keep Counsel?
Eu. I should do that without promising, and I hope you know me better than to doubt of it.

candidates.text: ...at once. **EV.** What birds do I see here? **CA.** It is the patriarch of the college. Do not withdraw; they have already finished drinking; sit down for a little while; when he has departed, we shall converse in our usual manner. **EV.** Come, I will ask of you what you were unwilling to tell me. Now that we are alone, tell me the whole story, for I would rather learn it from you. **CA.** Of so many friends, whom I thought to be the most steadfast, I now perceive there was not one who gave me more prudent and mature counsel than you, the youngest of all. **EV.** But how did you overcome the affection of your parents? **CA.** First, by the wicked exhortations of the monks and nuns; then also by my own: my mother’s spirit was weakened by prayers and blandishments; my father could by no means be persuaded. At last, with every engine brought to bear, he was conquered and overwhelmed, rather than consenting. It was done between drinks: they threatened horrible evil and ruin if he denied his daughter to Christ. **EV.** O the wickedness of fools! What happened then? **CA.** I was kept secretly at home for three days; meanwhile, certain women of that college, whom they call *Conversae*, were always present, adding spirit with their exhortations, that I should persist in the holy purpose, and anxiously guarding that none of my kinswomen or companions should approach me who might seem likely to change my mind. VIRGIN

EUPHEMIUS: What birds do I see here? 

CATHARINA: It is the patriarch of the college. Do not withdraw; they have already finished drinking. Sit for a little while; once he has departed, we will converse in our usual manner. 

EUPHEMIUS: Come now, I entreat you, tell me what you refused to tell me before. Now that we are alone, tell me the whole story; I would much rather learn it from you. 

CATHARINA: Of all the many friends whom I thought I valued most highly, I now realize there was none who gave me more prudent or mature advice than you, the youngest of them all. 

EUPHEMIUS: But how did you overcome the will of your parents? 

CATHARINA: First, through the wicked exhortations of the monks and nuns; then, my mother’s spirit was weakened by my own prayers and blandishments. My father could not be persuaded by any means. Finally, after all possible devices were employed, he was conquered and overwhelmed rather than convinced. It was done over cups of wine; they threatened a horrible, wretched end if he refused to deny his daughter to Christ. 

EUPHEMIUS: Oh, the wickedness of these fools! What happened then? 

CATHARINA: I was kept at home in secret for three days. Meanwhile, several women from that college, whom they call <term>Conversae</term> <gloss>lay sisters or converts</gloss>, were always present, giving me courage with their exhortations to persist in my holy purpose, and anxiously ensuring that no relative or companion who might seem likely to change my mind could approach me. Meanwhile, my clothing and other things belonging to the feast were being prepared. 

EUPHEMIUS: What was your state of mind in the meantime? Did you waver? 

CATHARINA: No, but I suffered something so horrendous that I would rather die ten times over than endure it again. 

EUPHEMIUS: I beg you, what is that? 

CATHARINA: I cannot say. 

EUPHEMIUS: Anything you tell me, you tell to your friend. 

CATHARINA: Do you promise silence? 

EUPHEMIUS: I would have guaranteed that even if you had not asked it of me. As if you did not know me yet.

they almost adopt the notion of the Manichæans, that the God of the Old Testament is a different being from the God of the New. But we shall easily get rid of such difficulties, if we direct our attention to that dispensation of God, which I have observed; namely, that during that period, in which he gave the Israelites his covenant involved in some degree of obscurity, he intended to signify and prefigure the grace of future and eternal felicity by terrestrial blessings, and the grievousness of spiritual death by corporal punishments.
IV. Another difference between the Old Testament and the New consists in figures, because the former, in the absence of the truth, displayed merely an image and shadow instead of the body; but the latter exhibits the present truth and the substantial body. And this is generally mentioned wherever the New Testament is opposed to the Old, but is treated more at large in the Epistle to the Hebrews than in any other place. The apostle is there disputing against those who supposed that the observance of the Mosaic law could not be abolished, without being followed by the total ruin of religion. To refute this error, he adduces the prediction of the psalmist concerning the priesthood of Christ; for since he has an eternal priesthood committed to him, we may argue the certain abolition of that priesthood, in which new priests daily succeeded each other. But he proves the superiority of the appointment of this new Priest, because it is confirmed with an oath. He afterwards adds that this transfer of the priesthood implies also a change of the covenant. And he proves that this change was necessary, because such was the imbecility of the law, that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to state the nature of this imbecility; namely, that the law prescribed external righteousnesses, consisting in carnal ordinances, which could not make the observers of them “perfect as pertaining to the conscience,” that by animal victims it could neither expiate sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it contained “a shadow of good things to come, but not the very image of the things;” and that consequently it had no other office, but to serve as an introduction to “a better hope,” which is exhibited in the gospel. Here we have to inquire in what respect the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical, the ministry of Christ with the ministry of Moses. For if the comparison related to the substance of the promises, there would be a great discordance between the two testaments; but as the state of the question leads us to a different point, we must attend to the scope of the apostle, in order to discover the truth. Let us, then, bring forward the covenant, which God has once made, which is eternal, and never to be abolished. The accomplishment, whence it derives its establishment and ratification, is Christ. While such a confirmation was waited for, the Lord by Moses prescribed ceremonies, to serve as solemn symbols of the confirmation. It came to be a subject of contention, whether the ceremonies ordained in the law ought to cease and give place to Christ. Now, though these ceremonies were only accidents or concomitants of the covenant, yet being the instruments of its administration, they bear the name of the covenant; as it is common to give to other sacraments the names of the things they represent. In a word, therefore, what is here called the Old Testament is a solemn method of confirming the covenant, consisting of ceremonies and sacrifices. Since it contains nothing substantial, unless we proceed further, the apostle contends that it ought to be repealed and abrogated, in order to make way for Christ, the Surety and Mediator of a better testament, by whom eternal sanctification has been at once procured for the elect, and those transgressions obliterated, which remained under the law. Or, if you prefer it, take the following statement of it; that the Old Testament of the Lord was that which was delivered to the Jews, involved in a shadowy and inefficacious observance of ceremonies, and that it was therefore temporary, because it remained as it were in suspense, till it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation; but that it was made new and eternal, when it was consecrated and established by the blood of Christ. Whence Christ calls the cup which he gives to his disciples in the supper, “the cup of the New Testament in his blood;” to signify that when the testament of God is sealed with his blood, the truth of it is then accomplished, and thus it is made new and eternal.
V. Hence it appears in what sense the apostle said, that the Jews were conducted to Christ by the tuition of the law, before he was manifested in the flesh. He confesses also that they were children and heirs of God, but such as, on account of their age, required to be kept under the care of a tutor. For it was reasonable that before the Sun of Righteousness was risen, there should be neither such a full blaze of revelation, nor such great clearness of understanding. Therefore the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them in such a manner, that they had yet only a distant and obscure prospect of it. Paul describes this slenderness of understanding as a state of childhood, which it was the Lord’s will to exercise in the elements of this world and in external observances, as rules of puerile discipline, till the manifestation of Christ, by whom the knowledge of the faithful was to grow to maturity. Christ himself alluded to this distinction, when he said, “The law and the prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached.” What discoveries did Moses and the prophets make to their contemporaries? They afforded them some taste of that wisdom which was in after times to be clearly manifested, and gave them a distant prospect of its future splendour. But when Christ could be plainly pointed out, the kingdom of God was revealed. For in him are discovered “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” by which we penetrate almost into the furthest recesses of heaven.

But we shall easily be disentangled from such scruples if we turn our mind to that dispensation of God which I have noted: that he wished, for the time when he was still delivering his Testament in some way wrapped up to the Israelite people, to signify and figure both the grace of future and eternal happiness by earthly benefits, and the gravity of spiritual death by bodily punishments.

4. Another distinction between the Old and New Testament is established in figures, in that the former, with the truth absent, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body: the latter exhibits the present truth and the solid body. And this is mentioned almost everywhere the new is opposed to the old testament: yet its discussion is fuller in the epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There, the Apostle disputes against those who did not think that the observances of the Mosaic Law could be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the whole of religion. To refute this error, he assumes what had been predicted of Christ’s priesthood by the Prophet. For since an eternal priesthood is conferred upon him, it is certain that that priesthood is abolished where successors were substituted for others daily. He proves that the institution of this new priest prevails, because it is established by an oath. He subsequently adds that the change of the Testament is also involved in that translation of the priesthood. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, since such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not render its worshippers perfect according to conscience, because by the victims of beasts, it could neither wipe away sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow in the very thing of future goods, not a living image of the things: and therefore it had no other office than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here it must be seen in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, a great disagreement would exist between the two Testaments: but since the state of the question leads us elsewhere, we must tend toward finding the truth. Let us therefore place in the middle the covenant which he once ratified as eternal and never to perish. Its complement, from which it finally has that it stands firm and ratified, is Christ. While such confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are as it were the solemn symbols of confirmation. This came into contention: whether the ceremonies that were ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. These indeed, although they were only accidents of the covenant, or certainly accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories: because, however, they were instruments of administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as is accustomed to be given to other Sacraments. Therefore, in sum, the Old Testament is called in this place the solemn manner of confirming the covenant, comprised in ceremonies and sacrifices. Now, since nothing solid lies underneath, unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it ought to have been made obsolete and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification has been once acquired for the elect: and the transgressions, which remained under the Law, were obliterated. But if you prefer, take it this way: the Old Testament was that which was delivered wrapped in the shadowy and ineffective observation of ceremonies; and therefore it was temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense, until it was supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. But then finally it became new and eternal, after it was consecrated and stabilized by the blood of Christ. Whence the cup, which Christ offers to the disciples at the Supper, he calls the cup of the New Testament in his blood: to signify that then the truth of God’s Testament truly consists, by which it is made new and eternal while it is sealed by his blood.

5. From this it is clear in what sense the Apostle said that the Jews were led to Christ by the pedagogy of the Law before he himself was exhibited in the flesh. He admits that they were also children and heirs of God: but who were to be held under the custody of a pedagogue because of their childhood. For it was fitting, with the sun of justice not yet risen, that there should be neither such splendor of revelation nor such perspicacity of understanding. Thus, therefore, the Lord dispensed the light of his word to them, so that they perceived it still from afar and obscurely. Therefore, Paul notes this thinness of intelligence with the word "childhood," by which the Lord wished them to be exercised with the elements of this world and external little observances, as rules of childish discipline, until Christ should shine forth: through whom the knowledge of the faithful people had to grow up. Christ himself marked this distinction when he said that the Law and the Prophets were until John: from then on the kingdom of God is evangelized. What did the Law and the Prophets profit the men of their time? Namely, they provided a taste of that wisdom which was one day to be manifested in clarity, and they pointed out that which was shining from afar. But when Christ can be pointed out with the finger, the kingdom of God has been opened. For in him are exposed all the treasures of wisdom and intelligence, by which one penetrates almost to the very inner sanctuaries of heaven.

Verùm talibus scrupulis facilè expediemur si animū referemus ad istam quam notaui Dei dispensationem, quòd tum futuræ ac æternæ fœlicitatis gratiam terrestribus beneficiis, tum spiritualis mortis grauitatem corporeis pœnis significare & figura-re pro eo tempore voluit quo Testamētum suum quodammodo adhuc inuolutum Israeli-tico populo tradebat.

4 Alterum Veteris & Noui testamenti discrimen statuitur in figuris, quòd illud absente veritate, imaginem tantùm & pro corpore vmbram ostentabat: hoc præsentem veritatem & corpus solidū exhibet. Atque huius fere fit mentio vbicunque veteri testamento nouum opponitur: fusior tamen est eius tractatio in epistola ad Hebræos quàm alibi vsquam. Illic disputat Apostolus aduersus eos qui Legis Mosaicæ obseruationes aboleri posse non puta-bant nisi vt secum traherent religionis totius ruinam. Quo hunc errorem refutet, assumit <margin>Psal. 110. b. 4</margin> quod de Christi sacerdotio prædictum apud Prophetam fuerat. nam quum æternum illi deferatur sacerdotium, certū est aboleri sacerdotium illud vbi alii aliis successores quoti-die substituebantur. Præualere autem noui istius sacerdotis institutionem probat, quòd <margin>Heb. 7. b. 11. c. 19. & 9. c. 9. & 10. a. 1</margin> iuramento stabilitur. Subiungit postea, in ea sacerdotii translatione verti etiam Testamē-ti mutationem. Atque id necessarium fuisse ratione cōfirmat, quoniam ea erat Legis im-becillitas quæ nihil adducere ad perfectionē posset. Tum deinde prosequitur quæ illa fue-rit imbecillitas, nēpe quòd externas carnis iustitias habuerit quæ cultores suos non possēt secundū conscientiam perfectos reddere, quòd pecudum victimis, nec peccata delere, nec veram sanctitatem conciliare poterat. Concludit ergo, vmbram fuisse in ipsa futurorum bonorum, non viuam rerum effigiem: ideoque non aliud habuisse officii nisi vt introdu-ctio esset in spem meliorem quæ in Euangelio exhibetur. Hic videndum est qua parte fœ-dus Legale cum fœdere Euangelico, Christi ministerium cum Mosaico conferatur. Nam si ad promissionum substantiam pertineret comparatio, magnum extaret inter duo Testa-menta dissidium: sed quum status quæstionis aliò nos ducat, eò tendendum est vt verū re-periamus. Fœdus ergo quod æternum & nunquam interiturum semel sanciuit, in medio statuamus. Illius complementum, vnde tandem habet vt statum ratúmque sit, Christus est. Talis confirmatio dum expectatur, ceremonias Dominus per Mosen præscribit, quæ sunt velut solennia confirmationis symbola. Id in contentionem veniebat, cederéne oporteret Christo quæ in Lege ordinatæ erant ceremoniæ. Hæ verò tametsi fœderis duntaxat acci-dentia erant, vel certè accessiones ac annexa, & (vt vulgus loquitur) accessoria: quia tamen instrumenta erant illius administrandi, fœderis nomen habent. qualiter & aliis Sacramē-tis dari solet. Proinde, in summa, Vetus testamentum hoc loco appellatur solennis confir-mandi fœderis ratio, ceremoniis & sacrificiis cōprehensa. En ia quoniā nihil solidū subest, nisi vlterius transeatur, oportuisse antiquari & abrogari cōtendit Apostolus, vt Christo po-tioris Testamenti sponsori ac mediatori locus daretur, per quem æterna sanctificatio ele-ctis semel acquisita est: & transgressiones obliteratæ, quæ sub Lege manebant. Quòd si ma-lis, ita accipe: vetus fuisse Domini Testamentum, quod vmbratili & inefficaci ceremonia-rum obseruatione inuolutum tradebatur. ideoque temporarium fuisse, quia veluti in su-spenso erat, donec firma & substantiali confirmatione subniteretur. SOROWE. I Am reprooued for praysing an vnworthie person.
Reason. That whiche is euyl, many times springeth from a good roter and good and innocent persons, iudge others to be suche as they are them selues. Hereof then it proceedeth, that they are more redy to prayse other, then reason requireth: and although I confesse it be euyll to prayse an vnwoorthie person, yet to disprayse a vertuous man, is farre more woorse.
Sorowe. I haue praysed one that was vnwoorthie.
Reason. If thou diddest it wittyngly, thou art blame woorthie: but yf through ignorance, thou art to be excused. It is not so euyl to be deceyued, as to deceyue: for, to be deceyued, belongeth to a man, but to deceyue, is the peculiar fault of the deceiuer.
Sorowe. Another mans prayse redoundeth to myne infamie.
Reason. Nay rather it was eyther thy fault, or thyne ignorance: For, as there commeth no prayse, so commeth there also no infamie from another.

Reason. ### On the shame derived from unworthy praise.

## D I A L. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you condemn later, it will be a part of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised someone unworthy.
<note>A woodcut depicts a large ornamental initial L at the start of the dialogue response.</note>

*Sorrow.* I praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* If you did it knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is less evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is foreign to one's nature, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Reason.* Rather, it is your own fault or ignorance. For just as there is no praise from another, so there is no infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly that I praised an unworthy person.

*Reason.* See to it, therefore, that you do not grieve over this same thing often. Beware that you do not rush rashly into praising and disparaging. For there is a lust for both, and (to speak properly) a disease and a certain itch of the tongue that is mobile and ignorant of rest. III. In the first place, it appears that a bona fide possessor is not bound to any restitution, if the thing be destroyed ; for he neither has the thing nor any gain from the thing : [a mala fide possessor is bound by his own act, besides the consequences of wrong doing.]
IV. Secondly, a bona fide possessor is bound to restore also the still extant produce of the thing : I say the produce of the thing ; for the produce of industry, even if it would not take place without the thing, is not due to the thing. The cause of this obligation is ownership : for he who is owner of a thing is naturally owner of the fruits of the thing.
V. Thirdly, that a bona fide possessor is bound to restitution both of the thing and of the produce of it consumed by him, if in any case he would have consumed as much : for by so much he is held to be richer. And accordingly Caligula is praised for having, in the beginning of his reign, when he restored governments to persons, given them also the income of the interval elapsed.
VI. Fourthly, a bona fide possessor is not bound to restore the produce which he neglected to take ; for he neither has the thing, nor anything which has come into its place.
VII. Fifthly, if a bona fide possessor has given to another a thing given to himself, he is not bound to restitution, except, in any case, without having this thing, he would have given something of equal value : for then he has gained by sparing his own property.
VIII. Sixthly, if he sell a thing which he have bought (belonging to another), he is not bound, except in so far as he sold it for more than he gave for it. If he have sold a thing given to him (belonging to another) he is held to restore the price; except it happen that he have spent the price, and would not otherwise have spent the money.
IX. Seventhly, a thing belonging to another which has been bona fide bought, is to be restored, and the price paid cannot be demanded back. To which rule it seems to me that this exception should be made ; — except in so far as the owner could not probably recover possession of his thing without some expense; as, for example, if it were in the hands of pirates : for then we may deduct as much as the owner would willingly have expended on it. III. First, it appears that a possessor in good faith <margin>Medina de contr. q. 10.</margin> (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the value of the thing by his own act) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither the thing itself is with him, nor any profit from the thing.

IV. Second, a possessor in good faith is held to restore even the existing fruits <gloss>products or profits</gloss> of the thing: I say fruits of the thing; for fruits of industry <margin>Zeff. l. II. c. 14. Navar. c. 17. n. 7.</margin> <note>profits arising from personal labor rather than the property itself</note>, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership <term>dominium</term>; for he who is the owner of a thing is naturally the owner of the fruits of that thing.

V. Third, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much anyway <note>if the possession saved him from spending his own funds</note>: for in this case he is judged to be enriched. Thus Gaius Caesar Caligula <margin>Suet. c. 16.</margin> is praised because, around the beginning of his empire, when he restored kingdoms to certain people, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.

VI. Fourth, he is not held to the fruits which he neglected to collect: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that succeeds in place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor gave a thing given to him to another, he is not held unless he would have given just as much anyway even without this thing: for then it will be a profit to have spared his own property. <margin>L. Quivæs. §. ult. D. furti.</margin>

VIII. Sixth, if he sold a thing he bought, he is not held, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sold a thing given to him, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price which he would not have squandered otherwise. <margin>L. si & rem. D. de petit. hereditatis.</margin>

IX. Seventh, a thing belonging to another bought in good faith must be restored, and the price paid out cannot be recovered. <margin>L. Sed & fi lege. D. eod.</margin> To this rule it seems to me this exception should be added: unless the owner probably could not have recovered possession of his thing without some expense, such as if the thing were with pirates. <margin>L. Si eum fervum. D. de rebus cre- ditis.</margin> For then as much as the owner would have been willing to spend can be deducted. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when difficult to recover, is something valuable; and in this the owner is judged to have been made more enriched after the loss of the thing. <margin>L. Mater tua. L. Si mancipia. D. de rei vin- dicatione.</margin> And therefore, while the purchase of one's own property is not valid by ordinary law, the Jurist Paulus says it is nevertheless valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession which is with another should be bought. <margin>L. Sucr. D. de cont. emt. L. 1. D. de evittionibus.</margin> And here I do not require that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner, in which case there are those who say an action for business managed <term>negotiorum actio</term> <gloss>a claim for services rendered without a contract</gloss> arises. <margin>L. Si laborav. §. Si navis. D. ad legem Rhodiam. Aegid. Reg. diff. 35. dub. 7. num. 126. Hoft. tit. de pern. v. quid de prædam ementibus. a L. Si in emtione §. rei. D. de contr. emt.</margin>

III. For first, it appears that a possessor in good faith (for a possessor in bad faith is held beyond the mere reason of the thing due to his own action) is not held to any restitution if the thing has perished: because neither is the thing itself with him, nor does he hold any gain from the thing.

IV. Secondly, a possessor in good faith is held to restore also the fruits <note>meaning the profits or products</note> existing from the thing: I say the fruits of the thing; for the fruits of industry, even if they would not have proceeded without the thing, are nevertheless not owed to the owner of the thing. The cause of this obligation arises from ownership. For he who is the owner of the thing is naturally also the owner of the fruits of the thing.

<margin>Zeff. b. II, ch. 14; Navar. ch. 17, n. 7.</margin>

V. Thirdly, a possessor in good faith is held to the restitution of both the thing and the consumed fruits, provided that he would have consumed just as much in any other case: for in this, he is considered to have been enriched. Thus, Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised near the beginnings of his reign, because to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he added also the fruits of the intervening time.

<margin>Suet. ch. 16.</margin>

VI. Fourthly, he is not held to the fruits which he neglected to gather: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that succeeds in the place of the thing.

VII. Fifthly, if such a possessor has given to another a thing that was given to him, he is not held unless he would have given just as much even without this thing: for then there will be a profit in having spared his own property.

<margin>L. "Quivas," § last, D. of theft.</margin>

VIII. Sixthly, if he has sold a thing he bought, he is not held, unless perhaps he sold it for more: but if he sold a thing that was given to him, he is held to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not otherwise have squandered.

<margin>L. "Si & rem," D. concerning the petition of an inheritance.</margin>

IX. Seventhly, a thing of another bought in good faith must be restored, and the price paid cannot be demanded back. To this rule, it seems to me that an exception should be added, unless insofar as the owner could not have recovered possession of his thing without some expense, for instance, if the thing had been with pirates. For then it will be possible to deduct how much the owner would have willingly spent. For the possession of the deed itself, especially when recovery is difficult, is something estimable, and in this, the owner is considered to have been enriched after the loss of the thing. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own thing is not valid under ordinary law, nevertheless, Paul the jurist says it is valid if it was agreed from the beginning that the possession, which is with another, be purchased. Anxiety led to the invention of a means of avenging so much bloodshed. The path it took when leaving its lair at night in search of prey, was carefully studied. The natives cut the road, digging a ditch which they covered over with boughs and earth. The tiger, which was a male, was incautious, and, falling into the ditch, remained there, stuck on the sharp points fixed in the bottom. Its roarings filled the neighbourhood and the mountains echoed with piercing howls. They killed the monster stuck on the points, by throwing great stones from the banks of the ditch. With one blow of its paw it broke the javelins thrown at it into a thousand fragments, and even when dead and no longer breathing, it filled all who beheld him with terror. What would have happened had it been free and unhurt! A civilian called Juan de Ledesma, a friend of Vasco, and his companion in danger, says that he ate the flesh of that tiger; he told me that it was not inferior to beef. When one asks these people who have never seen tigers why they affirm that this beast was a tiger, they reply that it was because it was spotted, ferocious, sly, and offered other characteristics which others have attributed to tigers. Nevertheless the majority of Spaniards affirm that they have seen spotted leopards and panthers.
After the male tiger was killed, they followed its track through the mountains, and discovered the cave where it lived with its family. The female was absent; but two little ones, still unweaned, were lying there, and these the Spaniards carried away; but changing their minds afterwards and wishing to carry them to Spain when they were a little larger, they put carefully riveted chains round their necks and took them back to the cave, in order that their mother might nurse them. Some days later they went back and found the chains still there, but the cave was empty. It is thought the mother, in a fury, tore the little ones to pieces, and took them away, in order that nobody should have them; for they could not possibly have got loose from their chains alive. The dead tiger's skin was stuffed with dried herbs and straw, and sent to Hispaniola to be presented to the Admiral and other officials, from whom the colonists of those two new countries obtain laws and assistance.
This story was told me by those who had suffered from the ravages of that tiger, and had touched its skin; let us accept what they give us.
Let us now return to Pacra, from whom we have somewhat wandered. After having entered the boios (that is to say, the house) abandoned by the cacique, Vasco sought to induce him to return by means of envoys who made known the conditions already proposed to other caciques; but for a long time Pacra refused. Vasco then tried threats, and the cacique finally decided to come in, accompanied by three others. Vasco writes that he was deformed, and so dirty and hideous that nothing more abominable could be imagined. Nature confined herself to giving him a human form, but he is a brute beast, savage and monstrous. His morals were on a par with his bearing and physiognomy. He had carried off the daughters of four neighbouring caciques to satisfy his brutal passions. The neighbouring chiefs, regarding Vasco as a supreme judge or a Hercules, a redresser of injuries, complained of the debaucheries and the crimes of Pacra, begging that he should be punished by death. Vasco had this filthy beast and the other three caciques, who obeyed him and shared his passions, torn to pieces by dogs of war, and the fragments of their bodies were afterwards burnt. Astonishing things are said about these dogs the Spaniards take into battle. These animals throw themselves with fury on the armed natives pointed out to them, as if they were timid deer or fierce boars; and it often happens that there is no need of swords or javelins to rout the enemy. A command is given to these dogs who form the vanguard, and the natives at the mere sight of these formidable Molossians and the unaccustomed sound of their baying, break their ranks and flee as though horrified and stupefied by some unheard-of prodigy. This does not occur in fighting against the natives of Caramaira or the Caribs, who are braver and understand more about war. They shoot their poisoned arrows with the rapidity of lightning, and kill the dogs in great numbers; but the natives of these mountains do not use arrows in warfare; they only use machanes, that is to say, large wooden swords, and lances with burnt points.
While Pacra was still alive they asked him where his people obtained gold, but neither by persuasion nor threats nor tortures could they drag this secret from him. When asked how he had procured what he had possessed,--for he had offered a present of thirty pounds of gold out of his treasury--he answered that those of his subjects who, either in the time of his parents or in his own, had mined that gold in the mountain were dead, and that since his youth he had not troubled to look for gold. Nothing more could be obtained from him on this subject.
The rigorous treatment of Pacra secured Vasco the friendship of the neighbouring caciques,

Having dug a pit, they covered it with hurdles and earth, and dispersed the unnecessary part. A tiger, a male, came incautious, fell into the pit, and stuck in the sharp stakes fixed in the bottom of the pit. With its roar, it was deafening the whole neighborhood, and the mountains were resounding with that strident noise. It was killed by huge rocks and stakes thrown at it from the edges of the ditch. It was breaking the spears fixed into it into a thousand splinters and a thousand pieces with its right paw, and thrown from above. Half-dead and bloodless, it filled those watching with fear; what it would have done if released and unharmed! A certain Ioannes Ledesma, a Hispalian and Vasco's friend and companion in labors, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than bovine meat. When asked whence they say it is a tiger—those who now saw the tiger—they respond that from the spots, from the ferocity, from the dexterity, and from other signs given by the authors, they judge it to be a tiger. Since most of them also declare that they have seen spotted leopards and panthers themselves. With the tiger destroyed, they followed its tracks toward the mountains and reached its den, its marital home. They take away two cubs, still unworthy of the mother's milk, while the mother is away. Having changed their plan to send them to Spain later when they were larger, they returned the little ones to the mother's den with iron chains carefully fastened around their necks. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains in nothing changed from their place. They think the mother, out of rage, tore them into pieces and carried them away so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have been loosened from the chains alive. The skin of the destroyed tiger was sent to Hispaniola, stuffed with dry herbs and straw, to the admiral and the leading men from whom the laws and aid of these new lands are expected. And both those who suffered hardships from the tiger and those who handled its skin told me these things, which we accept as given. We must return to Pacra, from whom we departed. Vasco, having entered the villages of Pacra—that is, his houses—strives to attract Pacra. Through envoys, he signifies the same things to Pacra that we recorded were signified to the others. For a long time, Pacra refused. Threats are added to the refusal. Finally, he comes accompanied by three petty kings. Vasco writes that Pacra is so deformed, sordid, and foul that he confesses he never saw anything more shameful. He says that nature gave him only human form; as for the rest, a wild, monstrous brute animal. He says his morals were equal to his habits and features. He was abusing the daughters he had seized by force from four neighboring petty kings with detestable lust. Many things regarding the obscene morals of Pacra and the infinite things of another kind were cast before Vasco by the neighboring petty kings, as before a praetorian judge or Hercules the avenger, so that punishment might be inflicted upon Pacra. He threw the monstrous beast, along with the three petty kings themselves who obeyed Pacra's word and labored under the same diseases, into the jaws of the war dogs, and ordered their lacerated corpses to be burned. Miraculous things are reported about the dogs with which they enter into battle. They were not ferocious against the armed natives; there was no need for swords, arrows, or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies, for when the signal was given and the dogs were released, the troop was terrified by the sight and the unusual barking of the Molossian hounds, and they, stupid, abandon their ranks and the battle at the prodigious invention. It happened otherwise, however, when hands were joined with the Caramairians and Caribs; for they are more ferocious and more apt for waging wars. Rushing upon the dogs, they aim their poisoned arrows faster than a lightning strike, and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows, but only with <term>maccanis</term> <gloss>wooden swords</gloss>, that is, broad, oblong wooden swords, and they act upon the enemies with missiles and fire-hardened spears. [context] But let us suppose that St. Peter had directed his Epistle to the Natural born Subjects, and those not private persons neither;
suppose he had writ to the Senate of Rome, What then? No Law that is grounded upon a reason, expresly set down in the Law it self, obligeth further than the reason of it extends. Be subject, says he, ὑποτάγητε : That is, according to the genuine sense and import of the word, be subordinate, or legally subject. For the law, Aristotle says, is order. Submit for the Lord's sake. Why so? Because a King is an Officer appointed by God for the punishment of evil doers, and the praise of them that do well. For so is the will of God: To wit, That we should submit and yield Obedience to such as are here described. There is not a word spoken of any other. You see the ground of this Precept, and how well 'tis laid. The Apostle adds in the 16th v. as Free; therefore not as Slaves. What now, if Princes pervert the design of Magistracy, and use the power that is put into their Hands, to the ruin and destruction of good men; and the praise and encouragement of evil doers? Must we all be condemn'd to perpetual Slavery, not private persons only, but our Nobility, all our inferior Magistrates; our very Parliament it self? Is not temporal Government call'd a humane Ordinance? How comes it to pass then, that mankind should have power to appoint and constitute, what may be good and profitable for one another; and want power to restrain or suppress things that are universally mischievious and destructive? That Prince, you say, whom St. Peter enjoyns Subjection to, was Nero the Tyrant: And from thence you infer, that it is our Duty to submit and yield Obedience to such. But it is not certain that this Epistle was writ in Nero's Reign: 'Tis as likely to have been writ in Claudius his time. And they that are commanded to submit, were private Persons and Strangers; they were no Consuls, no Magistrates:
