Senatum ipsum Romanum, cui hæc scripta sunt. Quid inde assequeris? cùm nullum præceptum cui ratio aliqua adjuncta est, quenquam ultra illam præcepti rationem obligare aut soleat aut possit. *Estote subjecti*, ὑποτάγητε, id est, si vim verbi spectes, subordinati, seu legitimè subjecti; ἡ δὲ τάξις νόμος inquit *Aristoteles*, lex est ordo. *Subjecti estote propter Dominum*. Quamobrem? quia cùm rex, tum præses constituitur à Deo ad ultionem facinorosorum, laudem benefacientium. *Quoniam ita voluntas est Dei*. Videlicet ut talibus obsequamur, quales hic describuntur; de aliis nullum hic verbum. Vides quam optimè hujus præcepti constet ratio; addit. v. 16. *ut liberi*, non ergò ut mancipia. Quid si versa vice ad crucem & perniciem bonorum, ad impunitatem & laudem & præmia facinororum regnent? an in perpetuum subjecti erimus non privati solùm, sed primores, sed magistratus omnes, ipse denique Senatus? Annon humana ordinatio dicitur? cur ergò potestas humana, ad constituendum quod hominibus bonum & salubre est, valebit, ad tollendum quod iisdem malum & exitiosum est, non valebit? Atqui rex ille, cui subjecti esse jubentur, erat Romæ eâ tempestate Nero tyrannus; ergò tyrannis etiam subjecti esse debemus. At inquam, & dubium hoc est, Nero an Claudius tunc temporis rerum potiretur, & illi qui subjecti esse jubentur, advenæ, dispersi, privati, non consules, non prætores,

[context] Neere vnto the kings palace standes the mint, hauing in the midst a fower-square court with certaine portals or cels rounde about it, wherein the money-minters dwell. Likewise there is another lodging
in the midst of the same court, where the gouernor of the mint with his scribes and notaries haue their aboad. Here, as well as in any other places, whatsoeuer commoditie is raised, redoundeth wholy to the king. Neere vnto the mint stande the gold-smiths shops, whose Consul or gouernour keepes the seale and stamps of the coine. In Fez neither ring nor any other Iewell or commoditie can bee made of siluer or golde, before the metall bee sealed, for the offenders are most seuerely punished. And, the metall being sealed, whatsoeuer is made thereof is weighed as if it were money. The greatest part of goldsmiths dwelling in new Fez are Iewes, who carrie their vessels of gold and siluer vnto a certaine place of old Fez, neere vnto the grocers shops, and there sell them. For in old Fez neither gold nor siluer is coined, nor any Mahumetans are suffered to be goldsmiths, bicause they haue vsurers among them, which will sell any peece of wrought siluer or golde deerer then the weight requireth; albeit the same priuilege is by the gouernours of the citie granted vnto the Iewes. Some there are also that onely make plate for the citizens, who are paied hire onely for their worke. That part of the citie which the kings attendants or guard once possessed,

QUESTION 112

OF BOASTING
(In Two Articles)

We must now consider boasting and irony, which are parts of lying according to the Philosopher (Ethic. iv, 7). Under the first head, namely, boasting, there are two points of inquiry:

(1) To which virtue is it opposed?

(2) Whether it is a mortal sin?

FIRST ARTICLE [II-II, Q. 112, Art. 1]

Whether Boasting Is Opposed to the Virtue of Truth?

Objection 1: It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But it is possible to boast even without lying, as when a man makes a show of his own excellence. Thus it is written (Esther 1:3, 4) that Assuerus "made a great feast . . . that he might show the riches of the glory" and "of his kingdom, and the greatness and boasting of his power." Therefore boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.

Obj. 2: Further, boasting is reckoned by Gregory (Moral. xxiii, 4) to be one of the four species of pride, "when," to wit, "a man boasts of having what he has not." Hence it is written (Jer. 48:29, 30): "We have heard the pride of Moab, he is exceeding proud: his haughtiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the loftiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that the strength thereof is not according to it." Moreover, Gregory says (Moral. xxxi, 7) that boasting arises from vainglory. Now pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore boasting is opposed, not to truth, but to humility.

Obj. 3: Further, boasting seems to be occasioned by riches; wherefore it is written (Wis. 5:8): "What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?" Now excess of riches seems to belong to the sin of covetousness, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore boasting is not opposed to truth.

On the contrary, The Philosopher says (Ethic. ii, 7; iv, 7), that boasting is opposed to truth.

I answer that, Jactantia (boasting) seems properly to denote the uplifting of self by words: since if a man wishes to throw (jactare) a thing far away, he lifts it up high. And to uplift oneself, properly speaking, is to talk of oneself above oneself [*Or 'tall-talking' as we should say in English]. This happens in two ways. For sometimes a man speaks of himself, not above what he is in himself, but above that which he is esteemed by men to be: and this the Apostle declines to do when he says (2 Cor. 12:6): "I forbear lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or anything he heareth of me." In another way a man uplifts himself in words, by speaking of himself above that which he is in reality. And since we should judge of things as they are in themselves, rather than as others deem them to be, it follows that boasting denotes more properly the uplifting of self above what one is in oneself, than the uplifting of self above what others think of one: although in either case it may be called boasting. Hence boasting properly so called is opposed to truth by way of excess.

Reply Obj. 1: This argument takes boasting as exceeding men's opinion.

Reply Obj. 2: The sin of boasting may be considered in two ways. First, with regard to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth; as stated (in the body of the article and Q. 110, A. 2). Secondly, with regard to its cause, from which more frequently though not always it arises: and thus it proceeds from pride as its inwardly moving and impelling cause. For when a man is uplifted inwardly by arrogance, it often results that outwardly he boasts of great things about himself; though sometimes a man takes to boasting, not from arrogance, but from some kind of vanity, and delights therein, because he is a boaster by habit. Hence arrogance, which is an uplifting of self above oneself, is a kind of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is very often its cause. For this reason Gregory reckons boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, the boaster frequently aims at obtaining glory through his boasting, and so, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory considered as its end.
[context] Reply Obj. 3: Wealth also causes boasting, in two ways.

->QUESTION 112<-

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next, we must consider boasting and irony, which are parts of lying according to the Philosopher in *Ethics*, book 4, chapter 7.
First, two things are asked regarding boasting: 1st, to which virtue it is opposed; 2nd, whether it is a mortal sin.

->ARTICLE FIRST<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, it proceeds thus. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes boasting can occur even without a lie, such as when someone displays their excellence. For it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast... to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom* <note>original: "divitias gloriæ suæ, ac regni sui"</note> *and the magnitude and excellence of his power.* Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory in *Moralia*, book 23, chapter 4, as one of the four species of pride, when someone boasts of having what they do not possess. Hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, saith the Lord, his boasting, and that his virtue is not according to him.* And in *Moralia*, book 31, chapter 7, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ART. I. — Boasting properly so-called is a vice by which someone outwardly elevates themselves above what is within them. Although boasting, regarding the usage of the word, may also be said of the ostentation of truth above the opinion or knowledge of others—as of a vice of its own genus (for thus it is only properly taken)—it is not spoken of except as an opposite of truth, by way of excess; since it is only in this way that it is the name of a vice of its own genus. For the ostentation of truth above the knowledge of others is not evil by its own genus, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil on account of an evil end (Cajetan).</margin>

<column-break/>

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by riches; whence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What hath pride profited us, or what hath the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of riches seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— But on the contrary, the Philosopher says in *Ethics*, books 2 and 4, chapter 7, that in both instances boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that boasting seems properly to imply that a person exalts themselves in words. For those things that a man wishes to boast about, he elevates on high. Now, someone properly exalts themselves when they say something about themselves that is above their own state. This occurs in two ways: first, when someone speaks of themselves, not above what is in them, but above what men think of them; which the Apostle, avoiding, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I spare, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or heareth anything of me.* — In another way, someone exalts themselves through words, speaking of themselves above what is in them according to the truth of the matter. And because one is to be judged more according to what is in them than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is that boasting is more properly said when someone elevates themselves above what is in them than when they elevate themselves above what is in the opinion of others; although it can be called boasting in both ways. And therefore **boasting properly so-called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds regarding boasting as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as said in the body; — in another way according to its cause, from which, although not always, it occurs more frequently. Thus it proceeds from pride as from an interior motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is interiorly elevated through arrogance above themselves, it follows for the most part that they outwardly boast of greater things regarding themselves, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and takes delight in it because such is their habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is elevated above themselves, is a species of pride; it is not, however, the same as boasting, but is its cause most frequently. And because of this, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. The boaster tends for the most part to obtain glory through their boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory according to the ratio of the end.

— On the contrary, is what the Philosopher says in the *Ethics*, books 2 and 4, chapter 7, in both places, that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that it must be said that boasting <term>jactantia</term> <gloss>a throwing or casting forth</gloss> properly seems to imply that a man extols himself in words. For those things which a man wishes to throw <term>jactare</term> far, he lifts up high. Now a person properly extols himself when he says something about himself that is above himself. This happens in two ways: — sometimes indeed someone speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in him, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> avoids, saying in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he sees in me, or that he hears from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in him according to the truth of the matter. And because a man is more to be judged according to what is in him than according to what is in the opinion of others, it follows that it is more properly called boasting when someone carries himself above what is in himself than when he carries himself above what is in the opinion of others; although it can be called boasting in both ways. And therefore **boasting properly so called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds from boasting insofar as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body of the article and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which it happens, if not always, yet quite frequently; and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an internal motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is inwardly lifted up above himself through arrogance, it follows for the most part that they boast of greater things about themselves externally, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not out of arrogance, but out of a certain vanity, and delights in this because they are such by habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is extolled above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is most frequently its cause. And for this reason Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, a boaster for the most part aims to obtain glory through his boasting; and therefore according to Gregory it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

->QUÆSTIO CXII<-

DE JACTANTIA. — In duos articulos divisa.

Postea considerandum est de jactantia — et ironia, quæ sunt partes mendacii, secundum Philosophum, in 4 Ethic., cap. 7.
Primo autem circa jactantiam quæruntur duo: 1° cui virtuti opponatur; 2° utrum sit peccatum mortale.

->ARTICULUS PRIMUS<-

Utrum jactantia opponatur virtuti veritatis.

Ad primum sic proceditur. 1. Videtur quod jactantia non opponatur virtuti veritatis. Veritati enim opponitur mendacium. Sed quandoque potest esse jactantia etiam sine mendacio; sicut cum aliquis suam excellentiam ostentat: dicitur enim Esther 1, 3: *Assuerus fecit grande convivium..., ut ostenderet divitias gloriæ suæ, ac regni sui* (1) ac magnitudinem, atque excellentiam potentiæ suæ. Ergo jactantia non opponitur virtuti veritatis.
2. Præterea, jactantia ponitur a Gregorio 23, Moral., cap. 4, a princ. una de quatuor speciebus superbiæ, cum scilicet quis jactat se habere quod non habet; unde dicitur Jerem. 48, 29: *Audivimus superbiam Moab (superbus est valde), sublimitatem ejus, et arrogantiam, et superbiam, et altitudinem cordis ejus. Ego scio, ait Dominus, jactantiam ejus et quod non sit juxta eum virtus ejus.* Et 31 Moral., cap. 7, a med., Gregorius dicit quod jactantia oriatur ex inani gloria. Superbia autem et inanis gloria opponuntur virtuti humilitatis. Ergo jactantia non opponitur veritati, sed humilitati.

<margin>ART. I. — Jactantia proprie dicta est vitium, quo quispiam exterius se effert, supra id quod in ipso est. Jactantia licet quoad vocabuli usum dicatur etiam de ostentatione veri supra opinionem seu cognitionem aliorum, ut de vitio ex suo genere (sic enim tantum proprie sumitur), non dicitur nisi de opposito veritatis, per modum excessus; quoniam sic tantum est nomen vitii ex suo genere. Ostentatio namque veri supra cognitionem aliorum, non est mala ex suo genere, sed quandoque bona juxta necessitatem aut utilitatem, quandoque mala, propter malum finem (Cajetanus).</margin>

(1) Vulgata: ... Divitias gloriæ regni sui.

<column-break/>

3. Præterea, jactantia ex divitiis causari videtur; unde dicitur Sap. 5, 8: *Quid nobis profuit superbia, aut diviliarum jactantia quid contulit nobis?* Sed superfluitas divitiarum videtur pertinere ad peccatum avaritiæ, quod opponitur justitiæ vel liberalitati. Non ergo jactantia opponitur veritati.
— Sed contra, est quod Philosophus dicit in 2 et in 4 Ethic., cap. 7, utrobique (1) jactantiam opponi veritati.

RESPONDEO dicendum quod jactantia proprie importare videtur quod homo verbis se extollat. Illa enim quæ vult homo longe jactare, in altum elevat. Tunc autem proprie aliquis se extollit, quando de se supra se aliquid dicit. Quod quidem contingit dupliciter: — quandoque enim aliquis loquitur de se, non quidem supra id quod in se est, sed supra id quod de eo homines opinantur; quod Apostolus refugiens dicit 2 ad Cor. 12, 6: *Parco, ne quis existimet me supra id quod videt in me, aut audit aliquid ex me.* — Alio modo aliquis per verba se extollit, loquens de se supra id quod in se est secundum rei veritatem. Et quia magis aliquis judicandum, secundum quod in se est, quam secundum quod est in opinione aliorum, inde est quod magis proprie dicitur jactantia, quando aliquis effert se supra id quod in ipso est quam quando effert se supra id quod est in opinione aliorum; quamvis utroque modo jactantia dici possit. Et ideo **jactantia proprie dicta opponitur veritati per modum excessus.**

Ad primum ergo dicendum quod ratio illa procedit de jactantia, secundum quod excedit opinionem.
Ad secundum dicendum quod jactantiæ peccatum considerari potest dupliciter: — uno modo secundum speciem actus, et sic opponitur veritati, ut dictum est in corp., et quæst. 110, art. 2; — alio modo secundum causam suam, ex qua etsi non semper, tamen frequentius accidit, et sic procedit quidem ex superbia sicut ex causa interiori motiva et impellente; ex hoc enim quod aliquis interius per arrogantiam supra seipsum elevatur, sequitur plerumque quod exterius majora quædam de se jactet, licet quandoque non ex arrogantia, sed ex quadam vanitate aliquis ad jactantiam procedat, et in hoc delectetur, quia talis est secundum habitum. Et ideo arrogantia, per quam aliquis supra seipsum extollitur, est species superbiæ; non tamen idem jactantiæ, sed ut frequentius ejus causa. Et propter hoc Gregorius jactantiam ponit inter superbiæ species. Tendit autem jactator plerumque ad hoc quod gloriam consequatur per suam jactantiam; et ideo secundum Gregorium ex inani gloria oritur secundum rationem finis.

(1) In Nicol. deest verbum utrobique.

THIRD ARTICLE [I, Q. 85, Art. 3]

Whether the More Universal Is First in Our Intellectual Cognition?

Objection 1: It would seem that the more universal is not first in our intellectual cognition. For what is first and more known in its own nature, is secondarily and less known in relation to ourselves. But universals come first as regards their nature, because "that is first which does not involve the existence of its correlative" (Categor. ix). Therefore the universals are secondarily known as regards our intellect.

Obj. 2: Further, the composition precedes the simple in relation to us. But universals are the more simple. Therefore they are known secondarily by us.

Obj. 3: Further, the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that the object defined comes in our knowledge before the parts of its definition. But the more universal is part of the definition of the less universal, as "animal" is part of the definition of "man." Therefore the universals are secondarily known by us.

Obj. 4: Further, we know causes and principles by their effects. But universals are principles. Therefore universals are secondarily known by us.

On the contrary, "We must proceed from the universal to the singular and individual" (Phys. i, 1)

I answer that, In our knowledge there are two things to be considered. First, that intellectual knowledge in some degree arises from sensible knowledge: and, because sense has singular and individual things for its object, and intellect has the universal for its object, it follows that our knowledge of the former comes before our knowledge of the latter. Secondly, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from a state of potentiality to a state of actuality; and every power thus proceeding from potentiality to actuality comes first to an incomplete act, which is the medium between potentiality and actuality, before accomplishing the perfect act. The perfect act of the intellect is complete knowledge, when the object is distinctly and determinately known; whereas the incomplete act is imperfect knowledge, when the object is known indistinctly, and as it were confusedly. A thing thus imperfectly known, is known partly in act and partly in potentiality, and hence the Philosopher says (Phys. i, 1), that "what is manifest and certain is known to us at first confusedly; afterwards we know it by distinguishing its principles and elements." Now it is evident that to know an object that comprises many things, without proper knowledge of each thing contained in it, is to know that thing confusedly. In this way we can have knowledge not only of the universal whole, which contains parts potentially, but also of the integral whole; for each whole can be known confusedly, without its parts being known. But to know distinctly what is contained in the universal whole is to know the less common, as to "animal" indistinctly is to know it as "animal"; whereas to know "animal" distinctly is know it as "rational" or "irrational animal," that is, to know a man or a lion: therefore our intellect knows "animal" before it knows man; and the same reason holds in comparing any more universal idea with the less universal.

Moreover, as sense, like the intellect, proceeds from potentiality to act, the same order of knowledge appears in the senses. For by sense we judge of the more common before the less common, in reference both to place and time; in reference to place, when a thing is seen afar off it is seen to be a body before it is seen to be an animal; and to be an animal before it is seen to be a man, and to be a man before it seen to be Socrates or Plato; and the same is true as regards time, for a child can distinguish man from not man before he distinguishes this man from that, and therefore "children at first call men fathers, and later on distinguish each one from the others" (Phys. i, 1). The reason of this is clear: because he who knows a thing indistinctly is in a state of potentiality as regards its principle of distinction; as he who knows genus is in a state of potentiality as regards "difference." Thus it is evident that indistinct knowledge is midway between potentiality and act.

We must therefore conclude that knowledge of the singular and individual is prior, as regards us, to the knowledge of the universal; as sensible knowledge is prior to intellectual knowledge. But in both sense and intellect the knowledge of the more common precedes the knowledge of the less common.

Reply Obj. 1: The universal can be considered in two ways. First, the universal nature may be considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality--viz. the relation of one and the same to many--is due to intellectual abstraction, the universal thus considered is a secondary consideration. Hence it is said (De Anima i, 1) that the "universal animal is either nothing or something secondary." But according to Plato, who held that universals are subsistent, the universal considered thus would be prior to the particular, for the latter, according to him, are mere participations of the subsistent universals which he called ideas.

Secondly, the universal can be considered in the nature itself--for instance, animality or humanity as existing in the individual. And thus we must distinguish two orders of nature: one, by way of generation and time; and thus the imperfect and the potential come first. In this way the more common comes first in the order of nature; as appears clearly in the generation of man and animal; for "the animal is generated before man," as the Philosopher says (De Gener. Animal ii, 3). The other order is the order of perfection or of the intention of nature: for instance, act considered absolutely is naturally prior to potentiality, and the perfect to the imperfect: thus the less common comes naturally before the more common; as man comes before animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of animal but goes on to the generation of man.

Reply Obj. 2: The more common universal may be compared to the less common, as the whole, and as the part. As the whole, considering that in the more universal is potentially contained not only the less universal, but also other things, as in "animal" is contained not only "man" but also "horse." As part, considering that the less common contains in its idea not only the more common, but also more; as "man" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Therefore "animal" in itself comes into our knowledge before "man"; but "man" comes before "animal" considered as part of the same idea.

Reply Obj. 3: A part can be known in two ways. First, absolutely considered in itself; and thus nothing prevents the parts being known before the whole, as stones are known before a house is known. Secondly as belonging to a certain whole; and thus we must needs know the whole before its parts. For we know a house vaguely before we know its different parts. So likewise principles of definition are known before the thing defined is known; otherwise the thing defined would not be known at all. But as parts
[context] of the definition they are known after. For we know man vaguely as man before we know how to distinguish all that belongs to human nature.

The third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

D The third [article] is proceeded thus: That more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us, but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. ### Question 85, Article 3

#### Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition

Regarding the third point, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition. For those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Therefore, universals are posterior in our knowledge.

Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things. But universals are more simple than particulars. Therefore, they are known later by us.

Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the thing defined first falls into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal; for example, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and thus universals are known later by us.

Furthermore, we arrive at principles through effects. But universals are principles. Therefore, universals are known later by us.

But against this is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that we must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its origin from sensitive cognition. And because the sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to the cognition of universals for us.

Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. Whatever proceeds from potency to act first reaches an incomplete act, which is halfway between potency and act, before reaching perfect act. Perfect act, which the intellect reaches, is complete science through which things are known distinctly and determinately. Incomplete act is imperfect science through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As it says in the first book of the *Physics*: things that are more confused are first manifest and certain to us. Later, we know them by distinguishing their principles and elements distinctly.

It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, one can know both a whole <note>a universal whole</note> in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; for example, knowing "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" as it is, while knowing it distinctly is knowing it as either rational or irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" rather than to know "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare anything more universal to something less universal.

<column-break/>

This order of cognition appears in the senses. For the sense judges more universal things before less universal ones, both in terms of space and time. For instance, when seeing something from a distance, we first perceive it to be a body, then we perceive it to be an animal, then a man, and finally Socrates. Similarly, it is clear that a child at the beginning distinguishes "man" from "not-man" before distinguishing individual men; children at first call all men "fathers" and later determine each one specifically, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. This is because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to knowing it distinctly, just as one who knows a genus is in potency to knowing the specific differences. And thus, indistinct cognition is midway between potency and act.

Therefore, sensitive cognition of singulars is prior to intellectual cognition of universals. But within the intellect itself, cognition of the more universal is prior to cognition of the less common.

To the first objection, it must be said that "prior" can be considered in two ways. In one way, regarding the intention of truth. Since the intention of truth and the true itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect arrives at this last. As is said in the first book *On the Soul*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior. But <term>Plato</term> <note>referring to the Platonic view</note> held universals to be substances, and in this consideration it would be true that particulars exist only by participation in the more universal subsistent things called Ideas.

In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, such as "animality" or "humanity" as found in particulars. In this, there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, where those things that are incomplete and in potency are prior. In this way, the more universal is prior in nature, as is clearly seen in the generation of a man and an animal; for the animal is generated before the man, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potency in nature, and the perfect prior to the imperfect. In this way, the less universal is prior in nature, just as "man" is prior to "animal." For nature's intention does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second objection, it must be said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole. The universal contains its parts in potency, such as "animal" containing not only "man" but also "horse." Therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man."

To the third objection, it must be said that a thing can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely as it is in itself. In another way, as it is a part of a whole. If we consider parts of a house like stones, we must first know the whole house in a confused way before knowing the parts. Thus it must be said that the defining parts, considered absolutely, are prior to the defined thing; otherwise, the defined thing would not be made known by them. But they are also parts of the definition.

But there is that which is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that from the universal we must arrive at particulars.

Now the perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is thus known is known both in act and in a certain way in potentiality. As is said in the first book of the *Physics*: first those things which are more confused are manifest and certain to us. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is either to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" in which is contained "rational" or "irrational," which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it first occurs to our intellect to know "animal" [rather than] to know "man." If both the sense and the intellect [are considered], cognition of the more universal is prior to cognition of the less common.

To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in two ways. In one way, as it is considered through the intention of truth; and when the intention of truth is both true and the same, it has a relation to many. And the abstraction of the intellect arrives at this end in such a way that it is truly posterior. In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's De Anima</note>, it is said that the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but [Plato] placed universals as substances; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are not except by participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called Ideas. He distinguishes between the order of nature and the order of discovery, using the example of how a child recognizes a "man" before recognizing their specific "father."</summary>

Question

<column-break/>

Article 3: Whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third article, the procedure is as follows: It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are simple; therefore, they are known later to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, *Physics* I</note> says that the defined <note>term: *diffinitum* <gloss>the thing defined</gloss></note> falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition, and parts of a definition are less universal; for instance, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," yet universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we encounter effects and causes and principles <unclear>by chance</unclear>, but universals are known later to us. But if it is true that, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*, we proceed from the whole to the singulars, I respond that it must be said that in our intellectual cognition, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its origin in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars is prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at the incomplete act, which is midway between pure potency and perfect act. The perfect act, to which the intellect arrives, is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as being in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*, what is first manifest and certain to us is more confused. Afterward, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, a whole, or that in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole can be known; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: just as knowing "animal" indistinctly versus knowing the animal in which rationality or irrationality exists, which is knowing a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "man." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less, just as sense goes from potency to act, so does the intellect. Such is the order

<column-break/>

of cognition appearing in sense. For in sense, we distinguish more, and when less is known, it is through being more remote by <unclear>corporeal being</unclear>, and <unclear>being</unclear> and "animal"; and more <unclear>observed</unclear> is "being animal," and <unclear>observed</unclear> is "good" and prior is "good" and "being." Or it pleases, and it is clear that a child from the beginning first distinguishes "good" and "not-good"; and children at the beginning call all men "father." Afterward, however, they determine each one, as stated in the first book of the *Physics*: it is manifest that one knows something indistinctly while it is still in potency, whether one knows the fiction or the principle; thus, one knows the genus and has the power to know the species. And so, by itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potency and act. And thus the cognition of singulars is prior to us, and the cognition of the universal is sensory cognition and intellectual cognition. If there is both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more universal is prior to the cognition of the lesser and common. As for the first objection, that can be considered in a double way. One way is considering the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect is the end of this mode, while the truth is posterior. As in the first book *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*</note>, the universal is either nothing or is posterior; but <unclear>Plato</unclear> posited universals as substances. And in this consideration, it is true, because particulars do not exist except by participation in the subsistent universals which are called "ideas." In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. In this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of man and animal. For the animal is generated before the man, as stated in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect; and in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for the nature of man is not arrested in the generation of the animal, but intends to generate a man. As for the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole is to a part; for the whole that is more universal contains not only the man and the horse, but it also contains the less universal, and it holds within it not only the more universal but others as well, just as "animal" contains not only man but also the rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "man," if "man" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so because of its reason. As for the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. In another way, when it is parts of this whole, and stones; it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house with a certain confusion. Thus, it must be said that the thing defined, considered absolutely, is prior to us and is defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be notified by those things, but rather, those things are the parts.

<summary>This page contains the third article of a question regarding the nature of intellectual cognition, specifically addressing the priority of universal versus singular knowledge in the human mind, and distinguishing between orders of generation and orders of perfection.</summary>

Tertius ar. utrum magis uniuersalia sint priora in nostra cognitione intellectuali.

Dtertium sic, proceditur. Ut quod magis uniuersalia non sint priora in nostra cognitione in-tellectuali: quia ea que sunt priora notiora secundum naturam sunt posteriora et minus nota secundum nos, sed uniuersalia sunt priora secundum naturam nostri intellectus. Preterea composita sunt priora quo ad nos et simplicia. sed uniuersalia sunt priora cioza: sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea philosophus dicit in primo physicorum diffinitus prius cadit in cognitione nostra et partes diffinitionis minus uniuersali: sicut animal est pars diffinitionis hominis: et uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Preterea effectus euenimus et casu et principia. sed uniuersalia sunt posterius nota quo ad nos. Sed si est quod or in in primo physicorum ex libris in singularia os deuenire. Respondeo dicendum quod in cognitione nostri intellectus duo os considerare. primo quidem quod cognitio intellectiua aliquo modo a sensitiua primordium sumit. et quia sensus est singularium in intellectus et uniuersalius: necesse est quod cognitio singularium quo ad nos sit uniuersalius cognitio. secundo os considerare quod intellectus nr de potentia ad actum procedit. et quod procedit de potentia in actum prius peruenit ad actum incompletum qui est medius inter potentia et actus et actus perfectus. aut perfectus ad quem peruenit intellectus est scia completa per quas distincte et determinate res cognoscuntur: actus et incompletus est scia imperfecta per quam sciuntur res indistincte sub quadaz confusione. quod enim sic cognoscitur tam quod cognoscitur in actu et quodammodo in potentia. ut in primo physicorum dicit in primo physicorum: sit primum nobis manifesta et certa confusa magis. posterius autem cognoscimus distinguendo distincte principia et elementa. manifestum est autem quod cognoscere aliquid in quo plura continentur sine hoc quod habeatur propria notitia uniuscuiusque eorum que continentur in illo est cognoscere aliquid sub confusione quadam. sic autem potest cognosci tam totum uel in quo partes continentur in potentia et totum integrale: utrumque enim totum potest cognosci in quadam confusione sine hoc quod partes distincte cognoscantur. cognoscere autem distincte id quod continetur in toto uel est habere cognitionem de re minus communi: sicut cognoscere animal indistincte et cognoscere animal in quo cum est rationale aut irrationale quod est cognoscere homine ut leonem. prius igitur occurrit intellectui nostro cognoscere animal et cognoscere homine. et cadere rone si comparem quodcumque magis uel ad minus ut sensus exit de potentia in actu sic intellectus: id et ordo

<column-break/>

cognitionis apparet in sensu. nam plus et sensu diuidicam magis et cum minus cognoscitur in remotius per opzebedit esse corp. et opzebedit et aial: et plus opzebeditur esse aial et opzebedit et ce bo et prius bo et sor. uel placet et patet at puer a principio prius distinguit bo et a bo: et in pueri a principio appellant omnes uiros pres. posterius autem terminat unumquemque ut or in in primo physicorum libri: rom manifesta et quod scit aliquid indistincte adhuc et in potentia uel sciat et fictio et principium sic et scit giis et potest: ut sciat oras. et sic per se cognitio indistincta media est inter potentia et actum. et quod cognitio singularium est prior quo ad nos et cognitio uniuersalis cognitio sensitiua et cognitio intellectiua. si et sensum et cum intellectu cognitio magis et est prior et cognitio minoris et cois. Ad primum et quod per duplex potest os siderari. uno et quod per os siderat sic et intentio ueritatis. et cum intentio ueritatis et uerum et idem beat habitudinem ad multa. pueniat et abstractio intellectus os finis hic modo dum uere sit posterius. in in primo de anima et quantitatem uniuersale aut nihil est aut posterius est: sed et plus tonem et posuit uniuersalia suba: et in hanc confide rationem uerem est: plus quia particularia et cum non sunt nisi per participationem uniuersalius sub sistentium que dicitur idee. alio modo potest conside rari et tum ad ipsam naturam. animalitatis et uel bu manitatis et put inuenitur in particularibus. et sic est duplex et ordo nature. unus fecundum uiam generationis et tempus cum uiam ea que sunt im perfecta et in potentia sunt priora. et hoc modo magis et est pus et in nam quod apparet manifeste in generatione bo minis et aialis. naz prius generatur animal bo: ut et or in in libro de generatione animalium. alius et ordo et perfectionis siue intentionis nature sicut actus simpliciter et pus et in naturam et quod per et pfectum per et quod ipse fecrum: et p hoc modo minus et est pus et in nam naz et bo aial. nature in intentio non sitit in generatione aia lis: et intendit generare hominem. Ad secundum et uniuersalius magis et est comparatur ad minus et est totum et per totum quod fit et magis et est uniuersaliter non solum co solum bo et equ: ut potest et minus et est et tinet in futurum non solum magis et est sed et alia ut bo in solum animal sed rona. sic igitur animal consideratum in se pus et in nostra cognitione et bo. si bo et pus i nra cognitione et animal sic per ronis eius. Ad tertium dicendum quod aliqua dupliciter potest cognosci. uno modo absolute secundum quod in se est et sic nihil et domum. alio modo cum sit partes huius totius et lapides necesse est quod prius cognoscamus totum et partes. prius enim cognoscimus domum quadam confusa sic igitur dicendum est quod diffinentia absolute consideranda fit prius nos et diffinitur. alioquin non no tificaretur diffinitum per ea. sed magis et sunt partes.

[context] This," he said, "the gods enjoin; and we have already shown how they admonish the soul to turn
to God, and command it to worship Him. But the ignorant and the ungodly, who are not destined to receive favours from the gods, nor to know the immortal Jupiter, not listening to the gods and their messages, have turned away from all gods, and have not only refused to hate, but have venerated the prohibited demons. Professing to worship God, they refuse to do those things by which alone God is worshipped. For God, indeed, being the Father of all, is in need of nothing; but for us it is good to adore Him by means of justice, chastity, and other virtues, and thus to make life itself a prayer to Him, by inquiring into and imitating His nature. For inquiry," says he, "purifies and imitation deifies us, by moving us nearer to Him." He is right in so far as he proclaims God the Father, and the conduct by which we should worship Him. Of such precepts the prophetic books of the Hebrews are full, when they praise or blame the life of the saints. But in speaking of the Christians he is in error, and calumniates them as much as is desired by the demons whom he takes for gods, as if it were difficult for any man to recollect the disgraceful and shameful actions which used to be done in the theatres and temples to please the gods, and to compare with these things what is heard in our churches, and what is offered to the true God, and from this comparison to conclude where character is edified, and where it is ruined. But who but a diabolical spirit has told or suggested to this man so manifest and vain a lie, as that the Christians reverenced rather than hated the demons, whose worship the Hebrews prohibited? But that God, whom the Hebrew sages worshipped, forbids sacrifice to be offered even to the holy angels of heaven and divine powers, whom we, in this our pilgrimage, venerate and love as our most blessed fellow-citizens. For in the law which God gave to His Hebrew people He utters this menace, as in a voice of thunder: "He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the Lord only, he shall be utterly destroyed."[659] And that no one might suppose that this prohibition extends only to the very wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom this philosopher calls very small and inferior,--for even these are in the Scripture called gods, not of the Hebrews, but of the nations, as the Septuagint translators have shown in the psalm where it is said, "For all the gods of the nations are demons,"--that no one might suppose, I say, that sacrifice to these demons was prohibited, but that sacrifice might be offered to all or some of the celestials, it was immediately added, "save unto the Lord alone." [note 661: Augustine here warns his readers against a possible misunderstanding of the Latin word for "alone" (soli), which might be rendered "the sun."] The God of the Hebrews, then, to whom this renowned philosopher bears this signal testimony, gave to His Hebrew people a law, composed in the Hebrew language, and not obscure and unknown, but published now in every nation, and in this law it is written, "He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the Lord alone, he shall be utterly destroyed." What need is there to seek further proofs in the law or the prophets of this same thing? Seek, we need not say, for the passages are neither few nor difficult to find; but what need to collect and apply to my argument the proofs which are thickly sown and obvious, and by which it appears clear as day that sacrifice may be paid to none but the supreme and true God? Here is one brief but decided, even menacing, and certainly true utterance of that God whom the wisest of our adversaries so highly extol. Let this be listened to, feared, fulfilled, that there may be no disobedient soul cut off. "He that sacrifices," He says, not because He needs anything, but because it behoves us to be His possession. Hence the Psalmist in the Hebrew Scriptures sings, "I have said to the Lord, Thou art my God, for Thou needest not my good." For we ourselves, who are His own city, are His most noble and worthy sacrifice, and it is this mystery we celebrate in our sacrifices, which are well known to the faithful, as we have explained in the preceding books. For through the prophets the oracles of God declared that the sacrifices which the Jews offered as a shadow of that which was to be would cease, and that the nations, from the rising to the setting of the sun, would offer one sacrifice.
[context] From these oracles, which we now see accomplished, we have made such selections as seemed suitable to our purpose in this work.

<meta>This page continues Augustine’s response to the philosopher Porphyry. Having previously cited pagan oracles that spoke well of Christ as a "pious man," Augustine now addresses Porphyry’s claim that Christians are in error for rejecting the worship of other spiritual beings or "demons."</meta>

### XIX

...warns concerning God and commands that he be worshipped everywhere. But the unlearned and those of such a nature to whom fate <term>fatum: In this context, Augustine is critiquing the Neoplatonic idea that some souls are destined to remain in ignorance, contrasted with Christian grace.</term> did not truly proceed from the Lord to obtain his gifts, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jupiter—not listening to either gods or divine men—have indeed rejected all gods. Yet, they have chosen not only to follow the forbidden demons with no hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things through which alone God is adored. For God indeed, as the father of all, needs nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. "For instruction," he says, "purifies; imitation deifies by working the affection toward him." He [the oracle or philosopher] indeed preached well concerning God the Father and said by what morals he is to be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the holy ones is being praised or censured. But regarding the Christians, they err so much—or rather, he slanders them as much as the demons (whom he thinks are gods) desire—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what filthy and disgraceful things were performed in service to the gods in theaters and temples <note>Augustine often contrasts the "obscenity" of Roman stage plays (which were part of religious festivals) with the moral sobriety of Christian worship.</note>, and to notice what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building up of morals lies and where their ruin. But who said this to him or inspired such a vain and obvious lie—that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whose worship was forbidden by the Hebrews—except a diabolical spirit? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and the holy heavenly angels and powers of God (whom we venerate and love as most blessed fellow-citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage), forbids sacrifice to be made to any other. He thundered this in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people, and he introduced it very threateningly, saying: *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out.* <note>original: "Sacrificans diis eradicabitur" — Reference to Exodus 22:20.</note> And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the worst demons and earthly spirits, whom that man [Porphyry] calls the least or lesser ones (who are themselves called "gods" in the holy scriptures, though not the gods of the Hebrews...

<column-break/>

...but of the Gentiles), the Seventy interpreters <note>Seventy interpreters: A reference to the Septuagint, the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by the early Church.</note> clearly placed this in the Psalm, saying: *For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons.* <note>original: "Quoniam omnes dii gentium demonia" — Psalm 96:5 (LXX 95:5).</note> Therefore, lest anyone should think that while it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, it was permitted to sacrifice to either all or some of the heavenly beings, he immediately added: *except to the Lord only*; that is, to the Lord alone. This is to prevent someone from believing that because he said "to the Lord alone," one should think there is only one God to whom sacrifice is due <note>Augustine is clarifying that "the Lord" refers to the specific God of the Bible, not a generic monotheistic concept.</note>. That it should be understood this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher provides such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations. In this law it is written: *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only.* What need is there to search out many things in his law and his prophets concerning this matter? Rather, there is no need to search, for they are not hidden or erased; it is easy to collect frequent and plain passages and place them in this discussion of mine, through which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God willed that sacrifice be offered to no one at all except to himself. Behold, let this one thing, spoken briefly—or rather grandly, threateningly, but truly—by that God whom the most learned of the pagans preach as so excellent, be heard: let it be feared; let it be fulfilled, lest the "rooting out" follow those who are disobedient. *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out,* he says, *except to the Lord only.* Not because he has need of anything, but because it is beneficial for us that we should be his property. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: *I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you have no need of my goods.* <note>original: "Dixi domino deus meus es tu: quoniam bonorum meorum non eges" — Psalm 16:2.</note> Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his City <note>This is a foundational statement for the book's title: the "City of God" is not a physical place, but the community of the faithful who offer themselves to God.</note>, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the oracles thundered through the Hebrew prophets that the animal sacrifices which the Jews offered as a "shadow of things to come" would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one single sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that even pagan philosophers acknowledge the God of the Hebrews, yet they falsely claim Christians revere demons. He cites the Mosaic law to prove that sacrifice is reserved for the one true God alone, culminating in the idea that the Christian community itself is the ultimate sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, demons, sacrifice, Hebrew Law, Exodus 22:20, City of God, Septuagint, worship, moral ruin vs building</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...as they take notice of</meta> God and command everyone to worship him everywhere. But the unlearned and the philosophers themselves, who do not truly proceed from the Lord to obtain his gifts, and do not have the knowledge of the immortal Jupiter, not listening to both the gods and the divine men, have indeed rejected all the gods. Yet, they have chosen not only not to hate the forbidden demons, but even to revere them. Pretending to worship God, they do not do the only things through which God is adored. For God, as the father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very lives a path to him through imitation and instruction from him. For instruction purges the mind, while imitation deifies the affection for him by working. He preached well indeed about God the Father and told with what morals he should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the <term>Hebrei</term> <gloss>Hebrews</gloss> are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy ones is either praised or blamed. But it was only among the Christians, or [these philosophers] calumniate them as much as the demons they fancy to be gods desire; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in theaters and temples regarding the service of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is the building up and where the ruin of morals. But who said this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians would rather revere than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love as the most blessed citizens, the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, forbids that sacrifice be offered to anyone in his law which he gave to his people, the Hebrews; and he thundered very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And so that no one would think that it was not forbidden to sacrifice to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom he <note>referring to Porphyry</note> calls mimes or lesser [gods]—who were also called gods in the holy scriptures, not by the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but by the Gentiles—which the seventy interpreters clearly placed in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons." Therefore, lest anyone think that sacrifice was indeed forbidden to these demons, but permitted to be offered to the celestial ones, either to all or to some, he immediately added: "unless to the Lord only," that is, unless to the Lord alone. Lest perhaps anyone, because he says "to the Lord only," might believe that God is the only one to whom he thinks he must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood that way is most easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives so great a testimony, gave a law to his own Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all the nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of his and in his prophets to search much about this matter? Or rather, not to search, for they are not hidden or erased, but clear and frequent to collect, and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he wished the true and highest God to be sacrificed to no one at all except to himself. Behold, this one thing, briefly or rather weightily, menacingly, but truthfully said by that God whom their most learned men preach as so excellent: let it be heard, feared, and fulfilled, lest the destruction follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," he says, "shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord only." Not because he needs any thing, but because it is expedient for us that we should be his. For to him it is sung in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you do not need my goods." And the most excellent and best sacrifice of him is we ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, as we disputed in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted through oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future were to cease, and that one sacrifice would be offered by the Gentiles from the rising of the sun even to its setting, as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine refutes the claim that Christians irrationally hate demons, arguing that the Hebrew law explicitly prohibits the worship of such spirits. He asserts that the one true God demands exclusive sacrifice, a tradition now fulfilled by the universal Christian sacrifice, replacing the temporary rituals of the Old Testament.</summary>
<keywords>Demonology, Hebrew Law, Sacrifice, Porphyry, Idolatry, Old Testament, Christian Liturgy, Psalm 96</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the gods command; and we have shown in the things above how they take notice of [God], advising that he be worshiped everywhere. But the unlearned, and indeed nature itself, because they truly did not receive the gifts of the Lord, nor did they have knowledge of the immortal Jupiter, not listening to both the gods and divine men, they indeed rejected all the gods; but they chose not only to harbor no hatred for prohibited demons, but even to revere them. Pretending to worship God, they do not do the only things through which God is adored. For God, indeed, as the Father of all, needs nothing; but it is good for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a path toward him through the imitation and instruction of him. For instruction purges the mind, [and] imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He preached well indeed that God is the Father and of the morals by which he must be worshiped. These precepts the prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of, when the life of the holy ones is either praised or blamed. But it was only among the Christians; or they are slandered as much as the demons—whom they suppose to be gods—wish: as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful things, what disgraces were performed in theaters and temples regarding the service of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God; and from this to understand where there is a building up and where there is a ruin of morals. But who said to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and suitable lie: that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we venerate and love—along with the celestial holy angels and the powers of God, whom we consider most blessed as fellow citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids in the law he gave to his Hebrew people that sacrifice be offered to him, and he decreed it very menacingly, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated. And so that no one might think that it was commanded not to sacrifice to the very worst demons and earthly spirits—whom he [Porphyry] calls mimics or lesser ones—because they also were called gods in the holy scriptures, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations: which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> clearly set down in a psalm, saying: For all the gods of the nations are demons. Lest anyone, therefore, think that it was forbidden to these demons indeed, but that it was permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, either to all or to some, he soon added: except to the Lord alone. That is, except to the Lord only, lest by chance anyone, because he says to the Lord alone, might believe that he is the only God to whom one thinks one must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in that way is found most easily in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews—to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony—gave a law to his own Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but already made famous among all nations, in which law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, except to the Lord only. What need is there in this law of his and in his prophets to search out many things about this matter? Indeed, there is no need to search, for they are not obscured or erased, but are clear and frequent to collect and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he wished the true and supreme God to be sacrificed to by no one at all except to himself. Behold this one thing, briefly—or rather, gravely, menacingly, but truthfully—spoken by that God whom their most learned men preach: let it be heard, feared, fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he needs anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be his. For it is sung to him in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, because you do not need my goods. But the most excellent and best sacrifice of him is we ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, as we disputed in the preceding books. For the oracles of the Hebrew prophets interpreted that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of what was to come were to cease, and that one sacrifice would be offered by the nations from the rising of the sun even to the setting, as we already see being done.

<summary>Augustine refutes Porphyry's claims by citing the Hebrew Law and Psalms to demonstrate that the God of the Hebrews strictly forbids sacrifice to any entity other than the Lord. He clarifies that the prohibition against "gods of the nations" targets demons, while defining the Christian sacrifice as the offering of oneself to God.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Hebrew Law, Sacrifice, Demonology, Septuagint, Idolatry, Christian liturgy, Divine Unity</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>God, and he commands that He alone be worshipped everywhere.
But the unlearned and those of a [base] nature—to whom, truly, the fate did not proceed from the Lord to obtain gifts, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jove <note>original: "Iouis"; Augustine often uses the Roman name Jupiter/Jove to refer to the supreme deity in a philosophical context</note>—not listening to both gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all gods. Furthermore, they have chosen not only not to pursue the prohibited demons with any hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things through which alone God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, stands in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore Him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through imitation and instruction concerning Him. For instruction purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward Him. Indeed, he <note>Porphyry</note> preached well concerning God the Father and said by what morals He must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy is either praised or blamed.

But among Christians, it was only so much, or he so much slanders them as the demons wish—those whom he thinks are gods—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in honor of the gods in theaters and temples, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building is and where the ruin of morals lies. Who, however, said this to him or inspired him, except a diabolical spirit, such a vain and obvious lie: that the demons prohibited from being worshipped by the Hebrews are revered rather than hated by Christians? 

But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped—and the celestial holy angels and powers of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids sacrifice to be made [to others], thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people; and He brought it in very threateningly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." <note>Exodus 22:20</note> And lest anyone should think that the command was not to sacrifice to the most wicked and earthly spirits, whom that man <note>Porphyry</note> calls the least or minor ones—since in the Holy Scriptures these are themselves called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the gentiles—which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> clearly placed in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the gentiles are demons." <note>Psalm 96:5</note> Lest anyone, therefore, should think that sacrifice was indeed prohibited to these demons, but permitted to be made to the celestial ones, either all or some of them, He immediately added: "except to the Lord alone"; that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" should believe God to be only one person to whom he thinks sacrifice must be made. That this is not to be understood so is very easily found in the Greek scriptures.

The God of the Hebrews, therefore, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> provides such a great testimony, gave the law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now made famous among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in His law and His prophets? Indeed, not to search for them—for they are not hidden or rare—but to collect those things which are plain and frequent and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that He, the true and supreme God, willed that sacrifice be made to no one at all except to Himself. 

Behold this one thing, spoken briefly, or rather grandly and threateningly, but truthfully, by that God whom the most learned of those [pagans] proclaim as so excellent: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," He says, "shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." Not that He has need of anything, but because it is expedient for us that we should be His. For to Him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, You are my God, since You have no need of my goods." <note>Psalm 16:2</note> Moreover, we ourselves are His most noble and best sacrifice. This is His City, the mystery of which thing we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, just as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets sounded oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and the nations, from the rising of the sun even to its setting, would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that even pagan philosophers acknowledge the God of the Hebrews, yet they fail to see that this God demands exclusive worship and forbids sacrifice to demons or lesser spirits. He identifies the Christian community and its "spiritual sacrifice" as the true City of God predicted by the prophets.</summary>
<keywords>Monotheism, Sacrifice, Porphyry, Demons, Hebrew Law, Septuagint, City of God, Moral virtue</keywords>

God, and he commands that he be worshiped everywhere.
But the unlearned and those of a [base] nature, to whom the true fate <note>original: "fatum"</note> from the Lord of obtaining gifts has not proceeded, nor have they a knowledge of the immortal Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, here used by Porphyry to refer to the supreme God</note>, not listening to both gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all gods; but they have chosen not only to not pursue the prohibited demons with any hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not do those things alone through which God is adored. For God indeed, as the Father of all, lacks nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. Instruction indeed purifies, he says; imitation deifies the affection by working toward him." The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy is either praised or blamed. But among the Christians there was only <note>or "at least"</note>, or there is only as much calumny as the demons whom they think are gods desire; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what base and disgraceful things were done in theaters and temples regarding the service of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where there is an edifice and where there is a ruin of morals. But who said this to him or inspired it, except a diabolical spirit, so vain and fit for a lie: that the demons prohibited from being worshiped by the Hebrews are revered rather than hated by Christians? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshiped, and the celestial holy angels and powers of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage: he forbids sacrificing [to others], thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people, and he brought it in very threateningly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." <note>Exodus 22:20</note> And lest anyone should think that the command was not to sacrifice to the worst demons and earthly spirits, whom that man <note>Porphyry</note> calls "least" or "minor"; because in the holy scriptures they themselves are called gods, not of the Hebrews

but of the gentiles; which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note> evidently placed in the psalm, saying: "Because all the gods of the gentiles are demons." <note>Psalm 96:5 (LXX 95:5)</note> Therefore, lest anyone should think it was prohibited to sacrifice to these demons indeed, but permitted to sacrifice to all or some celestial ones, he immediately added: "except to the Lord alone" <note>original: "nisi domino soli"</note>; that is, except to the Lord only; lest perhaps by saying "to the Lord alone," someone might believe he is only a God to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in his law and his prophets? "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out," he says, "except to the Lord only." Not because he lacks anything, but because it is expedient for us that we be his possession. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, you are my God, because you do not need my goods." <note>Psalm 16:2 (LXX 15:2)</note> Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice.
