For the Hebrew prophets sounded the oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun even to its setting, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine quotes Porphyry's own admission of the Hebrew God's supremacy to argue that sacrifice must be offered to Him alone. He contrasts the purity of Christian worship with the base rituals of pagan gods and identifies the true sacrifice as the City of God itself.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Hebrews, Sacrifice, Exodus 22, Psalm 96, Monotheism, Demons, Septuagint, City of God, Ritual purity</keywords>

XIX

<note>This text continues from the previous discussion on pagan philosophy and religious practices, contrasting them with the divine law revealed to the Hebrew people.</note>

...God, and to worship Him everywhere. Truly, the unlearned, and nature itself, did not advance in obtaining gifts from the Lord, nor in having the knowledge of immortal Jove. They did not listen to both the gods and the divine men. They indeed rejected all the gods, but they chose not only not to hate the demons who were forbidden, but even to revere them. Yet, while pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things alone through which God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, needs nothing. However, it is good for us when we adore Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very lives a path toward Him by imitation and instruction from Him. For instruction purges the mind, while imitation deifies the affection by working towards Him. He indeed preached well about God the Father, and said with what habits He should be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the lives of the saints are praised or blamed. But this was only among the Christians, or they are slandered as much as the demons—whom they suppose to be gods—desire. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were done in the theaters and temples in the service of the gods, and to pay attention to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to God, and from this to understand where there is the building up of morals and where there is ruin. But who said this to him or inspired it, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and fitting lie, that Christians should revere rather than hate the demons who were forbidden to be worshipped by the Hebrews? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and whom we, in this our mortal pilgrimage, venerate and love—along with the celestial holy angels and the virtues of God, whom we consider most blessed as fellow citizens—forbids sacrificing in His law which He gave to His people, the Hebrews. And He threatened very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." And lest anyone should think that it was commanded not to sacrifice to the worst demons and earthly spirits—whom he calls mimes or lesser ones—because they themselves were called gods in the Holy Scriptures, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations, the seventy interpreters clearly set this forth in the psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Lest, therefore, anyone should think that it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to celestial beings, whether to all or to some, He immediately added: "unless to the Lord alone," that is, unless to the Lord only. Lest perhaps someone, because He said "to the Lord alone," might believe that God is the only one to whom one thinks one must sacrifice. That this is not to be understood in this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this philosopher gives such great testimony, gave the law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but already made famous to all nations. In which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord alone." What need is there in this His law and His prophets to seek out many things about this matter? Indeed, do not seek them out. For they are not hidden or sparse, but open and frequent; one may gather them and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished that sacrifice be offered to no one at all except to Himself alone. Behold, this one thing, briefly—or rather, weightily—threatened, but truthfully spoken by that God whom their own most learned men preach: let it be heard, feared, and fulfilled, lest destruction overtake the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," He says, "shall be rooted out, unless to the Lord alone." Not that He is in need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be His. For to Him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my good things." But the most excellent and best sacrifice of this One is we ourselves. This is His city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have argued in the preceding books. For the prophets of the Hebrews interpreted the oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of things to come would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one sacrifice, as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine clarifies that the Hebrew law explicitly forbids sacrifice to any being other than the one true God, refuting pagan interpretations that equate Hebrew worship with the veneration of demons.</summary>
<keywords>De Civitate Dei, sacrifice, Hebrew law, one true God, demons, moral instruction, St. Augustine</keywords>

[context] Menstruation is promoted by using hare's gall,
in unwashed wool, as a pessary: Olympias of Thebe adds hyssop and nitre. Ashes, too, of deer's horns are taken in drink for the same purpose, and for derangements of the uterus they are applied topically, as also bull's gall, used as a pessary with opium, in the proportion of two oboli. It is a good plan, too, to use fumigations for the uterus, made with deer's hair, burnt. Hinds, they say, when they find themselves pregnant, are in the habit of swallowing a small stone. This stone, when found in their excrements, or in the uterus—for it is to be found there as well—attached to the body as an amulet, is a preventive of abortion. There are also certain small stones, found in the heart and uterus of these animals, which are very useful for women during pregnancy and in travail. As to the kind of pumice-stone which is similarly found in the uterus of the cow, we have already mentioned it when treating of the formation of that animal. A wolf's fat, applied externally, acts emolliently upon the uterus, and the liver of a wolf is very soothing for pains in that organ. It is found advantageous for women, when near delivery, to eat wolf's flesh, or, if they are in travail, to have a person near them who has eaten it; so much so, indeed, that it will act as a countercharm even to any noxious spells which may have been laid upon them. In case, however, a person who has eaten wolf's flesh should happen to enter the room at the moment of parturition, dangerous effects will be sure to follow. The hare, too, is remarkably useful for the complaints of females: the lights of that animal, dried and taken in drink, are beneficial to the uterus; the liver, taken in water with Samian earth, acts as an emmenagogue; and the rennet brings away the after-birth, due care being taken by the patient not to bathe the day before. Applied in wool as a pessary, with saffron and leek-juice, this last acts as an expellent upon the dead fœtus. It is a general opinion that the uterus of a hare, taken with the food, promotes the conception of male offspring, and that a similar effect is produced by using the testes and rennet of that animal. It is thought, too, that a leveret, taken from the uterus of its dam, is a restorative of fruitfulness to women who are otherwise past child-bearing. But it is the blood of a hare's fœtus that the magicians recommend males to drink: while for young girls they prescribe nine pellets of hare's dung, to ensure a durable firmness to the breasts. For a similar purpose, also, they apply hare's rennet with honey; and to prevent hairs from growing again when once removed, they use a liniment of hare's blood. For inflations of the uterus, it is found a good plan to apply wild boars' dung or swine's dung topically with oil: but a still more effectual remedy is to dry the dung, and sprinkle it, powdered, in the patient's drink, even though she should be in a state of pregnancy or suffering the pains of child-birth. By administering sow's milk with honied wine, parturition is facilitated; and if taken by itself it will promote the secretion of the milk when deficient in nursing women. By rubbing the breasts of females with sow's blood they are prevented from becoming too large. If pains are felt in the breasts, they will be alleviated by drinking asses' milk; and the same milk, taken with honey, has considerable efficacy as an emmenagogue. Stale fat, too, from the same animal, heals ulcerations of the uterus: applied as a pessary, in wool, it acts emolliently upon indurations of that organ; and, applied fresh by itself, or in water when stale, it has all the virtues of a depilatory. An ass's milt, dried and applied in water to the breasts, promotes the secretion of the milk; and used in the form of a fumigation, it acts as a corrective upon the uterus. A fumigation made with a burnt ass's hoof; placed beneath a woman, accelerates parturition, so much so, indeed, as to expel the dead fœtus even: hence it is that it should only be employed in cases of miscarriage, it having a fatal effect upon the living fœtus. Asses' dung, applied fresh, has a wonderful effect, they say, in arresting discharges of blood in females: the same, too, with the ashes of this dung, which, used as a pessary, are very good for the uterus. If the skin is rubbed with the foam from a horse's mouth for forty days together, before the first hair has made its appearance, it will effectually prevent the growth thereof: a decoction, too, made from deer's antlers is productive of a similar effect, being all the better if they are used quite fresh. Mares' milk, used as an injection, is highly beneficial to the uterus. Where the fœtus is felt to be dead in the uterus, the lichens or excrescences from a horse's legs, taken in fresh water, will act as an expellent: an effect produced also by a fumigation made with the hoofs or dry dung of that animal. Procidence of the uterus is arrested by using butter, in the form of an injection; and indurations of that organ are removed by similarly employing ox-gall, with oil of roses, turpentine being applied externally in wool. They say, too, that a fumigation, made from ox-dung, acts as a corrective upon procidence of the uterus, and facilitates parturition; and that conception is promoted by the use of cows' milk. It is a well-known fact that sterility is often entailed by suffering in child-birth; an evil which may be averted, Olympias of Thebes assures us, by rubbing the parts, before sexual intercourse, with bull's gall, serpents' fat, verdigrease, and honey. In cases, too, where menstruation is too abundant, the external parts should be sprinkled with a solution of calf's gall, the moment before the sexual congress; a method which acts emolliently also upon indurations of the abdomen. Applied to the navel as a liniment, it arrests excessive discharges, and is generally beneficial to the uterus. The proportions generally adopted are—one denarius of gall, one-third of a denarius of opium, and as much oil of almonds as may appear to be requisite; the whole being applied in sheep's wool. The gall, too, of a bull-calf is beaten up with half the quantity of honey, and kept in readiness for the treatment of uterine diseases. If a woman about the time of conception eats roasted veal with the plant aristolochia, she will bring forth a male child, we are assured. Calf's marrow, boiled in wine and water with the suet, and applied as a pessary, is good for ulcerations of the uterus; the same, too, with foxes' fat and cats' dung, the last being applied with resin and oil of roses. It is considered a remarkably good plan to subject the uterus to fumigations made with burnt goats' horns. The blood of the wild goat, mixed with sea-palm, acts as a depilatory. The gall of the other kinds of goat, used as an injection, acts emolliently upon callosities of the uterus, and ensures conception immediately after menstruation: it possesses also the virtues of a depilatory, the application being left for three days upon the flesh after the hair has been removed. The midwives assure us that she-goats' urine, taken in drink, and the dung, applied topically, will arrest uterine discharges, however much in excess. The membrane in which the kid is enclosed in the uterus, dried and taken in wine, acts as an expellent upon the after-birth. For affections of the uterus, it is thought a desirable plan to fumigate it with burnt kids' hair; and for discharges of blood, kids' rennet is administered in drink, or seed of henbane is applied. According to Osthanes, if a woman's loins are rubbed with blood taken from the ticks upon a black wild bull, she will be inspired with an aversion to sexual intercourse: she will forget, too, her former love, by taking a he-goat's urine in drink, some nard being mixed with it to disguise the loathsome taste.

For infants there is nothing more useful than butter, either by itself or in combination with honey; for dentition more particularly, for soreness of the gums, and for ulcerations of the mouth. A wolf's tooth, attached to the body, prevents infants from being startled, and acts as a preservative against the maladies attendant upon dentition; an effect equally produced by making use of a wolf's skin. The larger teeth, also, of a wolf, attached to a horse's neck, will render him proof against all weariness, it is said. A hare's rennet, applied to the breasts of the nurse, effectually prevents diarrhœa in the infant suckled by her. An ass's liver, mixed with a little panax, and dropped into the mouth of an infant, will preserve it from epilepsy and other diseases to which infants are liable; this, however, must be done for forty days, they say. An ass's skin, too, thrown over infants, renders them insensible to fear. The first teeth shed by a horse, attached as an amulet to infants, facilitate dentition, and are better still, when not allowed to touch the ground. For pains in the spleen, an ox's milt is administered in honey, and applied topically; and for running ulcers it is used as an application, with honey. A calf's milt, boiled in wine, is beaten up, and applied to incipient ulcers of the mouth. The magicians take the brains of a she-goat, and, after passing them through a gold ring, drop them into the mouth of the infant before it takes the breast, as a preservative against epilepsy and other infantile diseases. Goats' dung, attached to infants in a piece of cloth, prevents them from being restless, female infants in particular. By rubbing the gums of infants with goats' milk or hare's brains, dentition is greatly facilitated.

Cato was of opinion that hare's flesh, taken as a diet, is provocative of sleep. It is a vulgar notion, too, that this diet confers beauty for nine days on those who use it; a silly play upon words, no doubt, but a notion which has gained far too extensively not to have had some real foundation. According to the magicians, the gall of a she-goat, but only of one that has been sacrificed, applied to the eyes or placed beneath the pillow, has a narcotic effect. Too profuse perspiration is checked by rubbing the body with ashes of burnt goats' horns mixed with oil of myrtle.

Among the aphrodisiacs, we find mentioned, a wild boar's gall, applied externally; swine's marrow, taken inwardly; asses' fat, mixed with the grease of a gander and applied as a liniment; the virulent substance described by Virgil as distilling from mares when covered;
[context] and the dried testes of a horse, pulverized and mixed with the drink.

It is also useful for one suffering from uterine trouble. It is also applied as a salve, and bull bile mixed with two <term>oboli</term> <gloss>small weights</gloss> of opium is applied. It is also useful to fumigate the womb with stag hair. They report that when hinds sense they are pregnant, they swallow a small stone, which is found in their excrement or in the womb (for it is also found there), and is kept by the pregnant woman as an amulet. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb that are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. Regarding the pumice stone found in the same way in the uterus of cows, we have spoken of this in the nature of cattle. Wolf fat applied softens the womb. It can even be effective against harmful applications to alleviate their pains. And it is not useless. Or, if she is beginning to labor, let her stay near what she has eaten. So much so that it can even be effective against harmful applications. And it is truly a small thing to mention that it supervenes. There is great use of the hare for women. Dried lung, drunk, helps the womb. For fluxes, the liver with Samian earth in water, drunk. For the afterbirth, rennet. They avoid bathing on the previous day. Also, a salve made with saffron and leek juice, applied on a fleece, expels dead fetuses. If hare wombs are taken in food, they think male children are conceived. They believe this is also accomplished by their testicles and rennet. They believe that a hare's uterus, removed and given to those who have ceased to bear children, brings back fertility. Furthermore, the <term>magi</term> <gloss>Persian wise men</gloss> suggest a hare's conception for a man to drink. Likewise, nine grains of dung for a virgin, so that her breasts remain firm forever. Also with rennet. For this reason, smeared with honey, it is used on blood where they do not want hair to grow back after it has been plucked. For swelling of the womb, boar or swine dung mixed with oil is useful to apply. It is more effective if flour of dry dung is spread on it or added to a drink, in case it torments pregnant women or those who have just given birth. Drunk with honeyed wine, sow's milk aids the labor of women. Drunk by itself, it fills the failing breasts of those who have just given birth. The same, smeared with the blood of a female sow, makes the breasts grow less. If they are painful, soothe them with a drink of donkey milk. Taken with added honey, it also aids their purging. The old fat of the same animal also heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied on a fleece, it softens the hardness of the womb. Used by itself, whether fresh or old, applied in water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss>. The old spleen of the same animal, applied in water, increases the supply of milk in breasts. It stiffens the face. Donkey hooves burned as incense hasten labor, so that it may even induce an abortion; it is not used otherwise, for it kills the living fetus. If the dung of the same animal is applied while fresh, it is said to sedate fluxes of blood miraculously. And also the ash of the same dung, which, applied, is also useful for the womb. Horse foam, applied for forty days, causes the first hairs to stop growing before they are born. Likewise, stag horn, as taught. The horns are better if they are fresh. Wombs washed with mare's milk are aided. If one senses the fetus is dead, spleen drunk in sweet water expels it. Likewise, burning the hooves or using dry dung. It stops the face from drooping if infused with butter. Bull bile mixed with rose oil opens a hardened womb, applied externally on a fleece with turpentine resin. They also say that by burning the dung of a bull, drooping wombs are drawn back and labor is aided. Conception [is aided] by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility occurs due to the trauma of labor. The bile of others, however, softens the callus of the womb when sprinkled, and makes conception possible after purging. The power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss> is also brought about in this way: after the hairs are plucked, it is kept applied for three days. Midwives promise that a flux, however immense, is stopped by drinking goat urine, and if dung is applied. The membrane of goats, boiled in water and taken as a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. Regarding the pumice-like stone found in the wombs of cows in a similar way, we have spoken of it in the nature of cattle.

Wolf fat applied softens the womb. It is also effective against pains in those parts. It is beneficial if someone who has eaten it is near a woman beginning labor. Indeed, its mere arrival can be harmful <note>implying it might induce labor too quickly</note>. The use of the hare is also of great benefit to women. A dried lung, taken in drink, aids the womb. Its liver taken in water with <term>Samian earth</term> <gloss>a medicinal clay from Samos</gloss> stops discharges. Its rennet helps with the afterbirth, though they avoid bathing the day before. Applied with saffron and leek juice on a fleece, it expels a dead fetus. If the wombs of hares are taken in food, it is believed they conceive males; this is also achieved with their testicles and rennet. 

A fetus taken from a hare's womb is said to bring restored fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. Furthermore, a healthy hare is good for conception, and they give it to the man to drink more often. Also, nine grains of its dung given to a virgin keep the breasts firm forever. For inflation of the womb, it is beneficial to apply the dung of a wild boar or a sow with oil. If smeared with the blood of a female pig, the breasts grow less. If they are painful, they are soothed by drinking donkey's milk, which, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The aged fat of the same animal heals ulcerations of the womb, and when applied on a fleece, it softens hardness of the womb. Used by itself, fresh or aged and applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>a hair-removing paste</gloss>. The aged spleen of the same animal applied with water causes an abundance in the breasts. 

It beautifies the face. A fumigation with a donkey's hoof matures the fetus so as to even call forth an abortion; it should not be used otherwise, for it kills a living fetus. If the fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to wonderfully settle discharges of blood. Likewise, the ash of the same dung applied is beneficial to the womb. 

Horse foam applied for forty days before they are born suppresses the first hairs. Likewise, deer horn does this. It is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is aided by being washed with mare's milk. If a dead fetus is felt, the spleen drunk in sweet water ejects it. Likewise, a fumigation of the hoof or dried dung. Butter infused stops a prolapsed womb. Bull bile mixed with oil of roses opens a hardened womb when applied externally on a fleece with turpentine resin. They also say that a fumigation of dung from a male ox represses a prolapsed womb and aids the fetus. 

Conception is aided by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility can be caused by the trauma of childbirth. Olympias of Thebes affirms this is corrected by bull bile and snake fat with verdigris and added honey, applied to the medicinal areas before intercourse. Calf bile, if used during purgations and sprinkled on the womb during intercourse, softens hardness of the belly, reduces discharge if the navel is pricked, and is generally beneficial to the womb. If they eat roasted calf meat with <term>aristolochia</term> <gloss>birthwort</gloss> around the time of conception, it is promised they will bear males. Midwives promise that a discharge, however immense, is stopped by drinking goat urine, or if dung is applied. The membrane of goats, aged after the birth is produced and taken in wine, expels the afterbirth. 

They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. In a discharge of blood, the rennet is drunk or applied with henbane seed. Aeschines says that if a woman's loins are pricked with the blood of a black wild ox, she will develop a loathing for sexual intercourse. Similarly, he says goat urine drunk with nard causes love. 

Nothing is more useful for infants than butter, by itself or with honey; specifically for teething, the gums, and mouth ulcers. A wolf's tooth tied on prevents the fears of infants and diseases of teething. A wolf skin provides the same. Indeed, their largest teeth tied to horses are said to provide an untiring course. An infant's bowels are settled by hare's rennet applied to the breast. Donkey liver with a little <term>panace</term> <gloss>all-heal herb</gloss> dripped into the mouth protects infants from the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and other ills. They prescribe this for forty days. A donkey skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that horses lose first, when tied on, provide easy teething for infants, more effectively if they have not touched the ground. 

Calf spleen is eaten in honey or applied for pain of the spleen. For running ulcers, it is used with honey. Calf spleen boiled in wine, ground, and applied, heals sores of the mouth. A goat's brain passed through a gold ring and dripped into the mouths of infants before they taste milk protects against the falling sickness and other infant diseases. Goat dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat milk or hare brain make teething easy. 

Cato thinks that sleep is induced by taking hare in food. The common people also believe it brings grace to the body for nine days—a trivial saying, yet there must be some reason beneath such widespread persuasion. The Magi say that the bile of a sacrificed goat, if smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow, induces sleep. The ash of a goat horn with myrtle oil inhibits sweats when smeared on. Sexual intercourse is stimulated by applying boar bile. Likewise, swallowing pig marrow. Donkey fat mixed with the fat of a male goose, or even the [semen] from a horse's mating, as Virgil...

[margin] Solutions of the Arguments.
For the first, it is clear that there is no doubt but that, just as, with God's permission, they can kill men, so also can devils taken off that member, as well as others, truly and actually. But then the devils do not work through the medium of witches, concerning which mention has already been made. And from this the answer to the second argument is also made clear. But this is to be said: that God allows more power of witchcraft over the genital forces because, etc.; and therefore even allows that that member should be truly and actually taken off. But it is not valid to say that this always happens. For it would not be after the manner of witchcraft for it to happen so; and even the witches, when they do such works, do not pretend that they have not the power to restore the member when they wish to and know how to do so. From which it is clear that it is not actually taken off, but only by a glamour. As for the third, concerning the metamorphosis of Lot's wife, we say that this was actual, and not a glamour. And as to the fourth, that devils can create certain substantial shapes, and therefore can also remove them: it is to be said with regard to Pharaoh's magicians that they made true serpents; and that devils can, with the help of another agent, produce certain effects on imperfect creatures which they cannot on men, who are God's chief care. For it is said: Does God care for oxen? They can, nevertheless, with the permission of God, do to men true and actual harm, as also they can create a glamour of harm, and by this the answer to the last argument is made clear.

[margin] PART I. QUESTION X. Whether Witches can by some Glamour Change Men into Beasts.
Here we declare the truth as to whether and how witches transform men into beasts. And it is argued that this is not possible, from the following passage of Episcopus (XXVI, 5): Whoever believes that it is possible for any creature to be changed for the better or for the worse, or to be transformed into any other shape or likeness, except by the Creator Himself, Who made all things, is without doubt an infidel, and worse than a pagan.

And we will quote the arguments of S. Thomas in the 2nd Book of Sentences, VIII: Whether devils can affect the bodily sense by the delusion of a glamour. There he argues first that they cannot. For though that shape of a beast which is seen must be somewhere, it cannot exist only in the senses; for the sense perceive no shape that is not received from actual matter, and there is no actual beast there; and he adduces the authority of the Canon. And again, that which seems to be, cannot really be; as in the case of a woman who seems to be a beast, for two substantial shapes cannot exist at one and the same time in the same matter. Therefore, since that shape of a beast which appears cannot exist anywhere, no glamour or illusion can exist in the eye of the beholder; for the sight must have some object in which it terminates.

And if it is argued that the shape exists in the surrounding atmosphere, this is not possible; both because the atmosphere is not capable of taking any shape or form, and also because the air around that person is not always constant, and cannot be so on account of its fluid nature, especially when it is moved. And again because in that case such a transformation would be visible to everyone; but this is not so, because the devils seem to be unable to deceive the sight of Holy Men in the least.

Besides, the sense of sight, or the faculty of vision, is a passive faculty, and every passive faculty is set in motion by the active agent that corresponds to it. Now the active agent corresponding to sight is twofold: one is the origin of the act, or the object; the other is the carrier, or medium. But that apparent shape cannot be the object of the sense, neither can it be the medium through which it is carried. First, it cannot be the object, since it cannot be taken hold of by anything, as was shown in the foregoing argument, since it does not exist in the senses received from an object, neither is it in the actual object, nor even in the air, as in a carrying medium, as was treated of above in the third argument.

Besides, if the devil moves the inner consciousness, he does so either by projecting himself
[context] into the cognitive faculty, or by changing it.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the illusions of witches, specifically resolving previous arguments about the physical reality of "missing" limbs before moving into a new question regarding the transformation of humans into animals.</meta>

<margin>
# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill other humans when God permits it, they can also truly and physically remove a limb or other body parts. However, in those cases, **demons** are not operating through the **witches** <note>original: "maleficas"</note> currently under discussion. This also provides the solution to the second point. But as for the claim that because God permits the **generative power** <term>vim generativam: the biological ability to procreate</term> of witches more than other powers, He therefore permits that a limb be truly and physically removed—this is not a valid rule for every case. Such an act would not be performed by way of **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficii"</note>, nor do witches even desire this when they perform their works, because they want to retain the power to restore the limb whenever they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that the limb is not truly removed, but is taken away through the **art of illusion** <term>prestigiosa arte: the demonic skill of creating deceptive appearances</term>.

Regarding the third point about the transformation of **Lot's wife** <note>The biblical story from Genesis 19 where Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt</note>, we say that this was a real transformation and not done through the art of illusion; however, we are currently speaking of the deceptive arts. To the fourth point—that demons can introduce certain **substantial forms** <term>substantial forms: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "human-ness" or "snake-ness")</term> and therefore can also remove them—it is said regarding the **magicians of Pharaoh** <note>In Exodus 7, these magicians mimicked Moses's miracles</note> that they produced real serpents. Indeed, demons can produce certain effects regarding some "imperfect" creatures with the help of some other agent; however, they cannot do this to humans, for whom God has greater care. According to the scripture: *Is it for oxen that God is concerned?* <note>original: "Nunquid deo cura est de bobus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note> Nevertheless, as has been stated, they can always harm humans truly and physically, or through the art of illusion, if God permits it. This also makes the solution to the final argument clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into bestial forms through the art of illusion.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared regarding where humans are transformed into beasts. As to how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. In the **Canon Law** <note>original: "xxvi. q. v. Epi." referring to the Canon Episcopi, a famous 10th-century legal text on witchcraft</note> from the Council of Ancyra: "Whosoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is beyond doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan."

<column-break/>

Let us also use the arguments of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian</note> in the *Second Book of Sentences*, distinction 8, on whether demons can make impressions upon the **bodily senses** by deluding them with illusions. There, he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere. But it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not possess any **sensory image** <term>speciem: a mental representation of an object</term> unless it is received from real things. Furthermore, according to the legal authority cited above, there is no real beast there. Nor, again, can the form be in the thing that is seen (as when a woman appears to be a beast), because two **substantial forms** cannot exist in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that beastly form which is seen can exist nowhere, no **illusion of prestige** <term>illusio prestigiosa: a deceptive trick or hallucination</term> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that the form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be. Firstly, because the air is not capable of receiving a specific form or shape. Secondly, because the same air does not always remain around that person due to its fluid nature, especially when they are moving. Thirdly, because such a transformation would then be seen by everyone—which is not the case, since demons do not seem to deceive the visions of holy men, at the very least.

Furthermore, the sense of sight or the power of vision is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. Now, the active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one that originates the act (namely, the **object**), and another that conveys it (namely, the **medium**). But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor can it be the medium conveying it. Regarding the first—that it cannot be the object—this is because it cannot be derived from any real thing (as touched upon in the preceding argument), since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a real thing, nor is it in the object itself, nor even in the air as a conveying medium (as touched upon in the third argument). Furthermore, if the demon moves the internal **cognitive power**, he either does this by presenting himself as an object...

<margin># Solutions to the arguments.</margin>

The first point is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill by divine permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member <note>referring to the phallus, a frequent subject in the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now being made. Through this, the solution to the second point is also clear. But as for the argument that because God permits the generative power to be bewitched more [often] for the sake of something, therefore it is also permitted that such a member be truly and really removed, this does not hold because this does not happen by way of witchcraft, nor do witches even desire this when they perform such acts, since they do not have the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From which it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by the art of illusion. 

Regarding the third point, concerning the wife of Lot, we say: it was true and not by the art of illusion, but we are now speaking of the art of illusion. 

Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, concerning the magicians of Pharaoh, that they created true serpents. Demons can indeed produce certain effects around imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do around human beings, for whom God has greater care. According to that saying: "Is God concerned about oxen?" <note>1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. They can, however, always—as has been said—harm human beings truly and really by divine permission, or even by the art of illusion, and through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

However, certain superstitious individuals and children of this age, wishing to accumulate errors upon errors beyond the intellect and intention of <note>John</note> Duns Scotus and the canonists, attempt to defend themselves with these arguments: because natural things also possess certain occult virtues whose rationale cannot be assigned by man, such as the magnet attracting iron, and many other things which Augustine enumerates in book 21 of <note>The City of God</note> De civitate dei. Therefore, they argue, methods for obtaining health in matters where exorcisms and natural medicines fail should be permitted; it would not be illicit if one were to seek to procure health for oneself or another through images—not those involving necromancy or astrology, nor rings and the like—if it seems vain to do otherwise. 

They also argue: just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so too do artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain occult virtues resulting from the influence of celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also acquire some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects; consequently, to use them and others of this kind is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can multiply and transmute bodies, as Augustine says in book 3 of On the Trinity <note>De trinitate</note>, and this is evident in the bewitched. Therefore, it is licit to use even their power to remove those <note>afflictions</note>.

But in truth, the words of all holy doctors are to the contrary, as has been shown in various places. Hence, to the first point, it is said that if natural things are used simply to produce effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. If, however, they add any characters, or other unknown and vain observations which manifestly do not have a natural efficacy, this will be superstitious and illicit, as Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> treats at the end of question 96, article 2, in the second part of the second part of his work <note>Summa Theologica</note>.

<summary>This text addresses the theological debate regarding the legitimacy of using charms, images, and occult natural forces to achieve healing, ultimately concluding that such practices are superstitious and illicit if they rely on non-natural observations.</summary>

[context] After him came one who, in an unholy cause, made an even more shameful use of victory; for he did not stop at confiscating the property of individual citizens, but
actually embraced whole provinces and countries in one common ban of ruin.

28 And so, when foreign nations had been oppressed and ruined, we have seen a model of Marseilles carried in a triumphal procession, to serve as proof to the world that the supremacy of the people had been forfeited; and that triumph we saw celebrated over a city without whose help our generals have never gained a triumph for their wars beyond the Alps. I might mention many other outrages against our allies, if the sun had ever beheld anything more infamous than this particular one. Justly, therefore, are we being punished. For if we had not allowed the crimes of many to go unpunished, so great licence would never have centred in one individual. His estate descended by inheritance to but a few individuals, his ambitions to many scoundrels. 29 And never will the seed and occasion of civil war be wanting, so long as villains remember that bloodstained spear and hope to see another. As Publius Sulla wielded that spear, when his kinsman was dictator, so again thirty-six years later he did not shrink from a still more criminal spear. And still another Sulla, who was a mere clerk under the former dictatorship, was under the later one a city quaestor. From this, one would realize that, if such rewards are offered, civil wars will never cease to be.

And so in Rome only the walls of her houses remain standing — and even they wait now in fear of the most unspeakable crimes — but our republic we have lost for ever. But to return to my subject: it is while we have preferred to be the object of fear rather than of love and affection, that all these misfortunes have fallen upon us. And if such retribution could overtake the Roman People for their injustice and tyranny, what ought private individuals to expect? And since it is manifest that the power of good-will is so great and that of fear is so weak, it remains for us to discuss by what means we can most readily win the affection, linked with honour and confidence, which we desire.

30 But we do not all feel this need to the same extent;
[context] for it must be determined in conformity with each individual's vocation in life whether it is essential for him to have the affection of many or whether the love of a few will suffice.

[context] For this, indeed, is the cause why knowledge is free from falsehood, because of necessity each thing must correspond exactly with the knowledge which grasps its nature.
In what way, then, are we to suppose that God foreknows these uncertainties as about to come to pass? For if He thinks of events which possibly may not happen at all as inevitably destined to come to pass, He is deceived; and this it is not only impious to believe, but even so much as to express in words. If, on the other hand, He sees them in the future as they are in such a sense as to know that they may equally come to pass or not, what sort of foreknowledge is this which comprehends nothing certain nor fixed? What better is this than the absurd vaticination of Teiresias?


'"Whate'er I say / Shall either come to pass--or not."

In that case, too, in what would Divine providence surpass human opinion if it holds for uncertain things the occurrence of which is uncertain, even as men do? But if at that perfectly sure Fountain-head of all things no shadow of uncertainty
[context] can possibly be found, then the occurrence of those things which He has surely foreknown as coming is certain.

For if He thinks that those things are avoidable whose occurrence is not possible, He is deceived, which it is a sin even to imagine, let alone state. [context] The ends of the shaft are covered with iron. To the right and left of the screw are beams, with crosspieces fastening them together at both ends. In these crosspieces are holes sheathed with iron, and into them
pivots are introduced, and thus the screw is turned by the treading of men.

It is to be set up at an inclination corresponding to that which is produced in drawing the Pythagorean right-angled triangle: that is, let its length be divided into five parts; let three of them denote the height of the head of the screw; thus the distance from the base of the perpendicular to the nozzle of the screw at the bottom will be equal to four of those parts. A figure showing how this ought to be, has been drawn at the end of the book, right on the back.

I have now described as clearly as I could, to make them better known, the principles on which wooden engines for raising water are constructed, and how they get their motion so that they may be of unlimited usefulness through their revolutions.

[context] 3. “I,” saith the Lord, “taught the prophets from the beginning, and even now cease I not to speak unto all;
but many are deaf and hardened against My voice; many love to listen to the world rather than to God, they follow after the desires of the flesh more readily than after the good pleasure of God. The world promiseth things that are temporal and small, and it is served with great eagerness. I promise things that are great and eternal, and the hearts of mortals are slow to stir. Who serveth and obeyeth Me in all things, with such carefulness as he serveth the world and its rulers?

[margin] Isaiah xxiii. 4.
Be thou ashamed, O Sidon, saith the sea;
And if thou reason seekest, hear thou me.

For a little reward men make a long journey; for eternal life many will scarce lift a foot once from the ground. Mean reward is sought after; for a single piece of money sometimes there is shameful striving; for a thing which is vain and for a trifling promise, men shrink not from toiling day and night.”

4. “But, O shame! for an unchangeable good, for an inestimable reward, for the highest honour and for a glory that fadeth not away, it is irksome to them to toil even a little. Be thou ashamed therefore, slothful and discontented servant, for they are found readier unto perdition than thou unto life. They rejoice more heartily in vanity than thou in the truth. Sometimes, indeed, they are disappointed of their hope, but my promise faileth no man, nor sendeth away empty him who trusteth in Me. What I have promised I will give; what I have said I will fulfil; if only a man remain faithful in My love unto the end. Therefore am I the rewarder of all good men, and a strong approver of all who are godly.

5. “Write My words in thy heart and consider them diligently, for they shall be very needful to thee in time of temptation. What thou understandest not when thou readest, thou shalt know in the time of thy visitation. I am wont to visit Mine elect in twofold manner, even by temptation and by comfort, and I teach them two lessons day by day, the one in chiding their faults, the other in exhorting them to grow in grace. He who hath My words and rejecteth them, hath one who shall judge him at the last day.”

[context] The appearance of slowness in their motion is caused by their encountering the sun, as well as by
the character of their paths and the position of their orbits, which are at certain periods calculated to deceive the eye. Ships in the same way moving under full sail seem withal to be stationary. Men will some day be able to demonstrate in what regions comets have their paths, why their course is so far removed from the other stars, what is their size and constitution. Let us be satisfied with what we have discovered, and leave a little truth for our descendants to find out.

We cannot, Apollonius says, see through the stars what is beyond, but sight passes easily through the comets. Well, in the first place, if that is the case, it is not so in the part of the body which consists of dense solid fire, but only where the dispersed glow extends as it breaks up into the appearance of hair. One can see through the gaps in the fire and not through the fire itself. Stars again, it is said, are all round, comets extended; whence it is plain that they are not true stars. But who, pray, will allow that comets are long? Their tendency like that of other stars is to a globe shape, only the light from them is prolonged. The sun shoots out his rays far and wide, but has himself a shape different from that of the light that streams from him. So in comets, the body is rounded, but the glow from them presents the appearance of being longer than that of the other stars.

WHY is this so, you ask. Do you tell me first why the light the moon receives is wholly unlike the sun although she receives it from the sun. Why is it now ruddy, now pale? why is her colour ashen or black when she is cut off from the sun's view? Or tell me why all the stars have aspects to some extent dissimilar to one another and all as different as possible from the sun. It is no hindrance to their being true stars that they are not all alike; so there is nothing to prevent comets from being permanent through all time, sharing the same destiny as the other stars, even though they have not an appearance like theirs. Besides, is not the universe, if you will only examine it carefully, made up of contrarieties? Why is it that the sun should be always blazing hot in Leo, scorching the ground with his fierce glow, while in Aquarius he brings winter's chain and closes the rivers with ice? The one constellation is subject to the same law as the other, though its characteristics and influence are so different. Aries again rises in a moment, Libra lifts its scales very slowly; yet the one sign is of the same nature as the other, though that one mounts in a brief space, this comes forth very deliberately. Do you not see, too, how contrary the elements are to one another? They are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The whole concord of the universe is a harmony of discords. You say a comet is not a star, because its form does not correspond to the type,
[context] but is unlike other stars.

uiarum circulorumque sic positorum, ut certo tempore intuētes afflent. Sic naues quuis plenis uelis eant, uidentur tamē stare. Erit qui demonstret aliquādo, in quibus Cometæ partibus errent. Cum tam seducti a cæteris eant, quanti qualesque sint. Contenti sumus inuentis, aliquid ueritati & posteri conferant. Per stellas, inquit, ulteriora non cernimus, p Cometas aciem transmittimus. Primū si fit istud, non in ea parte fit, qua sydus ipsum spissi ac solidi ignis, sed qua rarus splēdor excurrit, & in crines dispergit. Per interualla ignium, nō per ipsos uides. Stellæ, inquit, omnes rotundæ sunt, Cometæ porrecti, ex quo apparet stellas non esse. Quis em̃ tibi concedet Cometas longos esse, quorum natura quidem ut cæterorū globus est? Cæterum fulgor extenditur quemadmodū sol radios suos longe lateque dimittit. Cæterum ipsi alia est forma, alia ei qui ex ipso fluit lumini. Sic Cometarum corpus ipsum corrotundat̃. Splendor autē longior q̃ cæterorū syderū apparet. Quare inquis: Dic tu mihi prius, quare luna dissimillimū soli lumen accipiat, cū accipiat a sole? Quare modo rubeat, modo palleat? Quare liuidus illi & ater color sit, cū a cōspectu solis excluditur? Dic mihi quare omnes stellæ inter se dissimile habeant aliquatenus faciem, diuersissimā soli. Quomodo nihil prohibet ita sydera esse, quuis similia non sint, ita nihil prohibet Cometas æternos esse & sortis eiusdē, cuius cætera, etiam si faciem illis non habent similē. Quid porro mundus ipse si consyderes illum, nōne ex diuersis cōpositus est? Quid est quare in leone semper sol ardeat, & terras æstibus torreat? in aquario astringat hyemē? flumina gelu claudat? Et hoc tamen & illud sydus eiusdem cōditionis <margin>† exoritur</margin> est, cum effectu & natura dissimile sit. Intra breuissimū tempus aries † excolitur, libra tardissime mergitur, & tamen hoc sydus & illud eiusdem naturæ est, cum illud exiguo tempore ascēdat, hoc diu proferatur. Non uides q̃ contraria inter se elementa sint? grauia & leuia sunt, frigida & calida, humida & sicca. Tota huius mundi concordia ex discordia constat. Negas Cometem stellam esse, quia forma eius non respondeat ad exemplar, nec sit cæteris similis. Vides enim, simillima est illa, quæ tricesimo anno reuertitur ad locum suum, huic quæ intra annum reuisit sedem suam. Nō ad unam natura formam opus suum præstat, sed ipsa uarietate se iactat. Alia morosiora, alia uelociora alijs fecit. Alia ualidiora, alia temperatiora, quædam autem eduxit a turba, ut singula & conspicua procederent, quædam in gregem misit. Ignorat naturæ potentiam, qui illi non putat aliquando licere, nisi quod sæpius facit. Cometas non frequenter ostendit, attribuit illis alium locum, alia tempora, dissimiles cæteris motus. Voluit ex his magnitudinem operis sui colere, quorum formosior facies est, q̃ ut fortuita putes, siue amplitudinem eorum consyderes, siue fulgorem, qui maior est ardentiorsq̃ q̃ cæteris. Facies uero habet insigne quiddam & singulare, non in angustum coniecta & artata, sed dimissa liberius, & multarum stellarum amplexa regionem. Aristoteles ait Cometas significare tempestatem & uentorum intemperantiam atq̃ imbrium. Quid ergo? non iudicas sydus esse, quod futura denunciat? Non enim sic hoc tempestatis signum est, quomodo futuræ pluuiæ scintillare oleum, & putres concrescere fungos, aut quomodo indicium est sæuituri maris, si marinæ in sicco ludūt Fulicæ, notasq̃ paludes deserunt, atq̃ altam supra uolat ardea nubem. Sed sic, quomodo æquinoctium in calorem frigusq̃ flectētis anni. Quomodo illa quæ Chaldæi canunt, quid stella nascentibus triste lætumue constituat. Hoc ut scias ita esse, non statim Cometes ortus, uentos & pluuias minatur, ut Aristoteles ait, sed <margin>Cometes ortus totū annum suspectū facit.</margin> annum totum suspectum facit. Ex quo apparet illum nō ex proximo, quæ in proximum daret signa traxisse, sed habere reposita & compressa legibus mundi. Fecit is Cometes, q̃ Patruculo & Vopisco cōsulibus apparuit, quæ ab Aristotele, Theophrastoq̃ sunt prædicta. Fuerunt enim maximæ & continuæ tempestates ubiq̃. At in Achaia, Macedoniaq̃ urbes terrarum motibus proru tæ sunt. Tarditas, inquit, illorum argumentum est grauiores esse, multumq̃ in se habere terreni. Ipsi præterea cursus, fere enim compelluntur in cardines. Vtrumq̃ falsum est. De priore dicam prius, quia quæ tardius feruntur, grauia sunt. Quid ergo?
